Cascades are mentioned only in three places, and none of them has a capability row behind it: the direct-lighting-shadows purpose text, gap-analysis B4, and the radar VSM fallback ("Clustered lighting + shadow maps"). The docs/00 §9 "technique selection" deferral does not cover this gap. The B4 ADR can only choose among techniques the framework owns, and lite3d configurations (mobile, standalone XR, Switch-class) have none to choose from.

This is not the capability-profile gating that docs/00 §5 lists. That section deliberately makes VSM std3d-only but offers no lite3d replacement. So this is a real, material coverage hole for agents building lite3d targets, and it sits squarely in K-RENDER's mandate. K-COMPLETE raised the same issue independently.

The proposal is technically sound. Adding E-class rows with no profile tag, owned by the skill already present in lite3d configurations, violates no check.py rule. The C-LIGHT "one lookup API per tier" clause fits the existing summary.

Splitting the change into three rows (csm, local-shadows, filtering) is a matter of granularity; K-COMPLETE proposed a single row, and either works. The finding should also point the radar fallback at the new rows.

Major severity is right. check.py still passes because closure is proved per skill, so the defect is not blocking. It does leave an entire base profile without a standard technique that every shipped engine has.

The finding holds on the data. In skills.json, vfx-particles has provides=[] and implements=[]. contracts.json has no C-VFX, and no contract summary covers spawning, attaching, parameterizing, pooling or stopping effects. C-RSCENE covers render features, primitive kinds and deformation flags. C-TRANSLUCENT covers translucent and decal submission. C-ATMOS covers media injection. C-SCALE covers actuators. C-SIGNIF covers per-entity tiers. C-ABILITY, C-SEQ and C-ANIM describe their own outputs and never define an effect request surface. C-AUDIO is the audio counterpart the critic names (emitter data, event triggering, parameters, busses), and VFX has nothing like it. The gap is concrete: capability GAM.SYS.impacts routes "audio, VFX, decals, haptics" from gameplay-systems-toolkit to vfx-particles, but no contract carries that route. None of gameplay-systems-toolkit, cinematics-sequencer, destruction-fracture, animation-runtime, atmosphere-weather or ui-architect consumes anything VFX-owned. check.py only checks that each contract has an owner and that each lead provides a contract. vfx-particles is an expert leaf, so check.py does not flag it. One part of the finding is overstated: vfx-particles already consumes C-PHYS? and C-ENV?, so the physics and environment data sources are partly declared, and the proposal to add C-PHYS? is redundant. Only C-ANIM, the skinned-surface source, is truly missing. That inaccuracy is minor and does not undo the main deficiency. Major severity fits: a whole domain has no request interface, and at least six consumers need one.

The finding holds, and "major" is the right severity. In data/skills.json, vfx-particles has provides: []. No contract in data/contracts.json lets anyone spawn, parameterize, pool or stop effects. Several capabilities do route effects into VFX. GAM.SYS.impacts (owned by gameplay-systems-toolkit, with vfx-particles as a contributor) routes impact effects to VFX. C-PREDICT mentions suppressing cosmetic effects during resimulation. C-ABILITY is a clear consumer. None of them has an interface to go through. Audio has the equivalent contract, C-AUDIO, so the gap is plain. Autonomous agents would each invent their own spawn API or reach into VFX internals. That is a real coordination defect, not a style point. I found no recorded scope decision against a VFX contract in docs/06 section C or docs/00. The proposal is technically sound against check.py. A layer-3 C-VFX requiring C-RSCENE creates no upward link and no build-dependency cycle. vfx-particles already consumes only contracts at layer 3 or below. The layer-4 consumers (the gameplay toolkit via C-ABILITY, and C-SEQ) are fine. A mutual optional dependency between atmosphere-weather and vfx-particles would only be flagged as an informational runtime-coupling cycle, not an error. The oracle author, gameplay-systems-toolkit, is not the implementer, which meets the oracle-author rule. Two small flaws, neither of which changes the verdict. First, vfx-particles already consumes C-PHYS?, so adding it is redundant. Second, C-ANIM? is a questionable source for skinned-surface deformation streams, which come from the render side through deformation-skinning and C-RSCENE. The milestone freeze entry would also need updating when the contract is added.

I checked the finding against data/*.json and it holds.

1. C-VT is consumed only by terrain (as C-VT?) and render-2d-vector (as C-VT) in skills.json. Milestones also mention it, but that is not a consumes edge.
2. material-system consumes C-SHADER, C-ASSET, C-MLGPU?, C-GPUTIER and C-LIGHTENV?, with no C-VT. The C-VT summary itself says it serves "terrain, materials and runtime-composited textures", so the missing edge contradicts the contract's own wording.
3. C-MATIF, which material-system owns, requires only C-SHADER and says nothing about VT sampling or feedback. So the gap is not hidden behind the material interface.
4. geometry-pipeline, translucency-decals and vfx-particles do not consume C-VT.
5. texture-streaming-vt consumes only C-RES, C-GPUMEM, C-RG, C-ML? and C-MLGPU?, with no C-RSCENE, C-INSTANCES or C-VIEW. C-VIEW's "streaming-source signals for sinks" therefore never reaches it.
6. C-RES carries generic load priority and deadline but no per-instance texel density or view data. RES.MGMT.gpu-requests covers only GPU-originated feedback buffers, not CPU-computed mip priority.
7. RND.TEX.mip-streaming ("Mip streaming & priority") is owned by texture-streaming-vt, but nothing supplies the scene or view inputs that priority needs.
8. check.py only proves structural things (closure, layering, acyclicity and similar), not semantic data paths like this, so it does not already cover the gap.

I could not confirm in the data that sampler feedback is std3d-only. That point only supports the argument, and the gap stands without it. Major severity fits: materials cannot sample VT, or CPU mip priority has no inputs.

The finding is right about the layers, but the framework already covers the case, so the deficiency does not exist as described. What checks out in data/contracts.json and data/skills.json: C-RTAS is layer 2 and requires only [C-RHI, C-GPUMEM]. C-RG is layer 3. ray-tracing-infrastructure consumes C-RG only as C-RG@C-RT. spatial-audio-acoustics consumes C-RTAS?. RND.GRAPH.external-work lists "AS builds" as registered producers. What the finding misses: (1) RND.GRAPH.external-work also covers "import of externally written resources, queue-ownership transfer & first-use acquire". L28's default stance says exactly this: "Render-graph-derived barriers; external work imported with queue transfers". So a layer-2 producer submitting through C-RHI (queues, command recording, completion tokens) and having its output imported by the graph is the sanctioned pattern, not a return of global sync. The same layer-2 producer shape already applies to C-GPUMEM uploads and C-IO GPU decompression, which are also below C-RG. (2) The render-side scheduling path already exists: C-RT is layer 3, requires C-RTAS, has "update policy" in its summary, and its module consumes C-RG@C-RT. RND.RT.as ("build, refit, compaction & update scheduling") belongs to the same skill, so render AS builds can be placed as graph passes through C-RT calling C-RTAS recording APIs, the way UE RDG does it. (3) Nothing in the data forces the C-RTAS module to "record its own barriers" outside the graph. The C-RTAS summary says it is independent of the render scene, which fits a layered API that other code records against. The one leftover gap is narrow: budget and priority arbitration for C-RTAS? builds from the non-render consumer spatial-audio-acoustics. That is at most minor, not a major dependency error, and the proposed layer move would break C-RTAS being "independent of the render scene" for audio. check.py does not prove this either way; its layering proof only enforces that nothing points upward, and it passes.

I checked this against data/*.json and the facts are correct. C-VT is consumed only by terrain (C-VT?) and render-2d-vector (C-VT). material-system consumes C-SHADER, C-ASSET, C-MLGPU?, C-GPUTIER and C-LIGHTENV?, but not C-VT. geometry-pipeline, translucency-decals and vfx-particles do not consume it either. texture-streaming-vt consumes only C-RES, C-GPUMEM, C-RG, C-ML? and C-MLGPU?, so it has no view or scene input.

The gap is not filled some other way:
- C-MATIF (layer 3, requires only C-SHADER) says nothing about VT or texture residency.
- C-RES carries priority/deadline load requests, but its owner, resource-streaming-architect, does not consume C-VIEW or C-RSCENE, so nothing computes per-primitive texel or mip priority.
- The C-VT summary names 'materials' as a consumer, yet no material skill consumes it. That internal inconsistency confirms the gap.

This is a material defect. Agents building material codegen (VT sampling and sampler-feedback writes) or CPU mip-priority streaming would have no contract path and would couple directly across skill internals. It covers established capabilities (RND.TEX.mip-streaming, RND.TEX.vt) in the lite3d and std3d profiles. No scope decision in docs/06 or docs/00 excludes it; B17 only leaves the mip vs SFS vs VT choice open.

The proposal is technically sound. I applied it to a copy of the data, and check.py reports 0 errors and 0 warnings. The layering is fine: C-VT and C-RSCENE sit at layer 3, C-VIEW at layer 2, and material-system provides C-MATIF at layer 3.

One caveat: the change adds a new runtime coupling cycle (material-system -> texture-streaming-vt -> render-architect -> material-system), which check.py reports as info. The baseline has no such cycle. Two ways to avoid it:
- Rely on the proposed per-instance texel-density registration in C-VT, where renderers push texel density to the streamer. That makes the C-RSCENE consume redundant; keep C-VIEW and C-INSTANCES?.
- Or mark C-RSCENE optional and declare the channel.

This is a refinement, not a reason to reject the finding. Major severity is appropriate: this is a missing data path that blocks a core rendering feature. It is not a style issue.

The finding's central inference does not hold. It claims that because C-RTAS (L2) does not require C-RG (L3), the AS-build module is barred from being scheduled by the graph and so has to issue its own barriers and submissions. The framework, however, consistently models external GPU work by inversion. Low-level producers expose work items, and the graph, at the higher layer, imports and schedules them. C-GPUMEM (L2) uploads and C-IO (L2) GPU decompression are listed as RND.GRAPH.external-work producers in exactly the same way, and neither requires C-RG. C-IO's summary spells the pattern out: work is "declared as external work items executed as render-graph nodes", and C-RG requires C-GPUMEM, not the reverse. For render-scene builds, the ray-tracing-infrastructure C-RT module (L3) already consumes C-RG@C-RT, so it can wrap C-RTAS build/refit calls in graph passes. That is the same arrangement the critic cites from UE RDG, where pass lambdas call a lower-level build API that knows nothing about the graph. The layering therefore does not force an L28 regression.

The proposed primary fix is unsound. Moving C-RTAS to L3 with a requirement on C-RG would break the recorded decision (docs/00 line 114, and the C-RTAS summary saying "independent of the render scene") that keeps AS/ray-query separate from rendering for non-render consumers such as spatial-audio-acoustics. The C-MLGPU comparison does not carry over: C-MLGPU is defined as a render-graph pass, while C-RTAS is deliberately a low-level library. The alternative C-GPUWORK contract duplicates the inversion pattern the framework already uses.

One real but small gap remains. Unlike C-IO, the C-RTAS summary does not say that builds are exposed as external work items for graph import. It is also not stated who schedules the GPU builds of the optional spatial-audio C-RTAS consumer. Both could be fixed with a one-line summary edit, so this is minor, not a major dependency-error.

The finding checks out against the data. In skills.json, path-tracing has provides: [] even though its purpose says "Reference path tracer as ground-truth oracle for validation". It consumes C-LIGHT and C-TEMPORAL (plus C-RT?, C-MATIF, C-RSCENE, C-INSTANCES, C-SCENETEX).

C-LIGHT is owned by direct-lighting-shadows, whose purpose covers light units and profiles. So a C-LIGHT bug would feed both the raster output and the reference it is compared against.

No contract in contracts.json covers a reference-render request or result under any name. The grep for reference, ground truth and undenoised found no such contract. render-validation's purpose names "comparisons against the reference path tracer", but it consumes only C-RG, C-RHI, C-RSCENE, C-RT? and C-SCENETEX. cinematics-sequencer lists "Path tracer" as a non-responsibility and consumes no path-tracing interface. Neither has a declared way to reach the oracle.

path-tracing, direct-lighting-shadows and reconstruction-upscaling share parent render-architect and workstream "rendering". There is no independence row for path-tracing vs direct-lighting-shadows or global-illumination.

check.py only proves oracle_author independence per contract, and independence pairs by workstream. Path-tracing provides no contract, so nothing checks the oracle's own independence. The deficiency is real, and a major missing-contract rating is justified.

One caveat on the proposed fix: check.py rejects an independence pair that shares a workstream. The proposed row (path-tracing vs direct-lighting-shadows/global-illumination, all "rendering") would fail unless path-tracing moves to another workstream. That limits the fix but not the finding.

The finding holds; I checked it against data/capabilities.json. RND.GEO.splat-relight ("Relightable/dynamic splats & hybrid raster/RT composition", owner geometry-pipeline) is labelled maturity "E" with profiles ["std3d"]. RND.GEO.splats ("Static Gaussian-splat...") is "M". In data/radar.json, the only splat entries cover RND.GEO.splats (M) and CNT.IMP.splats (X). Both entries have revisit "Standard format + relighting + shipped game use" and fallback "Photogrammetry meshes", and neither lists splat-relight. docs/07-research-plan.md:29 calls splatting "`experimental` for games". check.py's radar rule only covers non-established capabilities, and its X/S opt-in rule only covers X/S, so an E capability passes both. Nothing in check.py flags it. I ran model.cap_in_configuration and found splat-relight in every std3d client and tools configuration: standard-3d-client/tools, open-world, online-3d-client/console, racing, rts-3d, xr-pc, xr-console, coop, aaa client/tools and online-3d-tools. It is absent from server and bot configurations. So "all std3d shipping configurations" is accurate for client and tools builds. Nothing else in skills, contracts or crosscutting covers or qualifies relightable splats under another name. K-FUTURE raised the same issue independently. Major severity is justified: a research-grade capability sits in shipping builds with no radar entry and no fallback.

The data confirms the facts. In data/skills.json, path-tracing has provides=[] and consumes C-LIGHT and C-TEMPORAL, even though RND.PT.reference in data/capabilities.json calls it the "ground-truth oracle". QA.RENDER.reference (render-validation) and ANM.CINE.movie-render (cinematics-sequencer) both list path-tracing as a contributor, but neither skill consumes any contract from it. So the oracle every golden image is judged against has no declared request/output interface: no convergence criterion, seed, AOVs or variance. Autonomous agents coordinate through contracts, so this is a real missing contract.

The independence concern also holds. C-LIGHT covers light units and the many-light sampling API, and C-TEMPORAL covers denoiser signals. If the reference consumes them, a bug in either shows up in both the raster output and the reference. That weakens the framework's own oracle-independence rule (docs/00 L102/L124, QA.AGENT.oracle-independence). QA.RENDER.reference-validation, which checks the tracer against furnace scenes and an external renderer, reduces the risk but does not remove the coupling, and it defines no interface.

Neither docs/06 nor docs/00 records a scope decision against this, so the finding is within the K-RENDER mandate. Major is a fair severity: the defect is systemic to render QA, not cosmetic.

Most of the proposal is sound:
- C-PTREF at layer 3 requiring C-RSCENE and C-MATIF (both layer 3) fits the layering rules.
- An oracle_author of render-validation (workstream quality) is different from the owner path-tracing (workstream rendering).
- Optional consumption (C-PTREF?) is correct, because render-validation and cinematics-sequencer are in all profiles while path-tracing is lite3d/std3d only.

One part is unsound. The proposed crosscutting independence row "path-tracing vs direct-lighting-shadows/global-illumination" would fail scripts/check.py, because independence pairs must not share a workstream and all three skills are in rendering. The matrix also enforces staffing separation, not the code rule "no shared sampling code". That item needs a different mechanism, such as a rule that the reference module must not consume C-LIGHT or C-TEMPORAL, or a workstream move. This flaw is secondary and does not invalidate the core finding.

I confirmed this in data/capabilities.json. RND.GEO.splat-relight ("Relightable/dynamic splats & hybrid raster/RT composition") has maturity E and profile ["std3d"]. That means std3d shipping configurations include it (K-FUTURE confirms it sits in standard-3d-client). The base RND.GEO.splats is only M and is on the radar, and the radar's revisit trigger is "Standard format + relighting + shipped game use". docs/07 calls splatting experimental for games. So the more advanced child capability is rated more mature than its base, which is inconsistent. Because non-E capabilities must be on the radar (check.py line 409), an E rating keeps this one off it, so it carries no fallback, gets no radar review, and is not held to the experimental-only rule. For a framework whose agents choose what to build and ship from maturity and profile labels, that is a real correctness problem. Agents would treat research-grade technology as a shipping dependency. Major severity fits.

Nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 records a scope decision about splats, and the finding is within a rendering critic's mandate.

The proposed change is technically sound. check.py lines 470-471 require X/S capabilities to carry exactly the 'experimental' profile, and radar class must equal capability maturity. One caveat: the relight capability cannot join the existing M-class splat entry without failing the class check at line 456. It needs a new X-class radar entry owned by geometry-pipeline, which the critic's original text in gauntlet/round-3/K-RENDER.md does allow for ("or a new X entry").

Checked against the data and the finding holds. In data/capabilities.json, RND.RECON.denoise is a single row named "Spatiotemporal & ML denoising (ray reconstruction class)" with maturity M. It is owned by reconstruction-upscaling, with global-illumination as the collaborating skill. No other capability id or name covers denoising: grep for "denois" in capabilities.json returns only this row. The only other hits are in contract summaries (signal submission and guide buffers) and in the skill's purpose, none of which is a separate capability.

The radar entry in data/radar.json, "ML denoising & ray reconstruction" (class M), lists only RND.RECON.denoise and gives the fallback "Spatiotemporal denoisers". That fallback is part of the same M capability, so it is circular, as the finding says.

check.py (lines 406-407) only checks that a fallback string is present. It does not check that the fallback names a separate or established capability, so the problem is not already machine-proved. Severity minor is appropriate: it is a maturity labelling and modelling mistake, not a structural break.

I checked the facts in the data. In data/capabilities.json, RND.RECON.denoise is one row, 'Spatiotemporal & ML denoising (ray reconstruction class)', classed M. In data/radar.json, the entry 'ML denoising & ray reconstruction' (M) maps only to that capability, and its fallback is 'Spatiotemporal denoisers'. So the fallback is a technique inside the same M capability, which makes it circular. It does not point to an established capability that an agent could fall back to.

The defect is material. docs/00 section 7 says emerging techniques are reached through optional contracts or extension points. Labelling ordinary SVGF/ReBLUR/ReLAX denoising as emerging therefore pushes a baseline dependency of every RT/PT tier behind the emerging gate. An agent planning that tier would get the wrong maturity signal.

The framework is also inconsistent with itself. RND.RECON.upscalers, 'Temporal & ML upscalers', is classed established. Only denoise puts its established part behind an M label.

The proposed split matches the split rule in docs/00 (different rates of change and different literatures), and I found no scope decision in docs/06 section C or docs/00 against it. It is technically sound. The new ml-denoise row would stay owned by reconstruction-upscaling, and the radar entry would get a real, non-circular fallback, which satisfies the check.py radar rules.

Minor is the right severity. This is a labelling and fallback error, not a broken contract or dependency cycle.

The finding holds on substance, though one detail is wrong. In data/radar.json, RND.SHADER.autodiff already has its own class-M entry at about line 940, so it does not strictly share the RND.SHADER.neural entry. But that entry is a copy-paste of the neural one. Its tech is 'In-shader neural evaluation & differentiable shaders (RND.SHADER.autodiff)', and it repeats the same evidence ('SM 6.9 cooperative vectors (preview); Slang autodiff'), the same revisit ('Non-preview cross-vendor support') and the same fallback ('Standalone inference dispatch'). In capabilities.json, RND.SHADER.autodiff is 'Differentiable shader compilation (Slang-class autodiff)'. An inference-dispatch fallback does not apply to compile-time differentiation, and nothing else in the data gives autodiff a fitting fallback. check.py (lines 406-407 and 452-459) only checks that a fallback exists and that class and owner agree, not that the fallback is relevant, so it proves none of this. The neural entry (about line 284) also ties its evidence and trigger to SM 6.9 cooperative vectors. The claim that cooperative vectors moved to a DXIL linear-algebra direction and that the Vulkan extension is NV-only fits the public record. The capability description itself is already API-neutral ('matrix-vector/tensor intrinsics tier; API-neutral'), which shows the radar wording is behind the capability. The proposed change should become 'rewrite the existing autodiff entry' rather than 'create one'. Minor severity is appropriate.

The finding is confirmed in data/radar.json. The RND.SHADER.autodiff entry (around line 940, class M) is a copy of the RND.SHADER.neural entry (around line 284, class X): same tech name with an id suffix, same evidence ("SM 6.9 cooperative vectors (preview); Slang autodiff"), same revisit ("Non-preview cross-vendor support") and same fallback ("Standalone inference dispatch"). The critic says the two share one entry, which is slightly wrong: they are two entries with the same text. The practical effect is the same.

Why it matters: an inference fallback makes no sense for a compile-time differentiation feature. An autonomous agent writing the shader-system skill would get a meaningless fallback and a trigger that has nothing to do with autodiff.

The evidence and trigger also no longer match the framework's own definition. docs/01 defines RND.SHADER.neural as "matrix-vector/tensor intrinsics tier; API-neutral", but the radar entry is still keyed to cooperative vectors, a vendor/preview construct. The facts line up with the 2025 record: SM 6.9 shipped with cooperative vectors left in preview, Microsoft moved to a broader linear-algebra feature, and VK_NV_cooperative_vector is NV-only while cooperative matrix is KHR. As written, the revisit trigger could stay unfired or be misread.

Scope: this is within K-RENDER's mandate ("currency of rendering techniques", "technique maturity labels are honest"). It does not contradict any recorded scope decision. docs/06 A7 keeps the capability-tiered opt-in and only names the revisit trigger, and the proposal just brings that trigger up to date.

The proposal is technically sound: a separate M entry for autodiff with a gradient fallback done in tool code, and API-neutral trigger wording. It is incomplete, because the RND.MAT.neural and RND.TEX.ntc revisit triggers are also keyed to cooperative vectors, but that does not make it wrong. K-FUTURE raises overlapping points, which backs up the finding.

"Minor" is the right severity. This is advisory radar data at the experimental/emerging level, not a contract or a gate.

The finding is factually correct. legacy-patterns.json has 57 patterns (L01-L57). None covers a display-referred/LDR post pipeline, and none covers GS, HW tessellation or stream-out. A grep for geometry shader, tessellation, stream-out, LDR and scene-referred turns up nothing relevant: the only tessellation hits are RND.LOD.displacement (tessellation on virtualized geometry) and a radar note on Nanite. The leak into RND.POST.effects is real: capabilities.json L5019 reads 'Post chain ... applied after tonemapping on display-referred output', owned by post-color-hdr. L29's stance_capabilities are only RND.SHADER.pso-lists and RND.SHADER.cache. RND.SHADER.precache ('Load-time PSO precaching...') and RND.RHI.pso ('Pipeline-state models & caches ..., async creation', owned by rhi-core) exist but are not listed, even though L29's default_stance names async creation and pipeline libraries. check.py only proves that the stance capabilities a pattern names exist and that its justification owner owns, contributes to or leads them. It does not prove that the catalogue is complete, so this gap is not machine-covered. Minor severity fits an omission in the catalogue. One caveat for the fix: RND.RHI.pso is owned by rhi-core, not shader-system. Adding it to L29 would fail check.py unless shader-system contributes to or leads it, or rhi-core is made the justification owner.

The finding holds against the data files. No capability id, name, skill purpose or contract summary mentions transcoding, KTX2, Basis, UASTC or ETC1S. I searched all of data/*.json. The only hit is the fallback in radar.json:169 ("BCn/ASTC; transcode-on-load variant"), under the RND.TEX.ntc row, which matches the finding's claim that transcoding appears only as an NTC fallback phrase. RND.TEX.transcode does not exist. The nearest existing capabilities are RND.TEX.formats ("Runtime texture formats", a generic label), CNT.COOK.textures (cook-time BCn/ASTC encoding only), RND.TEX.runtime-decode (decoding player-supplied images, not device-format transcoding) and the PLAT.WEB/RND.RHI.webgpu rows. None of them states load-time selection or transcoding per device format. The untrusted-inputs registry has "assets" (serialization-schema) and "user-images" (texture-streaming-vt), with no transcoder parser registered. The check.py docstring proves only the registry's structure, not this coverage. One weakness: the RND.TEX.formats label is broad enough that someone could argue it implicitly covers this. Minor severity is appropriate.

I checked this against the data and it holds. data/legacy-patterns.json has 57 patterns (L01–L57). None covers the display-referred/LDR pipeline, and none covers geometry-shader, hardware-tessellation or stream-out pipelines. L29 lists only RND.SHADER.pso-lists and RND.SHADER.cache as stance capabilities, even though its default_stance promises "async creation with fallbacks". That promise is carried by RND.RHI.pso (owned by rhi-core, with shader-system contributing), and load-time precaching is RND.SHADER.precache (owned by shader-system). Both IDs exist.

The LDR gap is real, not hypothetical. RND.POST.effects still reads "applied after tonemapping on display-referred output", which is the leak K-RENDER-1 reported. The catalogue exists to catch exactly that kind of silent legacy stance.

The finding is within the critic's mandate. K-RENDER covers "currency of rendering techniques" and checks for "no ... DX11-era assumptions on capable tiers". Nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 records a scope decision that excludes these patterns. docs/00 only says the catalogue has 57 patterns, which is not a reasoned decision against adding more.

The proposal is technically sound and would pass check.py. The check requires every stance capability to exist and the owner to own, contribute to or lead at least one of them:
- L58's owner, post-color-hdr, owns both RND.POST.color and RND.POST.effects.
- L59's owner, geometry-pipeline, owns RND.GEO.mesh-shaders.
- shader-system owns RND.SHADER.precache.

The stance is advisory: a pattern needs an ADR, it is not forbidden. It is also scoped to capable tiers, so it does not break the scale-down paths. Two small weaknesses do not make the proposal unsound:
- L59 ties tessellation to RND.LOD.displacement, which is tagged emerging and applies to virtualized geometry.
- RND.POST.effects should be renamed per K-RENDER-1 before it serves as an L58 stance capability.

Minor severity is right. In PROTOCOL.md, minor means a small or placement issue. This finding adds guardrail entries and fixes a link, and the real data defect is already counted under K-RENDER-1 (major), so a higher rating would double-count it.

I confirmed the gap in data/docs. Transcoding from supercompressed universal formats appears only in the radar.json NTC fallback phrase ("transcode-on-load variant"). RND.TEX.formats ("Runtime texture formats") is generic. CNT.COOK.textures covers only cook-time BCn/ASTC encoding, and texture-streaming-vt explicitly hands encoding to asset-cook-processors. No PLAT.WEB, PLAT.MOB or RND.RHI.webgpu* capability covers choosing and transcoding a texture format per device at load time. KTX2/Basis is listed in docs/07 as a research source, but no capability owns it.

The gap is real for a framework with WebGPU and mobile targets: WebGPU exposes BC, ETC2 or ASTC depending on the device, so one download cannot carry one native format. I found no scope decision excluding it, and it is within K-RENDER's mandate, which includes a scale-down path per feature.

The proposal is technically sound. Ownership by texture-streaming-vt fits its existing formats and runtime-decode ownership, and registering the transcoder as a parser under the existing assets/user-images untrusted-input entries fits the registry's pattern.

Minor severity is appropriate: this is one small additive capability, and it is partly mitigated because per-platform cook variants (CNT.COOK.variants) could ship separate per-format builds. It does not break agent coordination.

The gap is real. K-RENDER's scope in data/critics.json is subtree:render-architect, render-validation, gpu-performance, terrain, vegetation-foliage, water-ocean, atmosphere-weather, deformation-skinning, xr-runtime, ml-inference-runtime, subtree:gpu-platform-architect, media-playback, voxel-worlds and platform-console. None of the three skills is in that scope or under those subtrees. world-editor-viewport and visual-debugging-tools sit under editor-architect, and text-fonts sits under ui-architect.

The ownership claims check out:
- world-editor-viewport contributes to RND.ARCH.editor-rendering (owner render-architect).
- visual-debugging-tools contributes to RND.SHADER.gpu-debug-draw (owner shader-system) and RND.TOOL.frame-debugger (owner render-graph-scheduling).
- text-fonts owns C-TEXT, whose summary says "glyph atlas/curve data". C-DRAW2D requires C-TEXT, and UI.TXT.raster covers "Glyph rasterization (SDF, MSDF, GPU curves)".

These skills are reviewed only by non-rendering critics: K-TOOLS covers subtree:editor-architect and K-GAMEPLAY covers subtree:ui-architect. check.py requires only some domain critic and an S3 critic per skill, so it does not prove rendering coverage.

The evidence is overstated in one place. Each of the three RND capabilities lists only one of these skills, not all of them, and text-fonts is not a contributor to any of the three. text-fonts' rendering link comes through C-TEXT and C-DRAW2D, not those capabilities. This inaccuracy does not undo the gap. Minor severity is appropriate.

This is not a material defect, and the finding's own evidence argues against it. The three cited capabilities are all owned by skills already in K-RENDER scope: RND.ARCH.editor-rendering belongs to render-architect, RND.TOOL.frame-debugger to render-graph-scheduling, and RND.SHADER.gpu-debug-draw to shader-system, all under subtree:render-architect. So K-RENDER already reviews the rendering side of debug draw, GPU picking and the frame debugger where it is decided. world-editor-viewport and visual-debugging-tools are only contributors to those capabilities. The claim that they "own the rendering-tooling surface" is therefore wrong. Both skills already have a domain critic, K-TOOLS, through subtree:editor-architect, with stages G1–S4. text-fonts has one too, K-GAMEPLAY, through subtree:ui-architect. None of the cited capabilities even lists text-fonts, so nothing in the evidence backs the C-DRAW2D glyph claim. check.py already enforces that every skill has a domain critic. Adding S1–S3 K-RENDER reviews for contributor skills would duplicate review of decisions whose owners K-RENDER already covers. A contributor's rendering-relevant work reaches K-RENDER through the owning skill's contracts anyway. If the finding held, "minor" would be the right severity, so severity is not inflated. It fails on materiality and on the accuracy of its premise.

The finding holds; I checked it against the data files. In data/capabilities.json around line 1903, CORE.JOBS.blocking reads: "Blocking & long-running tasks run inline on work-stealing workers (no dedicated lanes or compensating threads)". That is the policy the finding objects to.

It does conflict with other capabilities:
- RES.MGMT.no-stall (around line 2458) forbids blocking waits on frame-critical tasks and on threads bound to the host or OS.
- CORE.JOBS.degenerate (around line 1956) says 0–2 workers must have no blocking waits on host threads.

With only 0–2 workers, running blocking work inline stalls the frame. The only lanes in the model are CORE.JOBS.pinned (for work tied to a particular OS thread) and CORE.JOBS.priorities (latency-critical lanes). Neither provides a blocking or background lane.

Nothing already covers the fix:
- CORE.JOBS.thread-model only covers thread inventory and oversubscription detection. It has no compensation or suspend rule.
- CORE.JOBS.fibers only offers fibers as a mechanism. It does not require that waits suspend.
- The C-TASK summary only says "blocking rules", with no content.
- Legacy pattern L16 covers only file reads on a frame-critical thread. No legacy pattern covers blocking calls on frame-critical workers in general, and none has CORE.JOBS.blocking as its stance capability.
- scripts/check.py proves only structure (owners, layering, closure, whether ids exist). It checks no capability semantics like this.

Major is justified: a threading policy that is wrong at its base and contradicts shipping requirements for low-worker tiers.

This is a real, material defect. In data/capabilities.json, CORE.JOBS.blocking says "Blocking & long-running tasks run inline on work-stealing workers (no dedicated lanes or compensating threads)". That conflicts with other capabilities in the same file:
- RES.MGMT.no-stall: "no blocking waits on frame-critical tasks or host/OS-bound threads".
- CORE.JOBS.degenerate: "no blocking waits on host threads" on 0–2 workers.
- CORE.JOBS.priorities: "latency-critical lanes".
- CORE.JOBS.fibers: already exists as a mechanism for suspending waits.

The C-TASK contract summary lists "blocking rules", so autonomous agents implementing C-TASK would inherit the pool-starvation stance. That is the kind of silent legacy architecture PROTOCOL.md defines as major. The issue also falls within K-SYSTEMS's mandate (concurrency and scheduling; "no single-thread-first assumptions").

No scope decision in docs/06 section C or docs/00 covers this. Docs/06 B2 lists blocking/waiting patterns only as open research, not as a recorded decision for inline blocking. Docs/00 requires the same graph to run on 0–2 workers, which supports the finding.

The proposed change is technically sound. It matches the cited industry practice: TBB arenas, Go P handoff, .NET compensating threads, Naughty Dog fibers parking fibers, and Unreal background threads. The new legacy pattern would pass the check.py stance rules, because CORE.JOBS.blocking exists and is owned by job-system-task-graph.

K-ARCH, K-LEGACY and K-PERF raised the same finding independently, which confirms it. Major is the right severity: the defect would cause rework but does not block the whole framework.

The finding holds against the data. In data/capabilities.json (line 2133), CORE.OBJ.events is named "Events & messaging: global event bus with immediate synchronous listener dispatch by default" and is owned by entity-object-model.

In data/legacy-patterns.json, L19 is "Immediate synchronous observer callbacks across subsystems", and its stated default stance is "Deferred batched events at declared consumption points". L19 lists CORE.OBJ.events as its only stance capability. So the one capability meant to carry the deferred stance describes the very pattern it is supposed to replace.

check.py (docstring and the code around lines 473-488) only checks that stance capabilities exist and that the justification owner owns, contributes to or leads them. It does not check whether the capability's meaning matches the stance, so the contradiction passes the checker.

No other capability covers world-scoped deferred events under another name. CORE.OBJ.world-instances only forbids a current-world global. GAM.SYS.messages is "built on C-ID events", so it inherits the problem. The other event capabilities are domain-specific: PHY/ANM/AUD events and PLAT system-events.

The split ownership of messaging is also accurate. The C-ID summary (owner entity-object-model) lists "events", and the C-FLOW summary (owner frame-orchestration) lists "mailboxes ... between subsystems" as the default for runtime data flow. Neither states how the two relate.

Major severity is justified. The data states a legacy anti-pattern as the default, and GAM.SYS.messages builds on it.

I checked the finding against the source data and it holds. data/capabilities.json:2133 defines CORE.OBJ.events as "Events & messaging: global event bus with immediate synchronous listener dispatch by default". In data/legacy-patterns.json, L19 is "Immediate synchronous observer callbacks across subsystems" with the stance "Deferred batched events at declared consumption points", and CORE.OBJ.events is its only stance capability. So the one capability meant to carry out the stance is written as the pattern the stance forbids.

The capability also conflicts with three recorded principles. docs/00:100 says "No hidden globals". docs/00:92 requires multiple isolated worlds with no global. docs/00:47 makes C-FLOW the default way data moves between subsystems and derives ordering from declared access under C-FRAME, which callbacks fired mid-phase would bypass.

The ownership split is real. The C-ID summary (owner entity-object-model) lists "events", while the C-FLOW summary (owner frame-orchestration) lists "mailboxes".

This is material, not a matter of style. In a framework that coordinates autonomous agents, the text as written would lead agents to build exactly the legacy pattern. I found no scope decision in docs/06 or docs/00 that argues for keeping a global synchronous bus.

The proposed change is sound: the policy stays with entity-object-model and the transport moves to C-FLOW mailboxes. It also agrees with the independent findings of K-ARCH, K-LEGACY and K-PERF.

Major is the right severity. The problem is a direct contradiction inside an L2 contract that every gameplay skill consumes, but it can be fixed by rewording one capability and one contract summary, so it does not rise to critical.

Confirmed in the data. In data/capabilities.json, PHY.ARCH.stepping (owner physics-architect, contributor frame-orchestration) is named "Variable-timestep stepping on the render frame delta & frame sync". That is exactly the L30 pattern in data/legacy-patterns.json: "Frame-coupled variable-timestep simulation", detected as "simulation stepped by render delta". L30's default stance is "Fixed/declared step with interpolation per C-FRAME", and its only stance capability is CORE.FRAME.fixed-step. So the physics capability states the legacy pattern as its default, which contradicts CORE.FRAME.fixed-step and CORE.FRAME.sim-schedule.

Nothing else covers or fixes this. PHY.ARCH.async ("Decoupled/async physics stepping with input marshalling & interpolation") is a separate capability and leaves the stepping name unchanged. The physics-architect skill purpose and the K-SIM check only say stepping and sync must be "explicit". check.py only proves that stance capabilities exist and belong to the justification owner, so it cannot catch this contradiction in meaning.

One small overstatement: L30 does not "forbid" the pattern. The file header says a pattern is allowed if the justification owner writes an ADR. The proposed "variable step only by ADR" wording matches that rule. The proposed stance addition would also pass check.py, because frame-orchestration contributes to PHY.ARCH.stepping.

Major severity fits, since this default would break the determinism (C-DET) and rollback guarantees.

I confirmed the finding in the data. In data/capabilities.json around line 5590, PHY.ARCH.stepping reads "Variable-timestep stepping on the render frame delta & frame sync". It is owned by physics-architect, with frame-orchestration as contributor. In data/legacy-patterns.json, L30 is "Frame-coupled variable-timestep simulation", detected as "simulation stepped by render delta", with the stance "Fixed/declared step with interpolation per C-FRAME". Its stance_capabilities list only CORE.FRAME.fixed-step.

So a first-class capability states the forbidden legacy pattern as the physics default. An agent building physics from this would produce silent legacy architecture that breaks determinism and rollback. That matches the PROTOCOL.md definition of major, so the severity is right.

It is within the critic's mandate. K-SYSTEMS covers scheduling, and the finding's second-authority argument (physics picks its own cadence against frame-orchestration's fixed-step and sim schedule) is a scheduling and ownership concern.

I found no scope decision in docs/00 or docs/06 that endorses a variable step, and no seed-map entry covering this.

The proposed change is technically sound. Stepping inside the C-FRAME declared step with substeps, a catch-up clamp and interpolation hand-off is standard practice. Keeping variable step as an ADR exception is reasonable. Adding the capability to L30.stance_capabilities lets the checker tie the stance to it.

This finding duplicates K-ARCH, K-SIM and K-LEGACY in round 3. That affects the disposition (merge), not whether it holds.

The finding is confirmed. In data/capabilities.json:1244, PLAT.WEB.runtime reads "WASM threads (SharedArrayBuffer required; cross-origin isolation assumed on every host) & memory limits". Its owner is platform-web and its only contributor is job-system-task-graph. CORE.JOBS.degenerate (capabilities.json:1956) says "the same task graph on 0–2 workers ... yield to the host event loop", so the two contradict each other. Nothing else in the data covers a web path without cross-origin isolation. Searches for isolat, single-thread, no-thread and SharedArrayBuffer found no hosting-mode capability, no non-threaded web build variant and no detection or fallback wording. The platform-web purpose (skills.json:7222) only says "threads and cross-origin isolation". The M2 exit (milestones.json:293) says indie-2d ships on web, and the M4 web transports exit does not mention a web path without SharedArrayBuffer. check.py only checks that the web platform has an implementer (lines 594 and 624), so it does not prove this. Severity major is reasonable: on non-isolated hosts, such as iframe portals and pages with ad SDKs, a web build that requires SharedArrayBuffer does not start, and those hosts are the likely targets for the indie and web configurations. Seven other critics raised the same issue independently (K-ARCH, K-SEC, K-FUTURE, K-PLATFORM, K-LEGACY, K-PERF and K-SYSTEMS), which supports it. One small point: memory64 in the proposed change is new scope, not a fix for this defect, but it does not undermine the finding.

This is a real, material defect. data/capabilities.json says PLAT.WEB.runtime needs "WASM threads (SharedArrayBuffer required; cross-origin isolation assumed on every host) & memory limits". But CORE.JOBS.degenerate is a shipping mode meant to run on 0-2 workers and yield to the host event loop, with platform-web as a contributor. docs/00 (line 90) says the same graph runs inline on 0-2 workers on the web, and L25 in docs/09 expects correctness on one worker. So the platform capability rules out the fallback the core design promises. M2's exit requires indie-2d to ship on web, and non-isolated iframe portals are a main web-game channel, so the contradiction is on a milestone path. Nothing in docs/06 section C, docs/00 or radar.json records a reasoned decision to require cross-origin isolation, so the change is not out of scope. It also fits K-SYSTEMS's mandate (concurrency, memory, "no single-thread-first assumptions"). The proposed change is technically sound. It detects isolation at runtime via crossOriginIsolated, keeps COOP/COEP or credentialless as the threaded path, falls back to the existing 0-worker mode, and makes memory64 "where available". Credentialless and memory64 are not supported in every browser, and "where available" covers that. The evidence is accurate: Chrome 92 and Firefox 79 gate SharedArrayBuffer on isolation, and Emscripten and Unity keep single-threaded web builds. Making the M2 exit prove the non-isolated path is a sensible checked point. Major is the right severity: this is a cross-capability contradiction that breaks a milestone target on common hosts, not a style issue. Five other critics (K-ARCH, K-SEC, K-FUTURE, K-PLATFORM, K-LEGACY) raised the same issue independently.

Confirmed against data. CORE.OBJ.world-instances (entity-object-model), PHY.ARCH.multi-world (physics, with per-world budgets), NET.SRV.density ("Server tick cost & multi-instance density") and ED.ARCH.pie all exist, so the framework does require several worlds per process. No CORE.FRAME.multi-world exists. All CORE.FRAME.* capabilities describe one schedule: access-model is "the single frame scheduler that compiles the per-frame graph", and phases, time, amortized and headless are all single-graph. The C-FRAME summary says nothing about multiple worlds. CORE.JOBS.priorities covers generic task QoS, not fair share or overload isolation between worlds. The frame-orchestration, dedicated-server and job-system-task-graph purposes do not assign concurrent per-world scheduling, sync-point scoping or per-world pause/dilation to any owner. check.py proves nothing about this. The gap is real and cuts across skills, so major is justified.

This is a real gap. docs/00 line 92 makes "multiple isolated worlds per process, no current-world global" a design principle, and CORE.OBJ.world-instances, PHY.ARCH.multi-world ("match instances, preview worlds, server density ... per-world budgets"), NET.SRV.density and ED.ARCH.pie all assume several worlds in one process. The scheduling side is written for a single world, though. CORE.FRAME.access-model is "the single frame scheduler that compiles the per-frame graph". CORE.FRAME.time treats time domains, dilation and pause as process-level. The C-FRAME summary talks about "the minimal set of named global sync points" and never mentions worlds. I found no capability, contract or doc text covering per-world schedules, per-world pause or dilation (PIE paused while the editor world keeps running), fairness across worlds on the shared pool, or which sync points are process-wide and which belong to one world. Without an owner, physics-architect (per-world budgets), dedicated-server (density), editor-architect (PIE) and entity-object-model would each design world ticking their own way against one frame contract. That is exactly the kind of cross-agent drift this framework is meant to prevent. Nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 scopes this out. Section C's only multi-world mention is about PHY.ARCH.multi-world ownership load, which is a separate matter. Major fits because a stated principle has no scheduling owner at the core contract layer. The proposed change is technically sound and belongs in frame-orchestration, next to CORE.FRAME.time and access-model. One small gap: job-system-task-graph (CORE.JOBS.priorities/scheduler) and entity-object-model should also be listed as contributors, since fair share on the pool depends on the job scheduler. That does not weaken the finding.

I checked this against the data files and every factual claim holds. In contracts.json, C-SYNC (owner concurrency-primitives) has oracle_author entity-object-model, and C-TASK (owner job-system-task-graph) has oracle_author animation-architect. Neither skill's purpose or expertise covers memory models, lock-free code, reclamation or scheduling. entity-object-model lists object models, handle systems and lifetime design. animation-architect lists animation systems and pose pipelines, and its workstream is simulation. In capabilities.json, robustness-fuzzing owns QA.ROBUST.concurrency ("Concurrency stress & schedule perturbation") and contributes to CORE.CONC.correctness ("Thread-safety annotations & model checking"). Its workstream is quality, while both contracts sit in the foundation layer (layer 1). Its expertise includes TSan, and its purpose covers concurrency stress and schedule perturbation. Nothing in the data asks for model-checking or ARM/x86 litmus lanes in these conformance suites; model checking appears only in the implementer concurrency-primitives' own expertise. The only oracle rule check.py enforces is that the oracle author is not the sole implementer. It does not check whether the oracle is competent in the domain, so the finding is not already machine-proved. Because the hardest foundation contracts are graded by oracles with no concurrency expertise, rating it major is reasonable. One small note: robustness-fuzzing's expertise list names TSan but not model checkers, so the proposed change should also add that expertise. This does not weaken the deficiency.

The finding is confirmed. C-IPC (contracts.json, owned by core-runtime-architect) covers editor-runtime, tool-worker, crash-handler, profiler and script-debugger traffic, and its summary says only "dev-only port security". It has no untrusted-frame validation. CORE.LIFE.ipc and BLD.SYS.dev-surface-exclusion ("allowed shipping surfaces authenticated via C-IPC") exist as described. untrusted-inputs.json has no IPC or shared-memory entry. The nearest entries only partly overlap. 'crash-uploads' is remote upload of dumps, not the local crash-handler channel. core-runtime-architect registers only launch-args and config-layers. crash-diagnostics registers only crash-uploads. The robustness-fuzzing fuzz_targets list has no IPC target. check.py only checks entries that are already in the registry, so it cannot flag a class that is missing. Major severity is reasonable: the out-of-process crash handler ships, and the IPC surface has no validating owner, fuzz target or limits.

The finding is confirmed in data/contracts.json and holds. C-SYNC (owner concurrency-primitives) has oracle_author entity-object-model. C-TASK (owner job-system-task-graph) has oracle_author animation-architect. In data/skills.json neither author lists any concurrency or scheduling expertise: entity-object-model has object models, handle systems and lifetime design; animation-architect has animation systems and pose pipelines. robustness-fuzzing is in the quality workstream, lists TSan, fault injection and concurrency stress in its purpose, owns QA.ROBUST.concurrency and contributes to CORE.CONC.correctness (docs/01, lines 314 and 1674). It implements neither contract. The case is stronger than the critic states: entity-object-model is in the foundation workstream, the same one as concurrency-primitives. docs/00 line 35 says the implementer-vs-oracle-author pair is kept in different workstreams. check.py only tests that the author is not the sole implementer, so this breach goes undetected. Neither docs/06 section C nor docs/00 records a scope decision against this change. The proposal is sound: robustness-fuzzing is an independent quality-workstream author and passes the check.py rule, and the current skills stay on as consumer reviewers. The finding holds. In data/capabilities.json, PRF.METH.budgets (performance-architect) reads word for word "Budgets measured on the reference high-end PC and scaled proportionally to lower tiers". CORE.MEM.budget-enforcement and RES.MGMT.arbitration both exist, and RES.MGMT.arbitration enforces a "single physical budget on UMA", so budgets scaled from PC would feed the arbiter directly.

Nothing else fixes this. Some text is partly related, but it never says to measure on each tier's own reference hardware, never makes min-spec binding, and never derives memory budgets from physical or OS-reserved ceilings:
- The C-BUDGET contract (budgets "per hardware tier... derived from the performance model").
- PRF.METH.model and PRF.METH.scalability, which cover per-tier knob budgets.
- A milestone that mentions "within budget on min-spec PC".
- A console memory-model capability that mentions "reserved memory".

That related text actually contradicts the proportional-scaling rule instead of replacing it. scripts/check.py contains no budget or scaling checks. Rating it major is justified: the budgeting method is foundational, and on UMA, console and mobile tiers it would produce budgets that cannot be met.

I confirmed this against the data. data/untrusted-inputs.json has 48 input classes and none of them is IPC or shared-memory traffic. The nearest entries are dev-endpoints (validated by hot-reload-iteration), automation-commands (visual-debugging-tools) and collab-session. All three cover dev-only ports or other protocols. None covers the C-IPC transport, tool workers, or the crash-handler channel. That channel still exists in shipping builds, which is why BLD.SYS.dev-surface-exclusion (capabilities.json:9780) allows 'shipping surfaces authenticated via C-IPC'. The C-IPC summary (contracts.json:836) mentions only 'dev-only port security'; it says nothing about validating incoming frames. The docs require every untrusted input to be registered with a validating owner and a fuzz target (docs/04 'untrusted input' row, docs/00 line 37). A shipping trust boundary open to local privilege escalation, left out of that registry, is therefore a real, material omission, and it is within K-SYSTEMS's mandate. Nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 scopes IPC out. The proposed fix is technically sound. core-runtime-architect owns C-IPC and CORE.LIFE.ipc, crash-diagnostics and editor-architect are named contributors to CORE.LIFE.ipc, and the hostile-local / harness / TOCTOU-safe copy-out settings match the registry's conventions and the shared-memory double-fetch threat. Major severity is fair for a missing shipping-surface trust boundary. It is not critical, because the dev-only surfaces are already partly covered.

The finding is confirmed and material. In data/capabilities.json (line ~10754), PRF.METH.budgets reads "Budgets measured on the reference high-end PC and scaled proportionally to lower tiers". That contradicts the framework's own C-BUDGET contract (data/contracts.json:171), which sets budgets "per hardware tier × configuration × refresh class, derived from the performance model". It also contradicts docs/00, which says the submission strategy and bottlenecks differ per tier (TBDR, UMA). No recorded scope decision in docs/00 or docs/06 section C defends PC-first proportional scaling, so the finding is in scope. It is also not a re-raise: this is round 3 and no earlier rejection is recorded. The memory side falls within K-SYSTEMS's mandate ("memory, scheduling... low-level architecture"). Fixed UMA/OS-reserved pools feeding CORE.MEM.budget-enforcement and RES.MGMT.arbitration are exactly where an infeasible budget would be silently enforced. Major fits the protocol's definition: it would cause rework or silent legacy architecture, and it does not stop agents from coordinating, so it is not a blocker. K-PERF-1, K-LEGACY-7 and K-ARCH-13 independently raise the same issue at major, which supports the rating. The proposed change is technically sound and consistent with C-BUDGET: per-tier reference hardware, min-spec binding, and memory derived from physical and OS-reserved ceilings. Two caveats: it leaves out the configuration × refresh class axes and the reconciliation with PRF.METH.model, and "cross-tier scaling only as an initial estimate" is looser than the peer findings' "no proportional scaling". Merging it with K-PERF-1's wording fixes both, and neither makes the proposal unsound.

I confirmed this against the data files. In skills.json, memory-allocators consumes only ["C-PAL","C-BASE"]. In contracts.json, C-MEM requires only ["C-BASE"]. The same skill owns CORE.MEM.thread-caches ("Thread-local caches & NUMA-aware allocation") and CORE.MEM.fragmentation (defragmentation and relocation), which is concurrent machinery. C-SYNC is owned by concurrency-primitives and covers atomics, locks, lock-free queues and safe reclamation. It requires only C-BASE, and concurrency-primitives consumes only C-PAL and C-BASE. C-BASE offers only "raw thread primitives" as a bootstrap hook layer, not the engine's atomics or locks contract, so nothing else covers the gap under another name. check.py does not flag a missing edge, because it only checks cycles, layering and closure. I applied the proposed change to a copy of the data (memory-allocators consumes C-SYNC, C-MEM requires C-SYNC) and check.py still reported 0 errors and 0 warnings. So the new edge creates no cycle and breaks no layering, as the finding claims. One part is less certain: the claim that the allocator "escapes CORE.CONC.correctness review" is inferred, since the data does not model review. The missing dependency itself is real, and "minor" is a fair severity.

Confirmed in the data. In data/contracts.json, the C-TYPES summary (owner containers-core-types) says "vetted hashinggraphic primitives wrapper". That phrase is a garbled leftover of "cryptographic", and the same summary already lists "versioned stable hashing" separately. In data/capabilities.json, CORE.TYPES.crypto ("Vetted cryptographic primitives wrapper, CSPRNG, per-platform selection") is owned by security-runtime, not containers-core-types. security-runtime is also the owner of C-SIGN, whose summary begins "Crypto primitives and CSPRNG". So the C-TYPES summary claims crypto work that belongs to a different contract. check.py only proves structure (owners, layering, conformance and so on) and never checks summary wording, so it does not catch this. Rating it minor is fair: it is a text and naming inconsistency, and the ownership links themselves are correct.

Confirmed in data/contracts.json: the C-TYPES summary (owner containers-core-types) still says "vetted hashinggraphic primitives wrapper". The rendered docs/02 table repeats it. C-SIGN (owner security-runtime) summarizes "Crypto primitives and CSPRNG". In data/capabilities.json, CORE.TYPES.crypto is owned by security-runtime, and containers-core-types only contributes. docs/00 line 127 records the scope decision that security-critical crypto runtime code belongs to security-runtime (C-SIGN), so the C-TYPES text contradicts a recorded decision rather than an open question. This matters for autonomous agents. Contract summaries define what an owner implements, so the containers-core-types agent could reasonably build its own crypto wrapper next to C-SIGN's: duplicate security-critical code outside the owner that holds the trust store. The garbled word also shows the text was never properly cleaned up. Minor is the right severity: ownership in the capability data is correct, and only the contract prose is wrong. The main fix is sound: drop crypto from the C-TYPES summary. The second part is offered as an either/or. Renaming or moving the CORE.TYPES.crypto ID would be needless churn, since area prefixes do not decide ownership. Naming C-SIGN in its description is the cheaper, sound option. The critic's mandate covers this: it is a contract/ownership overlap. K-ARCH raised the same point independently in round 3, so this may be deduplicated against it.

The facts check out. memory-allocators consumes only [C-PAL, C-BASE] and owns CORE.MEM.thread-caches (thread-local and NUMA-aware allocation) and CORE.MEM.fragmentation (defragmentation and relocation). Atomics, locks and lock-free structures belong to concurrency-primitives through C-SYNC (CORE.CONC.atomics, sync, lockfree). C-BASE promises only "raw thread primitives", which is too vague to cover a memory model or atomics. So an agent building the allocator has no contract edge to the primitives it needs. It would either re-create them, blurring ownership, or rely on an unstated reading of C-BASE. For autonomous agents that is a real gap in the dependency contract, not a matter of style.

It is within K-SYSTEMS's mandate: docs/05 lists SYSTEMS as the domain critic for memory-allocators and concurrency-primitives. One claim is overstated. The finding says the allocator "escapes CORE.CONC.correctness review", but the same SYSTEMS critic already covers both skills, so the duplication and ownership problem is the stronger reason.

I found no recorded scope decision against this edge in docs/06 section C or docs/00. docs/00 relies on C-BASE to break the allocator/logging/config cycle, and the proposal keeps that intact by saying C-SYNC node storage uses the C-BASE raw allocator.

The proposal is technically sound. Foundation (L1) providers get no implicit universals (model.universals_for), and concurrency-primitives explicitly consumes only C-PAL and C-BASE, so the edge creates no cycle. I applied the change to a copy (scratchpad/r3/vt9): memory-allocators consumes C-SYNC and C-MEM requires C-SYNC. scripts/check.py still reported 0 errors and 0 warnings, so the bootstrap, layering and milestone freeze-order proofs all still hold.

Minor is the right severity. Nothing breaks structurally; the issue is a missing edge that invites duplicated primitives.

The claim is confirmed against the data. CORE.MEM.virtual exists as "Virtual memory reservation & mapping" (capabilities.json:1648) and says nothing about page size, large or huge pages, or commit/decommit granularity. PLAT.SRV.host-os (capabilities.json:1412) is the only place that names huge pages, and it covers server hosts only. The nearby entries do not own the policy either. The platform "System events & queries ... page size" entry (capabilities.json:605, contracts.json:9) only asks the OS what the page size is. The console memory model entry (capabilities.json:773) covers UMA and reserved memory, not page granularity. The memory-allocators skill's purpose mentions only "virtual memory" in general, and the GPU memory skill covers GPU heaps, not CPU page policy. A search for 64K, 2M, THP, large page, decommit and SeLockMemory found nothing else. This is an omission of an owner, not a structural check, so check.py cannot prove it. "Minor" is the right severity, since the gap is one fix: rename an existing capability.

The finding holds as a minor omission. In docs/01 and data/capabilities.json, CORE.MEM.virtual reads only "Virtual memory reservation & mapping" (memory-allocators). The only explicit large/huge page item is PLAT.SRV.host-os ("Server host OS & container specifics (Linux, ARM64 hosts, huge pages)"). PLAT.PAL.system-events only exposes a "page size" query and sets no policy. The memory-allocators entry in docs/03 does not mention page granularity either. Nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 records a decision to leave this out. Because the capability text is what autonomous agents scope their work from, a client allocator agent could reasonably miss 64K/2M page and commit-granularity policy. That affects console allocator design, TLB behaviour for multi-GB pools and decommit strategy, so the gap is real, not a matter of style. It is still minor, not major: the owner (memory-allocators, with "virtual memory" in its expertise) is arguably implied already, so the fix only makes scope explicit and no ownership is contested. The proposed rename is sound and cheap. It keeps the same owner, fits within K-SYSTEMS' remit, and "per platform" correctly leaves the platform numbers to the PAL/platform backends. Small caveat: Windows large pages are non-pageable and need a privilege, so they are rarely enabled in shipped clients. The capability should record the policy decision without implying that large pages are always used, but this does not make the proposal unsound.

The data supports the main claim, but the kick/ban part is overstated. C-SERVER (contracts.json, L3, owner dedicated-server) covers host lifecycle, per-connection budgets, overload state and the admin surface in one contract. dedicated-server targets only server and tools. NET.SRV.budgets, NET.SRV.overload and NET.SRV.admin are all owned by dedicated-server, and replication contributes to both overload and budgets. replication's consumes list does not include C-SERVER, so it has no contract through which to read the overload state. The configuration coop-3d-listen-client has target=client, so dedicated-server is not in it. That leaves the listen-server co-op reference game (required by a milestone exit) with no owner for per-connection memory/CPU quotas or overload degradation. I searched for time dilation, adaptive tick and similar degradation terms and found nothing that covers these on other targets. Two parts of the finding are already partly covered. Kick reasons and the ban hook exist as NET.SESS.disconnect, owned by net-session in all targets. Rate-limit policy is in C-INTEGRITY, owned by anti-cheat-integrity in all targets. The proposed C-HOSTAUTH should therefore reuse those instead of adding a new kick/ban surface. Even so, per-connection budgets and overload state are real gaps for non-dedicated hosts, and the wrong boundary is confirmed. Rating it major is reasonable because the gap affects a shipped reference configuration.

The central proposal (a host-authority contract for quotas and overload owned by net-session in all targets, with replication consuming it) is technically sound. I checked this against the data and it holds. C-PREDICT (data/contracts.json) promises "cosmetic-effect suppression during resim". 1. I checked the data and the finding holds, with some overstatement.

**Confirmed facts:**
- In data/capabilities.json, NET.DBG.profiler, NET.DBG.visualize, NET.DBG.session-replay and NET.REP.spectator are all owned by replication.
- In data/skills.json, replication's profiles are ["online"] only. network-transport and prediction-rollback cover online, online-lockstep and online-rollback.
- online-performance is profiles ["online"] and hard-consumes C-REP. It owns PRF.NET.bandwidth and PRF.NET.latency.
- fighting-2d-rollback-client (min2d + online-rollback) is claimed at M2. That milestone gates NET.PRED.rollback with the exit "8 frames under 150 ms / 5% loss".

So the configurations in scope get no prediction-error visualization, no spectator capability and no bandwidth or latency attribution. The only skill that would measure the rollback latency gate (prediction-rollback) is the one that builds the rollback netcode. That conflicts with the independent-validation principle in docs/00 (#4). This is material for agents coordinating by ownership: nothing assigns an owner to rollback stats overlays or lockstep observers, even though every shipped title in these genres has them.

**No scope conflict:** Nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 excludes this. Docs/00 explicitly split the netcode families so that input-only netcode does not link state replication. That split is what created the orphaning, so the fix is consistent with the recorded decision.

**Mandate:** K-NET's scope includes subtree:network-architect, which covers replication, prediction-rollback and network-transport. online-performance sits under performance-architect, so that part is adjacent to K-NET's scope rather than inside it. It is still a network-performance issue, which is defensible.

**The proposal is technically sound:**
- Channel-level attribution in transport works across all families, and replication can contribute the entity and property attribution.
- Optional C-REP? and C-PREDICT? consumes keep online-performance closed in rollback and lockstep configurations.
- New spectator and prediction-viz capabilities owned by prediction-rollback fit its existing lockstep-replay ownership.

**Overstatements:**
- "No network debugging" is too strong. NET.DBG.inspect is owned by transport and present in these configurations.
- The session-replay need is partly covered by determinism-replay (C-REPLAY, all profiles) and NET.PRED.lockstep-replay.

The remaining gaps (profiler, visualization, spectator, independent latency measurement) still justify the major severity.

The data files confirm the gap. The NET.REP group in capabilities.json holds state, compression, interest, priority, rpc, interpolation, replays, ids, spectator, killcam, change-tracking, parallel and moq-spectator. There is no NET.REP.compat, and no capability anywhere mentions layout hashes, per-class or per-connection layout negotiation, or tolerant decode of replicated bitstreams. Searches for wire, bitstream, layout negotiation and checksum found nothing relevant. The C-REP summary in contracts.json has no versioning or compatibility clause. L45 lists only NET.ARCH.versioning as its stance capability. Four things come close, but none covers the gap. (1) NET.ARCH.versioning and the C-NET summary are policy only: the compatibility window and handshake policy. (2) NET.SESS.handshake (net-session) does a session-level version check and capability negotiation, not negotiation of each replicated-schema layout. (3) CORE.SER.evolution ("Schema evolution, versioning & upgraders") is generic. The serialization-schema skill purpose describes formats and upgraders, which is stored-data work, and names no net role. (4) The "live changeability" crosscutting obligation (owner online-services-liveops) asks every skill to declare a patch-stable data layout under version skew. That is an obligation, not an implementing capability with a replication owner. The check.py docstring only proves that legacy patterns name existing stance capabilities. It does not prove this coverage. Release manifests (BLD.REL.compat, C-RELEASE keys) and skew tests (QA.FUNC.version-skew) exist, which matches the finding's description. The major severity is reasonable, because crossplay and live-ops patch lag depend on N-1 wire compatibility, and nothing implements the L45 stance at the replication layer. One caveat: the handshake capability and the crosscutting obligation partly soften the "nothing implements it" wording, but they do not fill the gap.

The finding holds as a major gap. I checked the data. NET.ARCH.versioning (network-architect) is only "Compatibility-window policy & handshake". BLD.REL.compat only emits manifests. QA.FUNC.version-skew only tests the skew matrix. NET.SESS.handshake does the connect-time version check and capability negotiation. None of the 13 NET.REP capabilities that replication owns covers compatibility of the replicated layout. C-REP's summary (data/contracts.json) has no versioning clause. CORE.SER.evolution and C-SER ("Formats, versioning, upgraders") are generic serialization-schema mechanisms. Replication separately owns its hand-packed delta and bit-packed bitstream (NET.REP.compression), so no owner is assigned to per-type layout hashing, negotiation or tolerant decode across the window. L45's stance is "Compatibility windows", but its only stance capability is a policy capability with no implementation behind it. An agent building replication to its contract would therefore produce an exact-layout protocol, which is the L45 pattern the stance rejects. For a framework that coordinates autonomous agents, a policy with no implementing owner is a real missing contract. I found nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 that places this out of scope, and it is within K-NET's mandate. Major is the right severity rather than blocker, because the policy, handshake and tests already exist and the missing piece is the implementing mechanism. The proposal is technically sound and fits existing patterns: a replication-owned capability with serialization-schema and network-architect as contributors, a C-REP summary clause that ties to the window defined in C-NET (which C-REP already consumes), and adding the capability to L45's stance_capabilities.
