Major severity fits: async PvP and leaderboards are a supported profile, and the standard integrity mechanism for them has no owner or configuration.

This is a real, material gap. online-async has only one configuration, mobile-async-client, which is a client target on the mobile platform. The server-side validation capabilities are tagged for the online profile only (XC.SEC.server-validation is gated to "online" at data/capabilities.json around line 11518), so an online-async game gets no server-validation route. NET.ARCH.async (owned by online-services-liveops) covers only backend-mediated play. XC.SEC.score-integrity has no contributors and nothing points it at re-simulation. Validating async PvP and leaderboard results by deterministic re-simulation is standard practice, as the Supercell and Trackmania examples show, and the framework already has what it needs: C-DET, C-SNAPSHOT and C-REPLAY under determinism-replay. Scope check: docs/06 C.3 and docs/00 exclude backend services, but the engine still owns the integration boundary, the server process lifecycle and server artifacts. A headless validator that runs the engine sim is an engine server artifact, not a backend service. Hosting it stays external, and online-services-liveops' external:backend sentinel keeps it that way, so the proposal does not conflict with a recorded scope decision. There is already precedent: online-3d-bot-client is a headless-client configuration on server-host. The proposal is technically sound. determinism-replay, anti-cheat-integrity and online-services-liveops all have profiles 'all' and all include headless-client in their targets, so the proposed configuration (minimal+online-async, headless-client, server-host) is plausible. Owner determinism-replay is the right choice. Claiming it in M2 alongside mobile-async-client makes sense. Major severity is fair: an entire netcode family has no anti-cheat validation path, and agents would otherwise have to improvise one. One caveat: I did not run check.py on the new configuration, so its closure is plausible but not proved.

I checked the finding against the data files and it is mostly accurate. One part is already covered: LAN discovery.

Confirmed:
- In skills.json, dedicated-server.consumes lists "C-LIVE" as a hard dependency, while other entries such as C-SVC?, C-WORLD? and C-SHARD? are marked optional.
- NET.SESS.host-mode reads "Hosting modes (dedicated, listen, P2P host, relay-hosted) & host migration". It names no self-hosted or community mode.
- NET.SESS.auth covers "Auth-ticket & service-identity validation in every host mode". It says nothing about auth without the first-party backend.
- BLD.REL.end-of-service promises "offline fallback, community server release, data export".
- I searched for server browser, server list, master server, self-host, community server and A2S. The only other "community" hit is end-of-service itself. There is no capability for internet server-list registration or query, and no NET.SESS.server-browser.
- PLAT.SVC.matchmaking covers only the matchmaking, lobby and session boundary, and it goes through C-LIVE (owner online-services-liveops).
- PLAT.SVC.emulation and the C-LIVE test_double ("service emulator") are for tests. Neither makes C-LIVE optional for a shipped server.
- check.py only checks optional ('?') dependencies for gated contracts. C-LIVE is not gated, so no check covers this.

Partly covered: NET.TRANS.local-network ("LAN/local-wireless session discovery & hosting without online services", owner network-transport, contributors platform-console and net-session) already handles LAN discovery. The proposed server-browser capability should not claim LAN discovery again. It should cover only internet and master-server listing and query. This does not overturn the main omission: the dedicated server hard-requires C-LIVE, and there is no internet server listing or self-hosted mode, which conflicts with the end-of-service promise. Major severity is reasonable.

The facts check out against the data. untrusted-inputs.json has 48 inputs and none of them is client RPCs or events. The closest is 'replicated-state' (owner replication, count/depth/rate), which is named and scoped as state. 'input-commands' and 'transaction-requests' cover other channels. The replication consumes list in skills.json (C-NET, C-NETLINK, C-ECS?, C-SER, C-ID, C-SPATIAL, C-WORLD?, C-SIGNIF?, C-REPLAY?, C-FLOW, C-SHARD?, C-FRAME, C-TASK) has no C-INTEGRITY. The skills that do consume it are platform-services, prediction-rollback, gameplay-systems-toolkit, character-movement and a few others. The replication-to-integrity link is only an optional C-INTEGRITY? in some skills, and anti-cheat does not consume C-REP. NET.REP.rpc ('RPCs & reliable events', owner replication) says nothing about validation or authority. The C-REP summary mentions RPCs but no validator or authority declaration. C-INTEGRITY registers validators only for movement, hits and economy. Partial coverage exists: NET.SRV.budgets sets per-connection RPC quotas (dedicated-server, with replication and anti-cheat contributing), and XC.SEC.server-validation is generic. Neither gives a per-RPC argument or authority validation path. check.py only proves registry well-formedness (one owner, fuzz target, limits per registered input), so it cannot detect a missing input class. Minor is the right severity given the partial coverage through budgets and generic server validation.

I checked this against data/*.json. dedicated-server.consumes does list a hard "C-LIVE", while net-session consumes "C-LIVE?". C-LIVE (owner online-services-liveops) is the live-ops backend boundary: matchmaking tickets, remote config, events, moderation. Its test double is a service emulator meant for tests, not a production local implementation. NET.SESS.host-mode lists only dedicated, listen, P2P host and relay-hosted, with nothing on who operates the server (first-party fleet vs self-hosted/community).

Some of it is already covered. NET.TRANS.local-network handles LAN discovery and hosting without online services. PLAT.SVC.matchmaking covers the backend lobby/session boundary. But nothing covers internet server-list registration or query for servers the studio doesn't run, or the query responder on the server itself (A2S-style). BLD.REL.end-of-service ("offline fallback, community server release") has dedicated-server as a contributor but no capability behind it.

Scope: docs/06 C.3 and docs/00 put backend services out of scope but keep the integration boundary and C-SERVER in the engine. A backend-free server mode and a server-browser client/responder are engine-side boundaries, so the finding does not contradict a recorded scope decision.

The proposal is technically sound. Making C-LIVE optional mirrors net-session and does not touch any check.py gated/upward-link rule. The new NET.SESS.server-browser should reference PLAT.SVC.matchmaking and NET.TRANS.local-network so it doesn't duplicate them, but that is a refinement, not a flaw.

Major severity is fair: a hard backend dependency in the server skill blocks an explicitly promised end-of-service outcome and a common genre hosting model, and autonomous agents would not fill the gap on their own. It is not critical, because LAN discovery exists and C-LIVE is an interface that could in principle be backed by an own-backend implementation.

The finding matches the data. In data/capabilities.json, NET.TRANS.web is class E and named "Browser transports (WebSocket, WebRTC data channels; WebTransport where available)". WebSocket is listed first and nothing says it is less preferred. WebTransport is only "where available", and the name never mentions WebRTC unreliable channels. In data/legacy-patterns.json, L42 ("TCP or all-reliable channels for real-time state") lists only NET.TRANS.reliability in stance_capabilities, not NET.TRANS.web. NET.TRANS.quic is class M, named "QUIC / WebTransport evaluation", and its radar entry says "QUIC/WebTransport game transport", class M, fallback "Custom UDP protocol". Searches for WebSocket, WebTransport, unreliable, datagram and browser across all data files found nothing that already prefers unreliable browser transports. The web-platform skill only says "browser transport constraints". check.py only proves that legacy stance capabilities exist and that radar classes match capability maturity. It does not check whether a stance covers the right capabilities or which browser transport is preferred. Minor severity is right: this is a wording and preference gap, not a broken structure.

I checked this against the data files and it holds. The untrusted-inputs registry has 48 classes and none of them is client-to-server RPCs or events. The closest ones are replicated-state (replication; limits count/depth/rate), input-commands and peer-inputs (both prediction-rollback). None of these covers per-RPC authority or argument bounds for server-authoritative RPC netcode. Replication owns NET.REP.rpc and C-REP names RPCs in its summary. But replication.consumes does not include C-INTEGRITY, whose summary is "validator registration per authoritative action". Only dedicated-server consumes C-INTEGRITY, so listen servers and P2P hosts, which run inside clients per docs/00, have no general RPC validator path. NET.SRV.budgets covers RPC quotas only under dedicated-server. I found no scope decision in docs/06 section C or docs/00 that excludes this. The finding is within the netcode critic's mandate, and a real attack surface (dupe and teleport exploits) is enough to make it material. Minor severity is right because pieces already exist nearby: replicated-state, C-INTEGRITY via dedicated-server, and NET.SRV.budgets. The proposal is technically sound. I applied it to a copy of the data: adding the optional C-INTEGRITY? to replication creates no layering or cycle error (both contracts are layer 3). Registering client-rpcs alone gives 2 check.py errors ("replication does not register it" and "has no fuzz target"). Both clear with the same mechanical follow-through already done for replicated-state, which is listed in two places in data/skills.json (lines 979 and 5301). That is an incomplete proposal, not an unsound one.

The facts check out. In data/capabilities.json, NET.TRANS.web is established (E), labeled "Browser transports (WebSocket, WebRTC data channels; WebTransport where available)" and shared with platform-web. It puts WebSocket first and says nothing about which transport fits which traffic class. In data/legacy-patterns.json, L42 ("TCP or all-reliable channels for real-time state", default stance "UDP-class channels with per-message reliability classes") lists only NET.TRANS.reliability in stance_capabilities. So the capability an agent building a web client reads first does not link to the stance that argues against WebSocket for real-time state. That is a real coherence gap for autonomous agents: one could reasonably pick the first-listed established transport. It is within K-NET's transport mandate, and I found no scope decision in docs/06 section C or docs/00 that excludes it. It is fairly rated minor rather than major: L42's own detection rule ("state over reliable ordered stream") still applies whatever the capability label says, so the pattern is not undetectable, only unsignposted. Two of the three proposed changes are sound and cheap: relabeling NET.TRANS.web to prefer WebRTC unreliable channels and WebTransport datagrams, with WebSocket as a fallback for async/turn-based play or by ADR, and adding NET.TRANS.web to L42 stance_capabilities. Both are schema-compatible, because check.py only requires stance_capabilities to be non-empty and valid. The third change, renaming NET.TRANS.quic to "native transport backend", is the weak part. The radar entry's recorded revisit trigger is latency parity with custom UDP on target platforms, and browser shipping status does not show that. Accepting the rename should therefore not be read as promoting its maturity. That caveat does not undo the core finding.

NET.TRANS.qos-probe does not exist; the only place it appears is the critic's own K-NET.md. I searched the data files for ping, QoS, probe, beacon, RTT, round-trip, region, datacentre and relay. The only matches that come close are about something else. NET.TRANS.nat covers NAT traversal and relays, NET.TRANS.congestion covers bandwidth estimation, NET.TRANS.simulation is the link-conditioner seam, and the "link statistics" in the transport contract (contracts.json line 1063) apply to connections that are already open. None of them covers probing latency or loss to candidate regions, data centres or relays before connecting. PLAT.SVC.matchmaking (owned by online-services-liveops) is described only as an "integration boundary", and neither network-transport's purpose nor online-services-liveops' purpose mentions QoS or ping probing. The only QoS matches are about thread priority. check.py does not check for this at all. It is a real but small gap, so "minor" is the right severity.

I checked each claim against the data files and all of them hold. prediction-rollback (skills.json) consumes C-NET, C-DET, C-SNAPSHOT, C-INPUT, C-FRAME, C-NETLINK and the optional ECS/PHYS/ANIM/REP/INTEGRITY contracts, but not C-NETSESSION. Only dedicated-server (required) and gameplay-architect (optional) consume C-NETSESSION. NET.SESS.baseline ("Join-in-progress baseline snapshot") lists only replication as a contributor, and NET.SESS.reconnect lists none. replication runs only in the 'online' profile, while net-session and prediction-rollback also run in online-lockstep and online-rollback. So in the lockstep and rollback configurations the baseline's only contributor is missing. net-session consumes neither C-SNAPSHOT nor C-PREDICT, and C-NETSESSION's summary says nothing about start frame, seed or input-delay agreement. Nothing else covers this under another name. NET.PRED has lockstep, rollback, clock, input-commands and lockstep-replay, but none of them handles session start agreement or late join and rejoin by snapshot plus command catch-up. The only "catch-up" match is sim time acceleration. check.py only proves structure (links, configuration closure, freeze order) and not this semantic path. Minor severity fits: C-NETSESSION does exist in these configurations, but no contract link carries lockstep or rollback join, baseline or reconnect.

I confirmed the gap in data/capabilities.json. No capability covers client-side latency or loss probing to regions, data centres or relays. The NET.TRANS set has sockets, reliability, mtu, congestion, crypto, nat, lifecycle, simulation, quic, web, voice, dos, platform-requirements, web-server, l4s and local-network. PLAT.SVC.matchmaking (owner online-services-liveops) is only an "integration boundary". NET.SESS turns matchmaking results into connections but does not produce latency input. A grep for ping, QoS or beacon finds only thread and task QoS, so nothing is implicitly owned. The purpose texts of network-transport and online-services-liveops do not mention probing either.

Scope: docs/06 section C puts backend services out of scope, but the engine keeps the integration boundary. Client-side probing is engine code running on the transport's UDP path, and the matching services (GameLift beacons, PlayFab QoS, SDR ping location) are backend-side. So the finding does not contradict the recorded scope decision.

Materiality: region and relay selection is a standard input to matchmaking. Without an owner, autonomous agents would either skip it or build it twice, once in the transport and once in the services boundary. That is a real, if small, omission.

The proposal is sound. network-transport owns the sockets, relays and NAT work, so it is the natural owner, and online-services-liveops as contributor fits how it consumes the results. "Minor" is the right severity: this is a single missing leaf capability with an obvious home, not a structural defect.

The gap is real. NET.SESS.local-players does not exist. The NET.SESS group has only handshake, join, baseline, reconnect, travel, disconnect, host-mode and auth. None of them, and neither the C-NETSESSION summary nor the net-session purpose, mentions several players per connection. NET.SESS.auth covers ticket and service-identity validation per connection, not per player. GAM.FW.local-players ("Local players & split-screen at gameplay level", gameplay-architect with input-system) is limited to gameplay, and its milestone use is local 2-player split-screen only. PLAT's platform-user model mentions guests, but only as local platform users, with no network join or auth. NET.PRED.input-commands covers delivery of command frames, not separate streams per player. The per-local-player mentions in the UI and view contracts are local only. No check.py rule covers this, and a minor omission is a fair rating.

I confirmed the facts in data/*.json. prediction-rollback owns NET.PRED.lockstep and NET.PRED.rollback, and its consumes list has no C-NETSESSION. Only dedicated-server and gameplay-architect (optionally) consume C-NETSESSION. net-session is in the online-lockstep and online-rollback profiles, but it consumes only C-REP?. NET.SESS.baseline lists replication as its only contributor, and NET.SESS.reconnect has no contributors. Per docs/00, input-only families must not link replication. So in lockstep and rollback configurations, late-join baseline and reconnect have no contract path to the skill that owns the command stream and C-SNAPSHOT-based restore. Start-frame and input-delay agreement also has no contract path. The milestones need a two-instance lockstep or rollback session. That makes this a real coordination gap for autonomous agents and not a style point.

It is not out of scope. docs/06 B10/B27 and docs/00 record the split by netcode family but no decision against this link. The proposal is technically sound. C-NETSESSION is layer 3, the same layer as C-PREDICT, which prediction-rollback provides, so check.py's no-upward-link rule holds. net-session does not consume C-PREDICT, so no cycle. Adding the contributors and rewording the capability is low-risk. One option is to add C-SNAPSHOT? to net-session, or simply accept prediction-rollback as the intermediary.

Minor is the right severity. It is a missing edge and contributor list, not a broken proof, and check.py passes with 0 errors.

The gap is real. The NET.SESS capabilities (handshake, join, baseline, reconnect, travel, disconnect, host-mode, auth) assume one player per connection. GAM.FW.local-players ("Local players & split-screen at gameplay level", owned by gameplay-architect with input-system), PLAT.SVC.user-model (guests), and the per-local-player UI/view contracts all cover the local side only. Nothing owns per-local-player sub-IDs, per-player auth or guest privileges on one connection, or per-player command streams. NET.PRED.input-commands carries C-INPUT frames per connection and does not mention sub-players.

It is not out of scope. docs/06 section C and docs/00 record no decision excluding online split-screen. docs/00 splits netcode by lifecycle and puts join and auth in net-session, so net-session is the right owner. The finding is within K-NET's mandate (online and multiplayer architecture, sessions, authority).

The proposal is sound. The owner and contributors fit (gameplay-architect for local-players, platform-services for guest and user identity, input-system for the command format). Adding replication or prediction-rollback as contributors would help, but leaving them out does not make the proposal wrong. K-GAMEPLAY filed the same gap independently, which supports it.

Minor severity fits. This is an omission of one capability in a common but not universal feature. It does not break any existing contract.

The finding is confirmed against the data. All ten skills exist in skills.json, and none of them is in K-NET.scope. The subtree:network-architect entry only covers network-transport, replication, prediction-rollback, dedicated-server, net-session and server-scaleout-persistence. The evidence is accurate: PHY.ARCH.stepping is owned by physics-architect and is literally "Variable-timestep stepping on the render frame delta & frame sync", a stance that clashes with rollback. The other skills also own net-relevant capabilities: PHY.ARCH.determinism and PHY.ARCH.multi-world (server density), PHY.2D.determinism, CORE.FRAME.headless (server tick model), PRF.NET.bandwidth/server-density/latency in online-performance (which measures against NET.ARCH.budgets), PLAT.SRV.* (contributed by dedicated-server), AUD.DSP.voip/voice-jitter (packet-loss concealment), platform-web's browser transport constraints, and XC.EXT.mod-compat (version compatibility is an explicit K-NET check). None of this is covered under another name. K-SIM reviews physics and crowd skills and K-SEC reviews modding-ugc, but only for their own domains, not netcode. check.py only proves that every skill has some domain critic, not that netcode-relevant stances reach K-NET. The weakest additions are rigid-body-dynamics and crowd-simulation (only indirect relevance through solver determinism and replication cost), but the core deficiency holds, and minor severity is appropriate.

The facts check out: none of the ten skills is in K-NET.scope, and PHY.ARCH.stepping ("Variable-timestep stepping on the render frame delta") is owned by physics-architect. But the stated evidence does not show a material coverage gap, and the proposed change is not sound as written. (1) The stepping stance is already reviewed by two critics. K-SIM covers subtree:physics-architect and its first check is "stepping and sync with frame phases are explicit". K-LEGACY has scope "all", and data/legacy-patterns.json lists "Frame-coupled variable-timestep simulation" as a catalogued pattern. Its netcode consequences also land on skills K-NET already reviews: prediction-rollback sits in subtree:network-architect, and determinism-replay and simulation-validation are named in K-NET's scope. So the example does not fall through review. If the real complaint is that the stance itself is wrong, that is a finding against the capability, not against critic scope. (2) The proposal adds ten skills in one block and gives evidence for only one. For several of them the netcode link is not argued: audio-dsp-mixing, platform-web, modding-ugc (already covered by K-SEC and K-GAMEPLAY), physics-2d and frame-orchestration. Adding them would dilute a blind critic's mandate. Two additions have a plausible case that the finding never makes: online-performance, which analyses bandwidth against network budgets and so matches K-NET's "bandwidth and scale budgets" check, and platform-server-host. Neither is part of the evidence, and check.py does not require netcode-critic coverage beyond a single domain critic per skill, which every skill already has. Minor severity would be right if the finding held, but as argued and proposed it is not a material defect.

Confirmed in data/capabilities.json around line 5590. PHY.ARCH.stepping is literally "Variable-timestep stepping on the render frame delta & frame sync" (physics-architect, E, contributor frame-orchestration). That restates the L30 legacy pattern ("Frame-coupled variable-timestep simulation", detection "simulation stepped by render delta") as an established default, which contradicts L30's stance. L30.stance_capabilities lists only CORE.FRAME.fixed-step ("Fixed-step simulation with interpolation"). CORE.FRAME.fixed-step is generic and belongs to the frame layer. The C-FRAME contract mentions "multi-rate cadences", so frame-level cadences are partly covered. But nothing covers physics solver sub-steps, per-subsystem physics sub-rates (tires, cloth), catch-up clamps or the interpolation hand-off. A grep for tire, sub-rate, substep and multi-rate finds no such capability; the tire mentions are only vehicle features, tools and validation. None of K-SIM's four checks is "no simulation stepped by render delta". check.py only proves that the stance capabilities named by legacy patterns exist. It does not detect a capability that contradicts a legacy stance. The deficiency is real and not covered elsewhere. Severity "major" is justified because the physics lead's core stepping capability endorses an anti-pattern that breaks determinism and resim.

The finding holds and "major" is the right severity. In data/capabilities.json (around L5590), PHY.ARCH.stepping is literally "Variable-timestep stepping on the render frame delta & frame sync", marked E, owned by physics-architect with frame-orchestration as contributor. That restates the anti-pattern that legacy pattern L30 in data/legacy-patterns.json lists as "Frame-coupled variable-timestep simulation" (detection: "simulation stepped by render delta"). It also contradicts CORE.FRAME.fixed-step and the C-PHYS resimulate conformance / C-DET determinism levels.

Why this matters: agents build from capability text, so the physics lead would be told to implement the legacy pattern as the established default. That is a real correctness defect, not a style point.

Scope and mandate: the change is inside K-SIM's mandate, since its first check is "stepping and sync with frame phases are explicit". Searching docs/ for timestep/stepping turned up no scope decision that keeps variable timestep. Section C of docs/06 and docs/00 were not opened directly.

The proposed fix is technically sound and consistent with check.py:
- frame-orchestration already contributes to PHY.ARCH.stepping (docs/03 L803).
- Adding PHY.ARCH.stepping to L30.stance_capabilities passes the rule that the justification owner must own, contribute to or lead the stance caps.
- The K-SIM check wording matches L30's detection text.
- Sub-steps, sub-rates, catch-up clamps and interpolation hand-off are standard practice and are not covered elsewhere. PHY.ARCH.async covers decoupled stepping but not sub-rates.

One weak spot: the claim that "nothing owns sub-stepping" is somewhat overstated given PHY.ARCH.async. That does not change the verdict.

The core claim checks out against the data. milestones.json freezes C-PHYS, C-MOVE, C-PREDICT and C-ENV at M2. collision-detection, rigid-body-dynamics, character-physics, vehicle-physics, terrain, water-ocean and atmosphere-weather first appear in M3, and dedicated-server in M4. The C-PHYS summary does list collider history for rewind, world instances, local simulation spaces and character controllers. check.py (lines 338-351 and the docstring) only requires that the owner and at least one consumer are built before a freeze, and that the contract's requirements are not frozen later. It has no rule about named implementers or oracle authors being present. I found no contract-versioning or extension-contract mechanism in the data (searched "breaking", "additive", "revision" and "extension contract"), so nothing already covers this.

The freeze problem is worse than the finding says. C-ENV's oracle author, collision-detection, and C-MOVE's oracle author, motion-synthesis, both arrive only at M3. So those conformance oracles are frozen before their authors exist.

Some details are inaccurate but do not change the verdict:
(a) C-PHYS has no implementers at all; physics-architect provides it. physics-2d only consumes it and is not the "only implementer".
(b) One of the four C-ENV implementers, voxel-worlds, arrives at M2, and fluid-simulation (a C-PHYS consumer) also arrives at M2. So not all C-ENV providers arrive at M3.
(c) The frozen features are not all without a consumer. character-movement, a C-PHYS consumer since M1, uses the character controllers, and prediction-rollback (M1) uses the rewind features.

The substance holds: the 3D and server consumers of the frozen surface are absent at freeze, and check.py does not catch this. Major severity is reasonable.

The data backs the finding. In data/milestones.json, M2 freezes C-PHYS, C-MOVE, C-PREDICT and C-ENV. The only physics implementer available by then is physics-2d (M1). collision-detection, rigid-body-dynamics, character-physics, vehicle-physics, terrain, water-ocean and atmosphere-weather arrive at M3, and dedicated-server arrives at M4. The C-PHYS summary names collider history for rewind, world instances, local simulation spaces and character controllers, so the frozen surface covers features no 2D implementer has built or used. It is worse than the critic says: C-ENV's oracle author (collision-detection) and C-MOVE's oracle author (motion-synthesis) both arrive at M3, after the freeze. So the named oracle authors cannot write the conformance suites that check the frozen contracts, and check.py (lines 528-530) checks only that an oracle author is valid, not when it arrives. For a framework that coordinates autonomous agents, freezing a contract before its implementers and its oracle exist forces breaking change requests later, through C-ORCH/C-API, for every M2 consumer. That makes this a material dependency error, not a style point. Nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 records a decision to freeze before implementers arrive. docs/06 C4 ("may be built") is about which skills a configuration includes, not when contracts freeze. The proposed fix is sound: either delay the freezes or split 3D extension contracts that freeze at M3/M4, and add a rule that every named implementer class must have arrived first. The rule is also checkable by machine. Two minor overreaches do not undermine the finding. First, voxel-worlds, a C-ENV provider, does arrive at M2. Second, moving C-PREDICT all the way to M4 is debatable, because rollback is already shown at M2 by fighting-2d. However, lag compensation and server rewind do depend on M4 skills, and the split option covers this. Major is the right severity.

The data confirms the finding. In data/contracts.json, the C-PHYS summary (owner physics-architect, workstream simulation, oracle_author gameplay-architect) includes 'character controllers (movement modes, move requests, root-motion hand-off)'. The C-MOVE summary (owner character-movement, workstream gameplay, oracle_author motion-synthesis) is 'Movement modes, move requests, resimulatable move API, root-motion hand-off.' So the same API appears under two owners, in two workstreams, with two oracle authors, and both have conformance set to true. character-physics lists 'Movement modes & networked movement' as a non-responsibility that belongs to character-movement. The capability registry gives GAM.MOVE.modes and GAM.MOVE.root-motion only to character-movement. check.py only checks for duplicate ids, not for overlapping text in contract summaries, so nothing in the checks already proves this. The proposed fix matches what character-physics is for ('Character controllers (kinematic and dynamic), moving platforms and physical interaction'). Rating it major is reasonable, since two conformance suites would be testing the same surface.

The finding is confirmed in the data. In data/contracts.json, C-PHYS (owner physics-architect, oracle gameplay-architect, conformance true) includes "character controllers (movement modes, move requests, root-motion hand-off)". C-MOVE (owner character-movement, oracle motion-synthesis, conformance true) covers "Movement modes, move requests, resimulatable move API, root-motion hand-off". So the same API surface sits in two conformance-tested contracts, with different owners, different oracle authors and different workstreams (simulation vs gameplay). The C-PHYS wording also contradicts the rest of the data: character-physics lists "Movement modes & networked movement" as a non-responsibility belonging to character-movement, and character-movement owns GAM.MOVE.modes and GAM.MOVE.root-motion. It also lists "Collide-and-slide controller primitive" as a non-responsibility belonging to character-physics. The proposed change matches that split and the production split (Jolt CharacterVirtual and PhysX CCT vs UE CharacterMovement/Mover), so it is technically sound. It is within K-SIM's mandate (physics boundaries). No recorded scope decision in docs/06 or docs/00 conflicts with it: those only confirm character-movement as an engine skill. Major is right: the protocol defines major as a wrong boundary that would cause rework, and here it would produce conflicting API definitions and duplicate oracles. It is not quite the "two owners" blocker, because capability ownership (GAM.MOVE.*) is unambiguous and only the contract summary overlaps.

This is not a material defect, and the main proposed change does not fit how the framework works.

1. **needs_implementer does not fit.** In this framework, needs_implementer means a contract must have a backend on every platform. check.py (lines ~269-276) verifies an implementer for each platform in each configuration. It is used for C-PAL, C-RHI and C-TARGETPLAT, whose backends really do differ by platform. Physics backends differ by profile or by a one-time build-vs-integrate decision instead. That decision is recorded as an ADR (docs/06 B6 and B23, PHY.ARCH.build-integrate, PHY.ARCH.middleware-layer), and it picks one backend per engine, not per platform. Profile membership already puts a backend in every configuration that uses physics: physics-2d is in min2d, and rigid-body-dynamics and collision-detection are in lite3d/std3d. Adding needs_implementer would add a platform check with nothing to prove.

2. **Implementers consuming the contract is the house pattern.** Owner-provides plus sub-skill-consumes is used for layer-3 subsystem contracts such as C-ANIM and C-AUDIO too. At most this is a naming nicety.

3. **The 2.5D claim is wrong.** Planar 2.5D simulation is covered by PHY.DYN.dof-lock ("Planar / DOF-locked simulation (2.5D)"), owned by rigid-body-dynamics in lite3d/std3d. The seed-map entry for 2.5D games is render-focused. No physics2d add-on is needed.

4. **Boundary and test double is a nice-to-have.** Boundary contracts in this framework cover platform, first-party service, allocator and GPU edges. A scripted kinematic physics double is a reasonable testing suggestion, but its absence does not stop agents from coordinating correctly. C-PHYS already has a restore-and-resimulate conformance suite and determinism levels. Treating C-PHYS dimensionality as a world-creation parameter is a design preference.

(4) UGC meshes arrive as registered hostile inputs 'mods' (modding-ugc) or 'assets' (serialization-schema, limits size/depth/count). The only gap left is an explicit check for degenerate geometry and extents on UGC meshes, which is much narrower than what the finding states. I don't think this finding holds as a material defect. The registry lists hostile data that crosses a trust boundary, and each entry has a parser. Collision geometry is not such an input. It is built on the server from data that already has an entry with limits. Remote voxel and construction edits arrive as input-commands or replicated-state (hostile-remote, with rate/tick-window and count/depth/rate limits). UGC meshes arrive as mods or assets (size/depth/count, validated by modding-ugc and serialization-schema). Voxel chunk meshes are well-formed by construction and bounded per chunk, so the real denial-of-service lever is how often and how many edits a player can make. NET.SRV.budgets covers that explicitly ("limits on client-triggered work"), and PHY.COL.runtime-build is already defined as "async and budgeted". So the claim that there is "no validating owner or limits" overstates the gap. The proposal is also unsound as written: voxel-worlds and modding-ugc would not parse "runtime-collision-geometry", so listing them as parser_owners misuses the field. And registering a derived data product as an input class blurs the registry's one-validator-per-boundary model. There is a small leftover point: collision cooking should be robust to degenerate or oversized UGC meshes (a fuzz and limit concern). That fits better as a limit on the existing mods/assets entries or as a note on the PHY.COL.runtime-build budget than as a new entry. The minor severity is right for what remains.

The finding is correct. critics.json K-SIM.scope is subtree:physics-architect plus 11 named skills, and neither gameplay-systems-toolkit nor navigation-pathfinding is among them. Other critics do cover them: K-GAMEPLAY through subtree:gameplay-architect, and K-NET, which lists gameplay-systems-toolkit by name. Neither of those critics has any simulation or determinism checks, so the gap is real, and check.py only proves that every skill has some domain critic. The evidence is also accurate. GAM.SYS.projectiles is owned by gameplay-systems-toolkit and reads "batched sweeps... predicted projectiles, server-side rewind validation", with contributors prediction-rollback and physics-architect. GAM.AI.local-avoidance ("Local avoidance (ORCA/RVO)") is owned by navigation-pathfinding. Both skills consume C-DET? (optional), and C-SIGNIF exists as a contract with a tier-transition protocol. On the checks: K-SIM's current list is "stepping and sync with frame phases are explicit", "determinism levels are declared", "simulation LOD exists for large scales" and "build-vs-integrate evidence". I checked the finding against data/critics.json and the docs, and it is correct. K-SIM's mandate covers "determinism of simulation", "crowds" and "large-scale simulation". The finding checks out against the data. In data/contracts.json, C-EDCMD is layer 5 (tool), owned by editor-architect, requires C-REFL, C-SER and C-IPC, and its summary is "Serializable, diff-based commands and transactions, undo/redo scopes... journal feed for recovery and multi-user". C-EDIT is layer 4, owned by modding-ugc, requires only C-SER, C-ID and C-FRAME, and its summary says "schema shared with C-EDCMD per ED.ARCH.transactions". C-EDIT cannot require C-EDCMD, because the layering rule in check.py forbids upward dependencies and check.py line 613 also rejects runtime code consuming a tool contract. So the "shared" schema has no reachable home. I found no layer-2 or layer-3 contract that covers commands, undo, journal or diffs: C-SER is "Formats, versioning, upgraders, canonical form, untrusted-input rules"; C-ECS "command buffers" and C-AUTOMATION are unrelated; C-VCS diff/merge is layer 5. No CORE.SER.commands capability or C-CMD contract exists. ED.ARCH.transactions is owned by editor-architect with contributors modding-ugc, collaboration-version-control and serialization-schema, but its only contract home is the layer-5 C-EDCMD. The milestone claim is right: C-EDCMD is drafted at M2 and frozen at M3, and C-EDIT is drafted at M4 and frozen at M5. check.py proves nothing about the cross-layer schema sharing. Rating it major is justified, since the likely result is two diverging undo/journal systems for the editor and runtime creation (XC.EXT.player-creation), plus multi-user editing (ED.COLLAB.multiuser) built on a tool-only journal.

The data confirms the finding. C-EDIT is layer 4, owned by modding-ugc, and requires C-SER, C-ID and C-FRAME. Its summary says its commands have a "schema shared with C-EDCMD per ED.ARCH.transactions". C-EDCMD is layer 5, owned by editor-architect, and requires C-REFL, C-SER and C-IPC. ED.ARCH.transactions is an editor-architect capability; modding-ugc, collaboration-version-control and serialization-schema only contribute to it. Neither docs/06 section C nor docs/00 records a scope decision that rules out a shared runtime command core. docs/09 L38 and the diff-based stance in C-EDCMD's summary back the direction.

This is a real wrong-boundary defect. Autonomous agents building modding-ugc and editor-architect would be left with parallel, divergent transaction systems, which is rework and silent drift. That matches the protocol's definition of "major", so the severity is right.

The fix is technically sound. A layer-2 C-CMD that requires C-SER, C-REFL and C-ID (all layer 2) is layer-legal. serialization-schema already provides C-SER at layer 2, so it is a sensible owner, whereas editor-architect is tool-side. Having both C-EDCMD and C-EDIT require C-CMD resolves the boundary. One small point: once C-CMD is frozen first, the extra condition "freeze C-EDCMD no earlier than C-EDIT's draft" is arguably unnecessary and would push the M3 editor freeze back. The data confirms the finding. In data/milestones.json, M1 contracts_frozen lists C-ASSET, C-COOK and C-TARGETPLAT, each drafted at M0. C-TARGETPLAT (needs_implementer, layer 5; summary covers cook format variants, the shader backend compiler hook, the packager and deploy/launch/debug on device) has these implementers: platform-desktop (M0), platform-console, platform-mobile and platform-web (all M2), and platform-server-host (M4). Its tool consumers are content-pipeline-architect (M0) and packaging-release-patching (M2). So at freeze the only implementer is desktop, and the packaging consumer arrives at M2. The M3 exit does require "on-device iteration to console and mobile". check.py (lines ~336-351) only proves that each contract is frozen once, after its owner and at least one consumer, and not before the contracts it requires. One imprecision: not every world-scope cook builder comes later. world-architect, procedural-generation and navigation-pathfinding are at M1 and tool-consume C-COOK. I checked this against data/contracts.json and data/milestones.json by comparing each skill's arrival milestone with each contract's contracts_frozen milestone. Exactly 29 frozen contracts have an oracle_author that arrives after the freeze, which matches the "about 29" in the finding. The four named examples are all correct: C-ASSET (frozen M1, ai-assisted-authoring arrives M6), C-SER (M1, collaboration-version-control M2), C-TEXT (M1, editor-ui-framework M2) and C-REPLAY (M1, physics-tools M2). C-SIGN (frozen M0), C-SPATIAL (M1), C-WORLD (M2) and C-SCRIPT (M2) all have oracles arriving at M4. check.py does not prove this: its oracle rule only requires the oracle_author to differ from the sole implementer, and its freeze rule only covers the owner, a consumer and requirements. Nothing requires the oracle to be present at freeze. docs/00 and docs/02 say acceptance suites are written by the oracle author, and docs/09 L56 says "tests before features", so the inversion goes against what the framework says it wants and is not covered elsewhere. Rating it major is reasonable because it affects the oracle-independence gate across the whole framework.

The core concern is real for C-TARGETPLAT. It is a needs_implementer contract (data/contracts.json) frozen at M1 while its only built implementer is platform-desktop (M0). platform-console, platform-mobile and platform-web arrive at M2, platform-server-host at M4, and packaging-release-patching at M2. The M3 exit requires on-device iteration to console and mobile. Freezing a device-deploy interface shaped by one platform is a material coordination hazard, and "major" is a fair severity for that part. It is not a style point, and nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 records a reasoned decision to freeze it early. Section C item 1 (NDA) covers filling the content, not when to freeze. Moving C-COOK and C-TARGETPLAT later is also sound: no contract frozen before M3 requires them, and C-VCS (M3) requires only C-ASSET.

The proposed change fails as written, though. It moves C-ASSET to M3, but check.py's rule "never before the contracts it requires" would then break. C-RES (layer 2, frozen M1), C-LOC (M2) and C-GAMEDATA (M2) all require C-ASSET. Following the proposal would either fail check.py or force a cascade: C-RES would have to move too, and many M1 rendering and runtime contracts sit downstream of it. The finding does not acknowledge any of this.

The case for C-ASSET is also weak. It is a layer-2 runtime contract (asset IDs and references), consumed by C-RES and runtime skills from M1. The arrival of the importer and editor is not evidence that asset identity needs to wait. Also, the importer and editor arrive at M2, not M2–M3.

The proposed rule "a layer-5 contract freezes only after a tool-side consumer has arrived" is vague. C-COOK already has a tool-side consumer, asset-cook-processors, from M0. Because the change as proposed is technically unsound and needs rework before anyone could apply it, holds=false. A narrower fix would be sound: move C-TARGETPLAT (and optionally C-COOK) to M2 or M3, and add a check requiring two implementers of different platform classes for needs_implementer contracts.

I checked the finding against the data files and it is factually correct.

- **Only four skills consume C-RELOAD.** In data/skills.json the only consumers are ecs-runtime, world-data-model, shader-system and scripting-runtime, all as the optional C-RELOAD?. hot-reload-iteration provides it.
- **All 13 named skills exist, and none of them declares C-RELOAD** in consumes or tool_consumes. Every one is kind runtime. Only some consume C-ASSET or C-RES, which give generic resource plumbing, not per-domain rebuilding of derived state.
- **C-RELOAD is not implicitly consumed by every skill.** Its entry in data/contracts.json has no 'universal' field, so it does not reach these skills by default.
- **Reload has no owned capability in these domains under another name.** The only reload capabilities are RES.MGMT.reload (resource-streaming), RND.SHADER.reload (shader-system), GAM.SCR.reload (scripting-runtime) and the four XC.ITER.* entries. RND.TOOL.material-editor mentions 'live update', but that is editor-tool preview, not a runtime reload path.
- **Ownership is as the finding says.** hot-reload-iteration's non-responsibilities hand 'Each system's own reload implementation (via C-RELOAD)' to the owning skill.
- **M3 does gate on iteration latency.** Its exit criteria in milestones.json require 'iteration-latency targets met'.
- **check.py does not already prove this.** Neither its docstring nor its code has a rule about C-RELOAD consumption.

One partial mitigation: crosscutting.json has a prose-only 'hot reload' obligation ('Declare what reloads live and how state is preserved.'). Nothing in the data records how any skill meets it, and no check enforces it, so it does not cover the gap. 'Cannot be met by construction' is slightly overstated, since the crosscutting obligation could in principle be met in prose. Even so, a missing contract edge across 13 content domains, tied to an M3 exit gate, justifies the major rating.

The facts check out against data/*.json. Exactly 29 frozen contracts have an oracle_author whose milestone comes after the freeze. C-ASSET freezes at M1 and its oracle, ai-assisted-authoring, arrives at M6. C-SER, C-TEXT and C-REPLAY freeze at M1 with oracles at M2. C-SIGN freezes at M0 with modding-ugc at M4. check.py only checks that a contract is frozen after its owner and one consumer; it never checks when the oracle author arrives.

The facts check out in data/capabilities.json. WLD.PART.grid, WLD.PART.sources and WLD.PART.hlod carry [lite3d, std3d], and ED.WORLD.partitioned ("Partition-aware world editing & loading", owned by world-editor-viewport with world-architect) carries only [openworld]. The same holds for C-PAL: platform-mobile alone covers iOS, Android and visionOS.

The current data happens to include all the backends, so nothing is broken today. What is broken is the proof. The docstring and docs/00 line 64 claim closure "for each of its platforms", and that proof passes falsely at the level where agents would actually lose a backend. The selftest only mutates the web family. The same gap applies to console holders: docs/00 line 115 says rhi-console is "instantiated per platform holder", but no holder instances exist as data, so no proof can reach them.

For a framework whose agents rely on check.py to know a configuration is buildable, that is material. It fits the protocol's definition of major: rework, or a silent missing backend.

No recorded scope decision blocks it. docs/06 section C lists no platform-granularity limit. C.4 ("may be built") is about using members, not about the implementer proof. docs/00 line 72 only lists the families, with no reasoning against finer granularity.

The proposed change is sound and fits the existing model. Variants default to all, implementers declare which variants they cover, and the per-variant loop replaces the per-family loop. Sealed holder ids match the NDA access classes. Generating ARCH.REQ.platform-matrix from the data is feasible.

Major is the right severity, and missing-contract is the right type.

I checked the finding against data/milestones.json, data/contracts.json and scripts/check.py, and it holds. In M0, C-PAL is in contracts_frozen, and the only platform/RHI skills present are platform-architect, platform-desktop, rhi-core and rhi-vulkan. In M1, C-RHI, C-IO, C-PRESENT, C-DEVICE, C-GPUTIER and C-TARGETPLAT are frozen, and the only platform/RHI skills added are platform-services, rhi-d3d12 and rhi-metal. platform-console, platform-mobile, platform-web, rhi-console and rhi-webgpu all arrive at M2. C-RHI declares platforms pc/console/mobile/web/xr-standalone, and C-PAL, C-RHI and C-TARGETPLAT are all marked needs_implementer. The freeze check in check.py (lines 330-351) only requires that the owner and some consumer are built by the freeze milestone, and that the contract's requirements are not frozen later. It has no rule about platform-family implementers or spikes. The data has no freeze_reviewer or conformance-spike mechanism either. ARCH.EVID.spike exists only as a general capability and is not tied to freezes. Some contract summaries mention non-desktop concerns by name: C-RHI lists bind-group and implicit-sync backends, and C-PAL lists a suspend/resume quiesce protocol. That is design intent written into the text, not proof against a real implementer, so it does not already cover the finding. One detail is slightly overstated: C-RHI's freeze is checked against D3D12 and Metal as well as Vulkan, not 'Windows/Vulkan only'. It is still desktop-only, so the core claim stands. Major is an appropriate severity for freezing platform contracts before their web, mobile and console implementers exist.

Confirmed against the data. In capabilities.json, PLAT.WEB.runtime reads word for word "WASM threads (SharedArrayBuffer required; cross-origin isolation assumed on every host) & memory limits" (owner platform-web, contributor job-system-task-graph). The PLAT.WEB area has runtime, storage, delivery, gestures, webgpu-target, pal and std3d. None of these covers a non-isolated or single-threaded variant, COOP/COEP detection, or hosting modes. The only "hosting modes" capability is the network one (dedicated/listen/P2P). CORE.JOBS.degenerate exists as described: a 0-2 worker inline/cooperative mode, with platform-web as a contributor. That supports the finding that the mechanism exists but nothing ties it to a web build variant. BLD.SYS.configs lists only debug/development/test/profile/shipping, with no web-nonisolated variant. The platform-web purpose says "threads and cross-origin isolation", which again assumes isolation. Searches for audioworklet, isolation detection and 0-worker/no-threads found nothing else covering this. minimal-client and indie-2d-client include web among their platforms, and indie-2d-online-web-client is web-only. The M2 exit says "indie-2d ships on ... web" with no requirement for non-isolated hosts. check.py only checks that each platform has an implementer and does not prove anything about threading or isolation. Major severity is reasonable: the smallest web configurations would fail to run on common hosts that cannot set COOP/COEP.

The data backs the finding. In data/milestones.json, C-PAL freezes at M0, where the only platform and RHI build skills are platform-architect, platform-desktop, rhi-core and rhi-vulkan. C-RHI, C-IO, C-PRESENT, C-DEVICE, C-GPUTIER and C-TARGETPLAT freeze at M1, which adds only rhi-d3d12, rhi-metal and platform-services. platform-console, platform-mobile, platform-web, rhi-console and rhi-webgpu all arrive at M2. The freeze rule that check.py enforces (lines 338-351) checks only the owner, one consumer and requirement order.

The finding is material. PLAT.PAL.lifecycle and PLAT.PAL.thread-affinity name platform-console and platform-mobile as collaborators. Both skills arrive two milestones after C-PAL freezes, so the declared co-designers of the suspend/resume quiesce protocol cannot review it before the freeze. The framework already uses the pattern the finding asks for elsewhere: M1 has network design authorities "review every freeze", and C-RHI's tensor tier is "reviewed by ml-inference-runtime before freeze". So adding a platform review is consistent with the framework's own rules, not a style preference. Nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 records a decision to freeze platform contracts against desktop only. C.1 (NDA parameters) says console skills can be structured now, which supports a conformance spike rather than ruling one out.

One factual correction: coverage at M1 is not Windows/Vulkan only, since D3D12 and Metal also land there. Both are still desktop-class backends with explicit sync, so web, mobile and console constraints remain unproven. The main proposal (a check rule that requires an implementer or a recorded conformance spike per claimed platform family, plus a console spike as a freeze reviewer) is sound and fits the existing check.py structure.

The alternative (deferring the C-PAL/C-RHI freezes to M2) is weaker than stated. The "never before its requirements" rule would force a cascade: every M0/M1 contract that requires C-PAL or C-RHI, such as C-TASK, C-IO and C-RG, would also have to move. The primary proposal carries the finding.

Major is the right severity rather than critical. The C-ORCH change-request process and C-API versioning give a path to amend a frozen contract. Even so, reworking 30-consumer interfaces after two milestones of dependent work is a significant coordination failure for autonomous agents.

Confirmed in data/capabilities.json: PLAT.WEB.runtime reads "WASM threads (SharedArrayBuffer required; cross-origin isolation assumed on every host) & memory limits", with owner platform-web and job-system-task-graph as the only contributor. That wording contradicts CORE.JOBS.degenerate ("Shipping inline/cooperative mode: the same task graph on 0–2 workers ...") and docs/00 ("The same graph runs inline on 0–2 workers (web, low-end)"). BLD.SYS.configs lists only debug/development/test/profile/shipping, with no threads-off variant. The M2 exit requires indie-2d to ship on web, but no gate checks a non-isolated host. docs/06 and docs/00 record no scope decision that makes COI mandatory; the listed non-goals are GLES/WebGL, not single-threaded WASM. So this is not an out-of-scope request. Seven critics raised the same point independently (K-ARCH, K-SEC, K-FUTURE, K-LEGACY, K-PERF, K-SYSTEMS, K-PLATFORM). The defect is material: agents following this text would build a web target that does not start on portals and iframe/ad-embedded hosts, which is where the indie-2d and online-web configurations ship. The finding sits within K-PLATFORM's platform mandate. The proposal is technically sound: a threaded WASM binary cannot degrade at runtime, so a separate non-threaded build variant plus load-time detection (crossOriginIsolated) is the right shape, and audio without SAB is a real sub-issue. One nit: a "web-nonisolated" variant arguably belongs in the platform/target configuration axis (C-TARGETPLAT) rather than BLD.SYS.configs, whose entries are optimization/instrumentation levels. That is a placement quibble and does not undermine the proposal. Major severity fits: it breaks a stated target configuration without affecting the whole framework.

The finding checks out. In data/capabilities.json, BLD.REL.staged-rollout is named "Simultaneous global rollout to all players with post-release kill switches". It is owned by packaging-release-patching and online-services-liveops is its only contributor. Milestone M4 in data/milestones.json lists this capability, and its exit criterion says "patch + DLC + staged rollout + rollback executed on the online reference game". So the M4 gate would pass an all-at-once release.

Nothing else in the data covers staged exposure. No capability mentions percentage or phased rollout, halt criteria or canary release; the only "canary" hit is about critic calibration. The rolling-server-deploy capabilities (compatibility window, server drain) handle server fleets, not staging player exposure.

check.py only verifies that ids quoted in capability names exist. It does not check whether a name means what it says, so it cannot catch this.

All four proposed contributors (online-services-liveops, platform-services, dedicated-server, crash-diagnostics) exist as skills. Rating it major is reasonable because the capability contradicts its own name and a milestone gate relies on it.

I confirmed this in data/capabilities.json. BLD.REL.staged-rollout (owner packaging-release-patching, only contributor online-services-liveops) is defined as "Simultaneous global rollout to all players with post-release kill switches". data/milestones.json lists it as an M4 gate, and the M4 exit requires a "staged rollout ... executed on the online reference game". The definition says the opposite of the id and of the exit criterion, and it states the all-at-once release that the framework is supposed to guard against. An agent that satisfies the text literally would pass the gate with a big-bang release. For a framework that coordinates autonomous agents, that is a real, material defect, not a style point. I found no recorded scope decision in docs/00 or docs/06 that justifies the global-rollout wording, so the finding contradicts no reasoned scope choice. It sits within K-PLATFORM's mandate: store phased release, the fact that console patches cannot be percentage-staged, and the fallback to server-side flags are platform matters. The proposed change is technically sound. Phased release per channel, with flag gating where the store cannot stage, halt criteria from crash data and telemetry, and kill switches, matches real practice on Play, the App Store and Steam and with server canaries. All four proposed contributors (online-services-liveops, platform-services, dedicated-server, crash-diagnostics) exist in data/skills.json. Major severity fits: the defect sits on a milestone gate and inverts what that gate validates. It is not critical, because the id, the M4 exit text and the kill switches partly limit the damage. Other critics (K-ARCH, K-SEC, K-TEST, K-PROD) report the same problem, but that does not reduce its materiality.

The data matches the finding. In data/capabilities.json, PLAT.PAL.cloud-streaming ("Cloud-streaming targets (latency, encode, input)") is maturity M and owned only by platform-architect, with no contributors listed. In data/radar.json, the "Cloud game streaming targets" entry is class M, cites GeForce NOW and xCloud as its evidence, and has the fallback "Treat as a PC target". Calling the capability M when the radar's own evidence cites services shipping since 2020 looks like a real maturity error.
