I confirmed the finding in the data. In data/capabilities.json, PLAT.PAL.cloud-streaming is maturity M, owned by platform-architect, with no contributors. In data/radar.json it is class M, and its fallback is "Treat as a PC target". The radar entry's own evidence already cites shipping services (GeForce NOW, xCloud). Nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 records a scope decision that keeps cloud streaming out or experimental, so no reasoned decision is being overturned.

The defect is material because the fallback is wrong for the largest services. Xbox Cloud Gaming and PlayStation stream console builds, so an agent following "treat as PC" would miss the console-package obligations: streaming-session detection and Touch Adaptation Kit bundles. The engine-side work the finding lists is real and has no owner. That covers touch overlays, the legibility/UI-scale tier, encode latency within the input-to-photon budget, and device changes mid-session. It sits in skills other than the PAL lead's.

The finding is within K-PLATFORM's mandate: platforms and packaging, with scope covering the platform-architect subtree.

The proposal is technically sound:
- check.py only requires non-established capabilities to be on the radar, so moving to E and removing (or reclassifying) the entry passes.
- The PLAT.CON.* and PLAT.DESK.* namespaces already exist.
- The named contributors (input-system, ui-architect, runtime-scalability, frame-orchestration) all exist in skills.json.

One part is weak but secondary: the "cloud variant" depends on K-PLATFORM-2. It arguably fits better as a deployment or packaging mode, because xCloud runs the console build. Major is the right severity: this is a wrong maturity class, a misleading fallback and unowned platform obligations, not a gate or blocker failure.

Some of the finding's structural statements are true. C-SVC is not needs_implementer: only C-PAL, C-RHI and C-TARGETPLAT are. Only platform-console lists C-SVC under implements. No configuration in skills.json has a storefront axis. The core claim, that store and service SDK backends have no owner and no closure proof, does not hold up against the data. platform-services has platforms=null, so it covers every platform, and profiles=["all"], so it is in every configuration. It provides C-SVC and owns the store-backend capabilities PLAT.SVC.entitlements ("Entitlements, store, DLC ownership"), identity, achievements, leaderboards, cloud-save, trials and first-party-emulation. Its purpose covers "entitlements and commerce through first-party stores", and its expertise lists "platform SDKs". The C-NETLINK summary in contracts.json says platform-SDK transports such as Steam and EOS are "implemented by platform-services and online-services-liveops", and platform-services lists C-NETLINK under implements. Third-party and own backends go to online-services-liveops through platform-services' non_responsibilities. So the Steamworks, EOS and similar backends already have a real owner that sits in every configuration. A per-platform closure proof adds nothing when the provider is platform-agnostic and always present. The evidence also has errors: QA.CERT.store-policy does have platform-services as a contributor, so "no implementer" is wrong. The store dimension is carried as the ARCH.REQ.platform-matrix capability, owned by engine-architect. What remains is a design preference: splitting backends into platform-tagged skills and adding storefront as a configuration axis. That is not a missing contract, so "major, missing-contract" overstates it.

The deficiency exists as described. In data/skills.json, rhi-d3d12 has platforms ['pc'] and its purpose covers only PC D3D12 (Agility SDK). rhi-console (platforms ['console'], access nda:per-platform-holder, one instance per holder) implements C-RHI on "each console graphics API" as an independent backend. RND.RHI.console, -validation and -quirks all sit in rhi-console. No capability, contract summary or skill purpose treats the Xbox backend as a shared D3D12 base with a confidential extension. Searches for superset, shared backend, base backend and similar wording found nothing. PLAT.PAL.confidential-extensions (in platform-architect) is only a generic mechanism for segregated modules and public stubs. It does not assign a D3D12 base to both backends. The C-LEDGER write-set convention (src/<skill-id>/, where contributors review and never write directly) means an NDA agent under rhi-console could not extend rhi-d3d12 code, so duplication and drift is a real risk. On the PAL side, platform-desktop is PC-only and lists Win32/GameInput, while platform-console is a separate NDA skill; nothing shares the GDK runtime between them. The check.py docstring only proves that console-only skills carry an NDA access class and that per-platform closure holds, so this boundary question is not machine-proved. Major severity fits: this is a structural ownership split that causes duplicated implementation of one of the core GPU backends.

The finding rests on "no owner", and that premise is weak. platform-services provides C-SVC and carries no platform tag, so it applies to every platform. Its purpose covers "First-party platform and store services... entitlements and commerce through first-party stores", and it lists "platform SDKs" as expertise. It also owns PLAT.SVC.entitlements ("Entitlements, store, DLC ownership") and PLAT.COMM.iap. platform-architect's non_responsibilities send "Store and online services" to platform-services. C-NETLINK already says Steam/EOS transports are backends implemented by platform-services and online-services-liveops.

platform-console implements C-SVC only because of the NDA access class. Steamworks, EOS, GameKit and Play Billing are public SDKs. So on pc, mobile and web, C-SVC is covered by its cross-platform provider, and the pc/mobile configurations close without a needs_implementer flag. Nothing is actually unowned; the only gap is that the store backends aren't listed by name.

The proposed change is also unsound:
- **Wrong axis.** Store SDKs don't split by OS. Steamworks runs on Windows, Linux, SteamOS and macOS. EOS covers PC, console and mobile. Moving them into platform-desktop, platform-mobile and platform-web would fragment one cross-store entitlement/achievement model across OS-integration skills.
- **Conflicts with a recorded decision.** docs/00 separates first-party platform services from third-party and live-ops backends. EOS/EGS partly belongs to online-services-liveops, which the proposal ignores.
- **Not needed for closure.** A null/DRM-free backend plus needs_implementer would add closure bookkeeping for a contract that already closes.

The one real point is that ARCH.REQ.platform-matrix names store as a dimension that no data carries. QA.CERT.store-policy (whose contributors include platform-services) is also thin on alternative stores. That is a minor gap worth a note on the matrix or configurations. It is not a major missing contract.

The finding is material and within the critic's mandate, and the proposal is technically sound, though it depends on K-PLATFORM-1.

Facts check out in data/skills.json. rhi-d3d12 has platforms ["pc"], no access class, and implements C-RHI. rhi-console has platforms ["console"], access nda:per-platform-holder, and implements C-RHI "on each console graphics API". platform-desktop (Win32/GameInput, pc) and platform-console (NDA, console) both implement C-PAL on their own. scripts/check.py lines 236-239 forbid an NDA class on any skill not tagged console-only. So the framework cannot express a confidential extension of a PC skill, and the only way to model the Xbox-class D3D12 backend is a second, independent NDA agent that re-implements D3D12. Given the stated bar (autonomous agents with strict write sets), that means duplicated backend code with no shared owner, plus drift in barriers, PSOs, DXC integration and quirks. That is a real structural defect, not a style preference.

Scope: docs/06 section C does not record a decision on this; its item 1 is only about NDA parameters. The docs/00 section 8 decision ("one skill per graphics API backend; console backends are rhi-console") rests on "each API has its own specification, validation layers and release cadence". The finding brings new evidence that this premise does not fully hold for the Xbox-class API, which is a D3D12 superset with a shared base, and that production engines (UE D3D12RHI plus a platform extension) share one backend. So it challenges the rationale with evidence rather than re-litigating a reasoned decision.

Mandate: K-PLATFORM covers graphics APIs and consoles, and rhi-d3d12 and the platform-architect subtree (platform-desktop, platform-console) are in its scope.

Soundness: a confidential module of rhi-d3d12 matches the framework's existing module granularity (the '@C-Y' module consumers, and module-level proof in check.py). It keeps a single owner for the shared base and confines NDA code to one cleared module. It does require the per-module access model from K-PLATFORM-1, because check.py currently rejects it, and the proposal states that dependency. Two minor points: the 'C-RHI@nda:xbox' syntax is new, and naming a specific holder departs from the generic per-platform-holder convention. Neither makes the proposal unsound.

Severity: "major" fits. It causes duplicated work and drift but does not block the framework, so it is not a blocker, and it is more than a minor issue.

The finding holds on the facts. In data/contracts.json, C-PAL has oracle_author "accessibility", boundary: true and conformance: true, and its summary covers OS services, lifecycle and system events, clock-domain correlation, suspend/resume quiesce, memory pressure, display, and thread affinity and QoS. Five skills in data/skills.json implement C-PAL: platform-desktop, platform-console, platform-mobile, platform-web and platform-server-host. platform-console has access "nda:per-platform-holder".

The accessibility skill's purpose covers subtitles, TTS and STT, colorblind modes, text scaling and similar features. Its access is null, so it has no NDA. It lists C-PAL only among what it consumes, and "OS accessibility settings" is one item in the C-PAL summary. No other capability or contract gives C-PAL a conformance suite under another name. RND.RHI.conformance exists for the RHI only.

check.py only proves that an oracle_author exists and is not the sole implementer. It says nothing about whether that author is competent or has NDA access.

The cited evidence is accurate. QA.HOST.runner and QA.HOST.fault-points are owned by test-runtime-harness. PLAT.PAL.event-injection lists test-runtime-harness and certification-compliance as contributors.

One caveat: the proposed "per-holder confidential partition" for certification-compliance does not exist yet. certification-compliance has access null, so the remedy would have to add that partition. This does not undercut the deficiency itself. Major severity fits a mismatched oracle on the widest boundary contract, which has an NDA implementer.

I confirmed the facts in data/contracts.json. C-PAL has oracle_author = accessibility and is a layer-0 boundary contract with conformance=true. It has five platform implementers: desktop, console (nda:per-platform-holder), mobile, web and server-host. Its summary covers lifecycle, suspend/resume quiesce, clock-domain correlation, thread QoS and affinity, memory pressure and display. Accessibility sits in the ui workstream, has no NDA access class, and owns no PLAT.PAL capability. The only part of C-PAL it plausibly consumes is the OS accessibility-settings event.

The competence the finding points to exists as claimed in docs/01. QA.HOST.runner and QA.HOST.fault-points belong to test-runtime-harness. PLAT.PAL.event-injection belongs to platform-architect, with test-runtime-harness and certification-compliance contributing.

The defect is material. The oracle author writes the read-only acceptance suite (tests/acceptance/C-PAL/), and that suite is the one gate the autonomous platform implementers cannot touch. An author that cannot write lifecycle, clock and threading cases, or see NDA certification timings, leaves the widest boundary contract effectively unverified. That undermines the framework's own principle of independent oracles (docs/00, QA.AGENT.oracle-independence).

I found no reasoned decision in docs/00 or docs/06 section C that picks accessibility or deliberately assigns oracle authors without regard to competence. check.py only proves that the oracle author is not the sole implementer and that independence pairs sit in different workstreams, and accessibility passes both. Other assignments also look like arbitrary cross-workstream rotation, which makes this a real defect rather than a design choice.

The finding is within K-PLATFORM's mandate (platform requirements, certification). The proposal is technically sound. test-runtime-harness is in the quality workstream and implements no C-PAL backend, so the independence rule still holds. A co-signature mechanism already exists in QA.AGENT.oracle-change-control. One caveat: certification-compliance has no NDA access class of its own, so the "per-holder confidential partition" co-signature has to be routed through PLAT.PAL.confidential-extensions and cleared agents. That is a refinement, not a flaw that invalidates the proposal. "Major" is appropriate for the wrong oracle owner on the foundational boundary contract; it is not critical, because the structural checks still pass and the defect is fixable in one field.

The data matches the finding. In data/radar.json, 'GLES / WebGL backends' has class S, non_goal=true and capabilities=[]. Its revisit trigger is 'Device DB shows >10% of a shipping configuration's audience without Vulkan/WebGPU', and its evidence is 'device DB share'. docs/01 defines speculative as 'watch only', but GLES and WebGL are established APIs, so class S is a mislabel. check.py does not catch it because it only compares radar class to the listed capabilities' maturity, and this entry lists none. Both WebGPU radar entries (RND.RHI.webgpu, and PLAT.WEB.webgpu-target owned by platform-web) give the fallback 'Web target limited to WebGPU-capable browsers (no WebGL backend)'. Meanwhile skills.json lists 'web' as a platform for minimal-client and indie-2d-client, and indie-2d-online-web-client is web-only. The trigger's circularity also holds: PLAT.PAL.device-db (platform-architect) stores device records, driver deny-lists and tier keys for devices that run the engine, and nothing in the data measures browser-capability share for the audience outside that set (grep found no browser-share, analytics-for-capability or no-WebGPU fallback entry). No WebGL2 or bounded 2D fallback path exists under any other name. check.py only proves that radar entries are present, that classes match and that fallbacks exist; it says nothing about whether a trigger can be measured or whether a web platform claim is reachable. Rating it major is justified: the smallest configurations claim web, with no fallback for a real share of their audience and a revisit trigger that can never fire.

The finding matches the data. In data/untrusted-inputs.json, 'saves' (validating_owner persistence-save, parser serialization-schema, mode harness, limits 'size/depth') is set to trust 'trusted-local'. It is the only 'trusted-local' entry in the registry: 16 are hostile-local, 20 hostile-remote, 6 semi-trusted-signed and 5 agent-input. Even 'cloud-saves' has a lower trust level (semi-trusted-signed). GAM.SAVE.integrity is 'Save signing & tamper policy' (owner persistence-save, contributor security-engineering). Nothing says the signature is only tamper evidence or that the parser is hardened anyway. No data file mentions save editors, save exploits or jailbreaks. XC.SEC.tamper (anti-tamper/DRM boundary) and the general security-incident capability do not cover how save files are trusted. check.py proves only that each input has a validating owner, registered parsers, a fuzz target and limits; it does not check whether a trust label is correct. Mode 'harness' means saves do get fuzzed, which helps, but the label is still wrong and the limits leave out count and version range. certification-compliance exists as a skill, so the proposed change is feasible. Rating it major is reasonable: save parsers are a documented console jailbreak route, and the label points holders the wrong way.

This is a real, material defect. data/untrusted-inputs.json lists 'saves' as trust trusted-local (validating_owner persistence-save, limits size/depth), while assets, mods and fonts are hostile-local. Players control save files, and save-parser exploits used for console jailbreaks are well documented. Agents reading the registry would treat saves as trusted and could lower their fuzzing and hardening priority. Neither docs/06 section C nor docs/00 records a reasoned decision to trust saves, so the finding does not conflict with a recorded scope decision. It is within K-PLATFORM's mandate, which covers consoles and tracing certification requirements, and certification-compliance is in its scope. The proposed change is technically sound: hostile-local, the added limits, "signature is tamper evidence only" and a certification-compliance contributor are all coherent. certification-compliance exists as a skill in data/skills.json. 'Major' fits, because a wrong trust class on a heavily attacked parser is a meaningful security gap but not a structural blocker. K-SEC and K-TEST raise the same point, which shows it is real; that duplication is not a materiality issue.

The finding is material, within the critic's scope, and new, and the proposed change is sound. Scope: K-PLATFORM's mandate covers graphics APIs and web constraints, and rhi-webgpu and the platform-architect subtree are in its scope. Nothing in docs/06 §C or the gauntlet records a reasoned decision on WebGL, and it has not been raised before. docs/00 only lists "GLES/WebGL backends" among the non-goals, with no rationale that answers this finding. Materiality: data/skills.json gives minimal-client and indie-2d-client the `web` platform, and M2 in milestones.json claims both "everywhere". indie-2d-online-web-client is web-only. The radar fallback confines web to WebGPU-capable browsers, so these configurations miss part of the audience that portal and 2D games serve. The revisit trigger is the key defect. It measures "device DB share", and PLAT.PAL.device-db is filled from device records and telemetry of devices the engine runs on. Browsers that cannot run the engine never enter it, so the trigger is effectively unfalsifiable and the non-goal can never be reconsidered. For an agent framework, a trigger that cannot fire is a real coordination flaw, not a matter of style. Adding a GLES-class path later would mean rework across rhi-core, shaders and C-GPUTIER, which fits the protocol's definition of major ("would cause rework or silent legacy architecture"). The S class is also wrong: WebGL/GLES are established. The other E-class non-goal ("Backend service implementation") shows the right pattern, and check.py only ties class to capability maturity for listed capabilities, so reclassifying this entry (which lists none) to E passes the checks. Proposal: an external browser-capability measure owned by platform-web is a trigger that can actually fire. The two options (a bounded WebGL2 path for min2d/minimal behind C-GPUTIER, or dropping web from those configurations and saying so in docs/00) are both workable and match the tiering model the framework already has. Severity major is neither inflated nor understated.

The central claim, that the Apple frameworks would be implemented twice, is wrong: in data/capabilities.json each named area already has one cross-platform owner rather than platform-desktop and platform-mobile. Owners: GameKit (achievements) is PLAT.SVC.achievements and StoreKit (store and entitlements) is PLAT.SVC.entitlements, both owned by platform-services. GameController is INP.DEV.gamepads (input-devices-haptics). CoreAudio and AVAudioSession are AUD.ARCH.devices (audio-architect). CAMetalLayer surfaces are PLAT.PAL.windowing (platform-architect) with RND.RHI.present (rhi-core) and RND.RHI.metal (rhi-metal). Signing and notarization are BLD.REL.packaging (packaging-release-patching). Only TCC and notarization interplay sits under PLAT.DESK.os-security, which is macOS-only, so it is not duplicated. The platform capabilities are the PAL backends (PLAT.DESK.pal, PLAT.MOB.pal), and it is normal for those to be split. The minor tvOS point is true: no data or doc file mentions tvOS, and ARCH.REQ.platform-matrix has no support or non-goal entry for it. That leftover is a small matrix gap. It does not justify the wrong-boundary finding or the proposed apple-common module, so the finding as written does not hold.

The main claim, that shared Apple frameworks get implemented twice, does not survive a check of data/skills.json and docs/01. Most of the named frameworks are already owned once by skills that span platforms, not by the form-factor experts. GameKit and StoreKit (achievements, commerce, entitlements) belong to platform-services, whose platforms field is unrestricted. GameController (gamepads, hotplug, haptics) belongs to input-devices-haptics, also unrestricted. CoreAudio and AVAudioSession device backends belong to audio-architect. Packaging and signing belong to packaging-release-patching. The swapchain and surface (CAMetalLayer) are listed as a non-responsibility of platform-desktop and go to rhi-core, and rhi-metal already spans pc, mobile and xr-standalone. That leaves some shared Darwin PAL code (Foundation, Mach threads) plus notarization and TCC, which PLAT.DESK.os-security gives to platform-desktop alone. AppKit and UIKit lifecycle and windowing really do differ, so this residue is small. The framework also deliberately groups platform experts by form factor: platform-mobile already covers both iOS and Android, and PLAT.MOB.thermal and PLAT.MOB.tbdr are organised by device class, not by vendor. The proposed fix is also questionable. Having platform-mobile own an apple-common module that platform-desktop then consumes adds coupling between the two experts. It also misplaces ownership of macOS-only concerns such as notarization. The tvOS gap is real but minor: tvOS is not in ARCH.REQ.platform-matrix or in the radar non-goals, and recording it either way would be a cheap improvement. It is not enough to carry the finding, whose main argument about duplicated implementation is not material. If the finding were accepted in narrowed form (tvOS only), minor would be the right severity.

I checked this against data/capabilities.json, skills.json and contracts.json, and all three parts of the finding hold.

1. **Browser lifecycle.** PLAT.PAL.lifecycle ("Process lifecycle (suspend, resume, constrained, terminate)") lists these contributors: platform-console, platform-mobile, async-io-storage, rhi-core, frame-orchestration and network-transport. platform-web is not among them. None of the PLAT.WEB caps (runtime, storage, delivery, gestures, webgpu-target, pal, std3d) mention page visibility, bfcache, tab discard or rAF throttling. platform-web's purpose does not either. A grep for visibility, bfcache, freeze, throttl and "hidden" finds no web lifecycle entry. CORE.FRAME.host-loop covers entering the frame through requestAnimationFrame, but not browser throttling or lifecycle.

2. **Dynamic HDR headroom.** PLAT.PAL.display is "Display enumeration, modes, DPI, HDR & VRR capability", which describes static capability. Its contributors are platform-desktop, platform-console and platform-mobile, not post-color-hdr. RND.POST.hdr-output ("platform calibration from C-PAL") and RND.POST.display-state do not cover headroom that changes with brightness. Grepping for EDR and headroom finds only thermal and async-compute headroom.

3. **Mobile windowing.** The PLAT.MOB caps are os, tbdr, thermal, storage, frame-pacing, notifications, links and pal. None covers resizable or multi-window apps, foldable posture, or desktop modes, and there are no hits for foldable, posture, multi-window, resizable or UIRequiresFullScreen. The generic PLAT.PAL.windowing ("Windowing & surfaces") and PLAT.MOB.pal ("...windowing...") only partly overlap. They name the backend slot, not these behaviours, so the gap is real, if narrow.

The data checks do not prove semantic coverage like this. "Minor" is the right severity: the gaps are real, but the general windowing and events slots of C-PAL give partial cover.

I checked this against data/capabilities.json, contracts.json and skills.json. The finding holds as a minor omission. Web lifecycle is the strongest part. PLAT.PAL.lifecycle ("suspend, resume, constrained, terminate") lists platform-console and platform-mobile as contributors but not platform-web. platform-web's purpose (threads, storage, delivery, gestures) never mentions page visibility, rAF throttling, bfcache or tab discard. C-PAL's suspend/resume quiesce protocol must still map those browser events. The finding holds, and minor is the right severity. The facts check out. PLAT.PAL.device-db explicitly includes "driver deny-lists ... remote updates". The proposal is technically sound, including the trust labels. For check.py to pass, the implementation must also add each id to the owner skill's untrusted_inputs and add a fuzz_target, since the proposed entries use harness mode. That is routine follow-through, not a flaw in the proposal.

This is a real defect. In data/capabilities.json (line 10754), PRF.METH.budgets reads "Budgets measured on the reference high-end PC and scaled proportionally to lower tiers". I checked this against data/capabilities.json around line 1902. CORE.JOBS.blocking exists, is owned by job-system-task-graph, and literally reads "Blocking & long-running tasks run inline on work-stealing workers (no dedicated lanes or compensating threads)". CORE.JOBS.degenerate covers only the 0–2 worker web/host mode. RES.MGMT.no-stall only covers loading. The legacy patterns (L03 render thread, L04 main-thread APIs, synchronous IO loads, modal editor ops) have no entry for blocking inside work-stealing workers. The contradiction the finding names is real. CORE.JOBS.priorities promises latency-critical lanes, CORE.JOBS.pinned promises pinned lanes, and RES.MGMT.no-stall forbids blocking waits on frame-critical tasks, yet the blocking rule bans dedicated lanes and parks workers. check.py's docstring checks only structure (ownership, layering, closure, radar, conformance existence), so it cannot prove anything about this semantic rule. "Major" is a fair severity: the rule sets the threading policy for the whole engine and would cause starvation on low-core tiers.

This is a real, material defect. data/capabilities.json and docs/01:327 define CORE.JOBS.blocking as "Blocking & long-running tasks run inline on work-stealing workers (no dedicated lanes or compensating threads)". That is an inverted, obsolete stance, and it contradicts the framework's own rules: CORE.JOBS.degenerate ("no blocking waits on host threads"), RES.MGMT.no-stall ("no blocking waits on frame-critical tasks or host/OS-bound threads"), and the latency-critical and pinned lanes of CORE.JOBS.priorities and CORE.JOBS.pinned. No reasoned scope decision covers it. Docs/06 section C does not mention blocking policy. Docs/06 B2 lists the task-model choice as an open research question and does not endorse inline blocking. Docs/00 principles also favor non-blocking, host-yielding execution. The finding is within K-PERF's mandate (serialization points, scalability bottlenecks, hidden sync). The proposed rewrite is technically sound and matches established practice: waits yield, OS-blocking calls go to a bounded, inventoried lane or compensation policy, background QoS lanes have preemption points. It also fits the existing thread-inventory ownership in CORE.JOBS.thread-model and the ADR rule for dedicated threads. Adding the rule to C-TASK (whose summary already names "blocking rules") and adding a legacy pattern are reasonable. Major severity is right: a normative capability tells agents to build a starving scheduler. Several independent critics (K-ARCH, K-LEGACY, K-SYSTEMS) raised the same finding, which supports that it is real.

I checked each claim against data/*.json and docs, and all of them hold.

I checked the data files and the finding is accurate. C-BUDGET (data/contracts.json) covers only time, transfer bytes and async-queue occupancy per tier. C-BENCH covers warm-up and variance but has no thermal soak or sustained-window rule. No capability in the framework covers whole-device energy or battery-hours. The framework explicitly targets mobile, xr-standalone and handheld PC and console modes (for example the TDP profiles in PLAT.PAL.performance-modes). The finding is within the performance critic's mandate. I confirmed the facts in the data. ARCH.ORG.ownership-ledger is only "Ownership ledger & territory locks". Materiality: the framework's stated purpose is coordinating many autonomous agents under exclusive territory locks. Agent crashes and context exhaustion are routine in that setting. Scope: this does not contradict any recorded scope decision. docs/06 section C covers NDA, game-specific systems, backends, membership semantics and critic misses. docs/00's `external:*` sentinels cover backends and model training, not agent runtime continuity.

**The data contradicts itself on C-RHI.** The M3 exit text says "C-RHI reviewed against the tensor tier by ml-inference-runtime before freeze", but C-RHI is already frozen at M1.

**Nothing else covers it.**

- C-API (semver and deprecation) is about public API stability. It does not set freeze scope per tier.

**One small overstatement.** "Before any consumer of them exists" is too strong at the contract level. check.py guarantees each contract has some consumer built by its freeze milestone. It is true at the tier level: RT, the tensor tier and neural features arrive at M3–M6 but are frozen at M1/M2. That does not undermine the core claim.

The defect is material. Without cross-origin isolation there is no SharedArrayBuffer, and a threaded WASM build does not start. Portal and iframe hosts, and pages with ad or payment SDKs, often cannot send COOP/COEP headers. That means the scale-down configuration fails on the hosts where it is most likely to ship. Agents following the capability would build threads-only.

A scale-down critic is clearly within its mandate here. At least seven other critics (K-ARCH, K-SEC, K-PLATFORM, K-LEGACY, K-PERF, K-SYSTEMS) found the same thing independently.

The proposal is sound. Threaded and non-threaded WASM are separate binaries, and a load-time check of crossOriginIsolated picking between them is standard practice (Godot 4.3, Unity, Emscripten). It also reuses the existing CORE.JOBS.degenerate. One caveat: the "gate" has to be a milestone exit or runtime test, because check.py only proves static structure. That is a wording detail, not a flaw.

Among the physics children, only cloth-deformables consumes C-ML?, through PHY.SOFT.ml (X, experimental, no contributors). The C-PHYS summary covers stepping phases, snapshot/resimulate and determinism conformance, but it has no hook for a learned policy or surrogate inside the substep. Two nearby items do not cover this. ANM.SYN.learned ("Learned motion matching & neural controllers", owner motion-synthesis) is kinematic animation, not physics-step actuation. C-AIAGENT does cover learned policies as recorded external inputs that are never re-invoked on resimulate, which is close to the proposed determinism rule, but it works at the gameplay-decision level (C-GAME), not inside the physics substep. check.py only proves that skills owning ML-named capabilities consume C-ML/C-MLGPU, and that gated extension points have conformance; it says nothing about this gap. On severity, "major" looks inflated: the proposal adds only experimental (X) capabilities for an emerging technique, PHY.SOFT.ml already sits at X, and the recorded-output determinism pattern already exists in C-AIAGENT and can be copied. Minor fits better, though the point about reopening C-PHYS gives some reason to fix it early.

The facts check out. ik-procedural-animation consumes only C-ANIM and C-PHYS, and rigid-body-dynamics consumes C-PHYS, C-TASK, C-DET, C-ANIM? and C-ENV?. Neither has C-ML?. ANM.IK.physical (active ragdoll, E) has no learned variant. The only ML-driven animation entries are ANM.SYN.learned, which is kinematic and owned by motion-synthesis, and GAM.AI.learned, which is agent-level. PHY.SOFT.ml covers only cloth and deformables. Gap A8 in docs/06 limits its scope to learned kinematic animation in motion-synthesis, and docs/06 section C records nothing that rules out physics-based RL characters. So this is not an out-of-scope request against a recorded, reasoned decision. The framework already gives far thinner-evidence neural techniques experimental (X) entries (RND.MAT.neural, RND.GI.neural-cache). A missing X/radar path for RL physics-based characters (the PHC/MaskedMimic line of work) is a real, if small, coverage omission within a future-tech critic's mandate. The core fix is sound: add ANM.IK.learned-physics (X, experimental, owner ik-procedural-animation) with a radar entry whose fallback is classic active ragdoll, plus C-ML? on ik-procedural-animation. check.py's rule that ML owners reach the inference runtime via contracts would then be met.

The severity is inflated, though. Anything X-class is confined to the experimental profile, so no shipping configuration depends on it. Adding an opt-in radar/capability entry is a minor change, not a major one. Parts of the proposal are also technically weak. (1) A C-PHYS "substep policy hook" is not required. These controllers usually run the policy at control rate and output PD/motor targets. The solver tracks those targets through the existing C-PHYS motor and stepping interface, so the "must reopen C-PHYS later" argument is overstated. Recording policy outputs for rollback can live on the consumer side (C-SNAPSHOT/C-DET). (2) PHY.ARCH.learned-surrogates largely duplicates PHY.SOFT.ml for deformables. Learned destruction and fluid surrogates have little production evidence, so at most they belong as a radar note, not a physics-architect capability. (3) C-ML? on rigid-body-dynamics has no concrete consumer. So the finding holds in trimmed form (one X capability, a radar entry, C-ML? on ik-procedural-animation), at minor rather than major severity.

Confirmed against the data. data/untrusted-inputs.json has 48 inputs. It includes generated-content (model output, validated by ai-behavior-perception with length/moderation limits), chat-text (player-to-player, validated by online-services-liveops), voice-streams (codec level, validated by audio-dsp-mixing with bitrate/frame-size limits) and project-content-to-llm (developer-side agent input). No entry covers player text or voice sent as a prompt to a runtime model, so there is no 'player-model-prompts' or anything like it. The surface itself is real in the capabilities: GAM.AI.llm-dialogue (LLM dialogue "guardrails per XC.SEC.genai"), AUD.CONTENT.speech (runtime TTS/ASR) and XC.EXT.generated-assets ("player-prompted generated assets"). XC.SEC.genai names prompt injection and cost DoS, but only as a threat-model capability owned by security-engineering. It does not give that input a validating owner, a red-team corpus or limits. check.py (lines 538-569) enforces owner, parser, fuzz/red-team and limits only for inputs listed in the registry, so it cannot catch this gap. Contract C-AIAGENT (contracts.json:1149) covers budget, timeout and moderation for provider decisions and outputs, not validation of prompt input. Minor caveat: the proposed mode 'redteam+harness' is invalid, because check.py only accepts 'harness' or 'redteam'. The fix would have to pick one or be split into two entries. That does not change whether the omission exists. Rating it major fits, since it is the main injection and cost-DoS entry point for shipped LLM features.

The gap is real. data/untrusted-inputs.json registers 'generated-content' (model output, validated by ai-behavior-perception), 'chat-text' (player-to-player), 'voice-streams' (codec limits only) and 'project-content-to-llm' (dev-agent redteam). No entry covers player text or ASR transcripts sent into a runtime model, even though GAM.AI.llm-dialogue (M) and AUD.CONTENT.speech ('Runtime neural TTS/ASR for gameplay dialogue', M) are milestone capabilities and XC.SEC.genai names prompt injection and cost DoS. The docs/06 A12 decision covers output moderation, budget, fallback and replay recording. It never scopes out the input side, so this finding does not contradict a recorded scope decision. The registry is the machine-enforced mechanism (check.py requires one validating owner, parser registration and fuzz/redteam coverage), so leaving out the main hostile-remote surface of a shipped M feature is material, and 'major' fits.

One caveat on soundness: the proposed mode 'redteam+harness' fails check.py, which accepts only 'harness' or 'redteam'. 'redteam' is also defined (docs/09 and the registry _doc) as covering development-agent inputs through XC.SEC.agent-redteam, with trust 'agent-input'. The entry should be mode 'harness' with a fuzz target and its limits. The prompt-injection corpus should hang off XC.SEC.genai, or the redteam definition should be widened explicitly. Every listed owner must also add the input to its untrusted_inputs. None of these are trivial copy edits, but they refine the fix rather than invalidate it, and the core change is sound.

The finding checks out against the data. In data/skills.json, ml-inference-runtime has profiles ['all'] and targets client, headless-client, server and tools. Model.in_configuration decides membership from profiles and targets alone, and no rule pulls the runtime in only when a consumer needs it.

Running cap_in_configuration for ML.RT.inference, ML.RT.os-models and ML.RT.residency returns True in minimal-client, indie-2d-client and indie-2d-online-web-client. All three capabilities are maturity M with no profile restriction.

Every consumer takes C-ML or C-MLGPU as optional (C-ML? or C-MLGPU?), across 17 skills. Both contracts are marked gated, and check.py enforces that they are only consumed optionally. The radar entry owned by ml-inference-runtime has the fallback "No ML features".

The profile addons (openworld, online, aaa, xr, ugc, massim, sandbox, vehicles, team-large, online-lockstep, online-rollback, online-async, experimental) include no 'ml' addon. check.py proves only that configurations are closed and that gated contracts are consumed optionally. It says nothing about keeping an optional-only module out of small builds, so the gap is not already covered.

Minor severity fits: this is a footprint and privacy-review concern, not a correctness break.

The overlap exists as described in the data. In data/capabilities.json, RND.GPU.hetero-offload (owned by gpu-platform-architect, maturity X, no contributors) reads "Heterogeneous adapter offload (inference, encode, async work on the integrated GPU/NPU)". ML.RT.npu (owned by ml-inference-runtime, maturity X, contributor platform-architect) reads "NPU backends via platform ML APIs". The C-ML contract summary also says ml-inference-runtime owns the "CPU and NPU backends". So two owners each claim inference on the NPU, and neither entry lists the other's skill as a contributor. Nothing in the data settles who decides placement. ml-inference-runtime's non_responsibilities does hand "GPU queue/budget arbitration of C-MLGPU work" to gpu-platform-architect, but that covers budgeting GPU queues, not choosing between the NPU and the iGPU. RND.RHI.adapter-selection only covers high-performance vs low-power adapters for rendering and present. check.py checks ownership, contract and untrusted-input structure, but it cannot catch two capability names that overlap in wording. Rating it minor fits: both entries are experimental. The proposed rewording plus a contributor link is a proportionate fix.

This is a real overlap. In data/capabilities.json, RND.GPU.hetero-offload (owned by gpu-platform-architect, X) is described as "Heterogeneous adapter offload (inference, encode, async work on the integrated GPU/NPU)". ML.RT.npu (owned by ml-inference-runtime, X, with platform-architect as its only contributor) is "NPU backends via platform ML APIs". Both claim NPU inference placement. That goes against the recorded principle in docs/00 line 120: ml-inference-runtime owns standalone networks (C-ML for CPU/NPU, C-MLGPU for render-graph passes) so that one runtime keeps a single budget. Two owners of NPU inference placement would split that budget and duplicate the placement policy. The overlap is a real coordination defect for autonomous agents, not a style issue. It is within the critic's overlap mandate, and nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 records a decision that the two should overlap. The proposal is technically sound. Rewording hetero-offload to non-inference async and encode work on a secondary adapter leaves it with a coherent scope that does not overlap. Adding gpu-platform-architect as a contributor to ML.RT.npu for adapter selection keeps its expertise without shared ownership. One nit: the evidence cites DirectML, which is now in maintenance and superseded by Windows ML execution providers, but the single-placement-API point still holds. Minor is the right severity because both capabilities are experimental (X, experimental profile only) and the fix is a rewording.

Confirmed in data/skills.json: ml-inference-runtime has profiles ['all'], so it is in every configuration. Every consumer of C-ML and C-MLGPU takes it optionally (C-ML?, C-MLGPU?), which check.py requires of gated contracts. Its own M capabilities (ML.RT.inference, os-models, residency, local-remote and others) have no profile tags, so they ship in minimal and min2d too. This is a real scale-down gap measured against docs/00 section 5 ("scaling down is proven, not asserted"). The framework already sets a precedent for gating: ray-tracing-infrastructure, which provides the gated C-RT and C-RTAS, is limited to lite3d and std3d. No recorded scope decision in docs/00 or docs/06 section C justifies putting ML in 'all'. docs/00 only explains why the skill sits under core-runtime-architect. The finding is within K-FUTURE's scale-down mandate, and 'minor' is the right severity: the cost is binary size and wasted agent scope, and nothing breaks. The proposal is sound in its main option (an 'ml' add-on, or membership derived from an enabled consumer capability). Its suggested default list (aaa, xr, experimental) is incomplete, though. Some M capabilities in lite3d and std3d need the runtime today: ANM.DEF.ml (deformation-skinning) and ANM.SYN.learned (motion-synthesis). So do AUD.CONTENT.speech in audio-content-runtime (all profiles) and XC.SEC.behavioral-detection on servers. These would need the new profile tag, or the consumer-derived rule, so they don't silently lose their provider. The consumer-derived variant avoids that problem. This caveat is about how to implement the fix and does not undo the finding.

The finding is factually right about one thing. WLD.PCG.ml ("ML-generated content", owned by procedural-generation) is class X, carries only the "experimental" profile, and radar.json lists it as X with the fallback "Rule-based PCG". But the data does not show the gap the finding claims: tool-side ML generation already has mature (M) coverage under other ids.

- ED.AI.generative, "Generative asset tools & editor copilots", is class M.
- ED.AI.provenance, "Provenance of generated content (consumer of CNT.ID.rights)", is class M.
- ED.AI.evaluation, "Evaluation harness for generative & ML-assisted tools", is class M.
- CNT.COOK.ml-assisted, "ML-assisted retopology/UV/LOD techniques as processor options", is class M and runs in the cook.
- The ai-assisted-authoring skill's purpose explicitly covers "generative asset tools, editor copilots, ML-assisted retopology/rigging/UV/LOD, provenance and licensing of generated content". It also delegates "Runtime inference" to ml-inference-runtime.

So the tool-side versus runtime split already exists. The shipping editor tools the finding cites (Unity AI, Roblox Cube 3D) map to ED.AI.generative, which is M, and nothing blocks them from being used. The proposed WLD.PCG.ml-bake would largely duplicate ED.AI.generative plus CNT.COOK.ml-assisted, and it names ED.AI.provenance, which already exists.

What is left is a wording nit: procedural-generation's purpose ("evaluates ML generation") and WLD.PCG.ml's label don't say "runtime/stream-in". That is not the maturity error the finding claims.

The claimed harm does not hold. WLD.PCG.ml ("ML-generated content", X, experimental only) is one line, but the framework already covers tool-side ML generation at M. ED.AI.generative ("Generative asset tools & editor copilots", M) and ED.AI.provenance (M), both owned by ai-assisted-authoring in the aaa profile, cover exactly the editor tools cited as evidence: Unity AI and Roblox Cube 3D (ML terrain, texture and layout generation). So putting WLD.PCG.ml in the experimental profile does not block tool-side ML use that already ships. The radar entry's revisit trigger ("Deterministic, licensable models with provenance") and its evidence ("Research & tool demos") show that WLD.PCG.ml is aimed at ML generation inside the PCG framework, which runs in the editor and at stream-in. The proposed WLD.PCG.ml-bake (M) would largely repeat ED.AI.generative + ED.AI.provenance. It would also blur the boundary between procedural-generation and ai-assisted-authoring, rather than add coverage. The one residual point is small: an ML node in the PCG graph that runs only at cook time. That could be clarified with a note on the capability that points to ED.AI.generative, not with a new M capability. Given that, the finding is immaterial as stated. "Minor" would be the right severity for the residual clarification point, so the severity is not inflated.

The finding holds. Every construct it names is in the data as described. In skills.json, ml-inference-runtime's purpose says "GPU (cooperative-vector / tensor) and CPU backends" and its expertise lists "cooperative vectors". In capabilities.json, RES.IO.gpu-decompress is titled "GPU decompression (GDeflate class)". In radar.json, the neural evidence for RND.SHADER.neural and RND.SHADER.autodiff reads "SM 6.9 cooperative vectors (preview)". The revisit triggers for neural materials and NTC (RND.MAT.neural, RND.TEX.ntc) wait for "cross-vendor cooperative-vector support" or "non-preview cooperative-vector support", and the two shader entries wait for "Non-preview cross-vendor support". Those events may never happen if a linear-algebra API replaces cooperative vectors, so the triggers risk going stale. The capability rows themselves are API-neutral, as the finding says. The in-shader row reads "matrix-vector/tensor intrinsics tier; API-neutral", and the C-SHADER contract says "neural/tensor intrinsics tier". So the wording clash between briefs and capabilities is real. Nothing else covers Zstd for GPU decompression: zstd appears only in the CPU codec-library capability. The check.py docstring was not read. A grep of check.py for preview/vendor/cooperative/gdeflate found nothing, so no sign it checks this wording. The outside facts are cited and plausible but I did not check them online: SM 6.9 kept cooperative vectors in preview with a linear-algebra successor planned, and DirectStorage announced Zstd. Minor severity fits: this is wording and freshness, with no structural gap.

I checked the data and every construct the finding names is there. data/skills.json has the ml-inference-runtime purpose "GPU (cooperative-vector / tensor)" and the expertise item "cooperative vectors". In data/radar.json, the RND.SHADER.neural and RND.SHADER.autodiff entries both give the evidence "SM 6.9 cooperative vectors (preview)" and the revisit "Non-preview cross-vendor support". The neural materials and NTC entries have revisit triggers keyed to "cooperative-vector support". data/capabilities.json has RES.IO.gpu-decompress as "GPU decompression (GDeflate class)".

The defect is real and material, though minor. The capability RND.SHADER.neural and C-SHADER already say "API-neutral matrix-vector/tensor intrinsics tier", so the skill brief and radar contradict the framework's own neutral wording. More important, the radar revisit triggers are tied to a construct that may never leave preview. If cooperative vectors are superseded rather than promoted, those triggers never fire, which breaks the radar's promotion mechanism in docs/00 section 7. The briefs also steer the agents who write SKILL.md toward a vendor or preview API.

This is within a future-proofing critic's mandate. No scope decision in docs/06 section C or docs/00 is contradicted, since docs/06 B18 already lists zstd as a candidate. The proposed rewording is technically sound and low-risk: "matrix/tensor intrinsics tier" and "GPU-decodable codecs (GDeflate/Zstd class)" keep the fallbacks intact, and check.py does not depend on the wording.

Minor is the right severity: it is wording and evidence staleness with a mandatory fallback in place, not a structural gap. The finding overlaps K-RENDER's stale-evidence finding, but it adds the ml-inference-runtime brief and the gpu-decompress codec.

The finding is factually correct and nothing else covers it. In data/capabilities.json, PLAT.PAL.cloud-hybrid ("Split client/cloud compute boundary") is owned by platform-architect with maturity X, an empty contributor list and an experimental tag. In data/radar.json, the "Cloud-hybrid compute (split client/cloud simulation)" entry also names platform-architect as owner, with Crackdown 3 as its evidence.

platform-architect's purpose covers OS services, discovery and lifecycle, and evaluating new targets such as cloud streaming. Its expertise is OS internals, porting and CPU topology. Nothing in it touches authority, replication or latency hiding.

network-architect's purpose covers the authority model and netcode model. Its expertise lists "latency hiding" and "distributed systems". It, frame-orchestration and online-services-liveops all exist in skills.json. No other capability, skill purpose or contract summary covers split client/cloud simulation; the grep hits for cloud-streaming, RND.GPU.hetero-offload and cloud-save are different topics.

check.py does not already prove this. It checks only that an owner exists, and that the radar owner owns or leads the capabilities it lists. It says nothing about whether the owner has the right domain expertise.

The proposed change is feasible as long as the radar owner is updated too, which the finding already calls for. One caveat: network-architect's profiles are online-only, but a split client/cloud simulation is online by nature.

Minor severity is appropriate because the capability is experimental (X) with a local-only fallback.

This holds as a real minor defect, and the proposed fix is sound. In data/capabilities.json, PLAT.PAL.cloud-hybrid ("Split client/cloud compute boundary", class X, profile experimental) has platform-architect as owner and an empty contributor list. That leaves no netcode input at all. data/radar.json and docs/09 name the same owner. What the capability actually covers is deciding what runs where, reconciliation and what happens on disconnect. That is authority and latency-hiding work, and in data/skills.json it sits with network-architect: its purpose names the "authority model" and its expertise lists "latency hiding". network-architect also already owns NET.ARCH.authority and NET.ARCH.distributed-authority (docs/03 line 1671). Nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 records a reasoned decision to keep this with the PAL lead, so the finding does not conflict with a scope decision.

The change is technically sound. network-architect, frame-orchestration, online-services-liveops and platform-architect all exist as skills. network-architect is a lead, so it can take a capability, and making it owner of both the capability and the radar entry passes check.py's rule that the radar owner must own or lead the capabilities it lists. The X class stays opt-in through the experimental profile.

Two small caveats that do not change the verdict:
- The PLAT.PAL.* id prefix would sit oddly under a NET owner. A rename to something like NET.ARCH.cloud-hybrid would be cleaner, but it is not required.
- Azure Remote Rendering was a rendering-streaming service, not split simulation, so it is weaker evidence than Crackdown 3.

On mandate, this is borderline but acceptable. K-FUTURE covers whether the architecture handles emerging technologies, and deciding who owns an experimental radar item decides how it gets designed and promoted.

Minor is the right severity: the capability is experimental and opt-in, and it has a local-simulation fallback.

I checked this against the data files and the omission is real. RND.LIGHT in data/capabilities.json has nine rows: units, clustered, stochastic, area, vsm, rt-shadows, contact, profiles and channels. RND.LIGHT.vsm and RND.LIGHT.rt-shadows are both limited to the std3d profile. Nothing in any data file mentions cascaded, CSM, PCF or a shadow atlas. The "shadows" entry in seed-map.json lists only vsm and rt-shadows. So the lite3d configurations (lite-3d-mobile-client and xr-standalone-client have lite3d in their profiles) get only contact shadows for dynamic shadows. The skill purpose in skills.json says "cascaded, virtual and ray-traced shadows", but no capability row covers cascaded shadows. The radar fallback text "Clustered lighting + shadow maps" is in radar.json. check.py only proves that configurations are closed; it does not prove that a shadow technique is present. One inaccuracy: that radar fallback belongs to the stochastic many-light row, not to a VSM entry. There is no VSM radar entry, so the proposal's "point the radar VSM fallback at it" should say the stochastic row's fallback. The deficiency itself still holds, and major is a reasonable severity because shipping lite-tier 3D without conventional shadow maps is a real gap.

I confirmed this in data/capabilities.json. RND.LIGHT has 9 rows: units, clustered, stochastic (M, std3d), area, vsm (std3d), rt-shadows (std3d), contact, profiles and channels. None of them is a cascaded, directional or local-light shadow-map technique, so every lite3d configuration (mobile, portable console, standalone XR) gets no dynamic shadow-map path. The direct-lighting-shadows purpose (skills.json:3706) promises "cascaded" shadows. Gap-analysis B4 lists "cascades" as an option for the shadow ADR, but that ADR can only choose among capabilities the skill owns. docs/00 line 77 deliberately limits VSM to std3d, and nothing gives lite3d a replacement. docs/06 section C and docs/00 record no scope decision that excludes conventional shadow maps, and docs/00 line 95 treats the TBDR/lite3d path as first-class. That makes this a real, material, in-mandate omission (a completeness sweep against shipped engines), and major is the right severity. The proposed row is technically sound: CSM plus a local-light atlas with PCF/PCSS/EVSM filtering is the standard lite-tier technique, and adding one E row with no profile restriction keeps check.py's invariants intact, since E rows need no radar entry. One small inaccuracy: VSM is an E capability and has no radar entry. The "Clustered lighting + shadow maps" fallback belongs to the Stochastic many-light sampling entry (radar.json:167-180, RND.LIGHT.stochastic), so the pointer should be added to that entry, not a VSM entry. This does not weaken the finding. The same finding also appears as K-RENDER round 3, with a finer split into csm, local-shadows and filtering.

The core claim holds against the data. CNT.COOK (data/capabilities.json around lines 2819-2955) has cook steps for textures, meshes, images, geometry-ops, ml-assisted and the rest, but none for audio or video. asset-cook-processors' purpose and expertise cover only textures, BCn/ASTC, meshes, images and domain builders. CNT.IMP.audio is 'Audio source formats' (import only). AUD.DSP.codecs is 'Codecs & decoding (Opus, Vorbis, ADPCM, hardware)', a runtime cap owned by audio-dsp-mixing. It has no cook, encode-quality, SRC, seek-table or chunking wording. AUD.CONTENT.authoring ('Audio authoring tool integration') and AUD.ARCH.middleware are about integration and the middleware decision, not a per-platform encode step. RND.MEDIA has decode, sync, surfaces, hdr and middleware only, with no transcode or bitrate-ladder cook. media-playback's non_responsibilities hand 'Movie rendering (producing video)' to cinematics-sequencer. A grep for encode, transcode, bank, seek, sample rate and loudness+cook found no owner. check.py does not prove media cook coverage. Two small caveats, neither of which breaks the finding. First, the third proposal (RND.MEDIA.encode) partly overlaps existing caps: ANM.CINE.movie-render ('High-quality movie rendering') arguably owns movie-render output, and PLAT.SVC.capture ('Media capture & share integration', platform-services) arguably owns runtime clip capture. So that part is weaker and should be framed as naming the encode step, not as a missing owner. Second, loudness exists at runtime (AUD.DSP.dynamics) but not as a cook-time normalization step. Major severity fits: audio ships in every configuration, and CNT.COOK.incremental-equivalence and determinism-check cannot be enforced on a step nobody owns.

I checked the data files and confirmed the omission. CNT.COOK in data/capabilities.json has texture, mesh, image and geometry processors but no audio or video processor. AUD.DSP.codecs reads "Codecs & decoding" and CNT.IMP.audio reads "Audio source formats". asset-cook-processors' purpose covers only texture and mesh processing plus hosting domain builders. audio-content-runtime (events, music, VO, authoring integration) does not claim bank builds or encoding. Nothing in the data mentions audio encoding, sample-rate conversion, cook-time loudness normalization, seek tables or video transcoding. Loudness appears only as a runtime or QA metric (AUD.DSP.dynamics, QA.SIM.audio).

The gap is material. Audio ships in every configuration. Per-platform, per-tier encoding is a real cook step, and without an owner CNT.COOK.variants and CNT.COOK.incremental-equivalence have nothing to bind to. Autonomous agents would have no owner to route the work to.

Scope is not a problem. Neither docs/06 section C nor docs/00 excludes this, and the critic's completeness mandate covers omissions. "Major" is the right severity: the missing step is core pipeline work in every configuration, not a whole subsystem, so it is not critical.

The first two proposed capabilities are sound: CNT.COOK.audio owned by audio-dsp-mixing, and CNT.COOK.video owned by media-playback. The third, RND.MEDIA.encode, is weaker and partly duplicates existing capabilities. Runtime clip export already falls under PLAT.SVC.capture ("Media capture & share integration", platform-services). Movie-render output belongs with ANM.CINE.movie-render (cinematics-sequencer), since media-playback explicitly hands off "producing video" to that skill. The residual offline encode should be a contributor note on ANM.CINE.movie-render, not a new media-playback capability. This caveat is about the proposal, not whether the finding holds; the core omission stands.

The data files confirm the gap. QA.CERT.licenses reads "Third-party license compliance & SBOM" and says nothing about notices shown to players. OBS.LOG.consent reads "Telemetry consent mechanism (policy in XC.SEC.privacy)", and the privacy-data-protection skill's purpose covers only consent policy for telemetry and analytics. I found no capability, skill purpose or contract summary that mentions EULA, ToS, terms of service, privacy-policy presentation, acceptance records, re-acceptance, OSS or third-party notices, credits, splash or logo obligations. Nearby items cover different things: the children's-data item is about parental consent flows, ARCH.PROD.licensing-model is about engine terms for game teams, the asset rights manifest is about content rights and the ad-SDK/ATT item is about ad consent. No QA.CERT.legal-surfaces id exists; its only mention is the critic's own proposal in gauntlet/round-3/K-COMPLETE.md. check.py cannot prove semantic coverage like this. Rating it major is reasonable, because shipping or certification is blocked without these surfaces (store in-app privacy policy, licence notice clauses, GDPR proof of consent).

I confirmed the gap in data/capabilities.json and docs/01. QA.CERT has privacy, store-policy, licenses ("compliance & SBOM"), regional and similar entries, but no capability anywhere covers presenting ToS/EULA or a privacy policy, versioned acceptance or re-acceptance gating, in-game OSS attribution notices, or middleware logo/splash obligations. A search for notice, EULA, terms, splash and acceptance in the data found nothing relevant. OBS.LOG.consent covers telemetry consent only.

The finding is material. The engine ships its own third-party dependencies inside every title, so the end-user notice obligations under Apache-2.0 §4(d), BSD and MIT land on every configuration. Because the SBOM already exists, generating notices from it is a natural and sound extension. The store rules on in-app privacy-policy access are also real ship blockers. Nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 scopes this out.

One caveat on soundness. Storing acceptance records server-side falls under the backend non-goal (06 C.3), so the new capability should be worded as the client-side presentation and gating flow plus the integration boundary to the backend, not as the record store itself.

Major is a fair severity: this is a cross-configuration legal and certification omission, not a style issue. Owner certification-compliance with contributors ui-architect, platform-services and privacy-data-protection fits the existing QA.CERT pattern.

The gap is real. I searched data/*.json for geoloc, location, GPS, GNSS, geofence, VPS, compass, Lightship and earth, and found no device-geolocation or VPS/geospatial-localization capability. The PLAT.MOB set covers only os, tbdr, thermal, storage, frame-pacing, notifications, links and pal. This is a material omission, not a style point. The framework has a mobile target and xr profiles. Location permission (precise vs approximate, background) is a real App Store and Play review gate. It also carries privacy-class, battery and geofence policy that an autonomous agent would otherwise have no owner for; at best it would fall silently into the vague PLAT.MOB.os.

It is within K-COMPLETE's mandate ("compare against platform requirements", shipped engines: Unity LocationService, Unreal LocationServices). No recorded scope decision in docs/06 section C or docs/00 excludes it. Section C item 2 is about game content, not platform services.

The proposal is technically sound:
- PLAT.MOB.location as E, owned by platform-mobile with privacy-data-protection contributing, matches how existing capabilities are structured (PLAT.XR.anchors, PLAT.MOB.links).
- PLAT.XR.geospatial as M with a radar entry fits its emerging maturity (ARCore Geospatial, Lightship VPS) and the existing planetary/geospatial radar rows.

Severity: "major" is defensible under PROTOCOL.md. The permission and privacy-class wiring, plus geo-referenced anchoring against the world coordinate model, would need rework if added late. It is on the lower edge of major, but not clearly inflated.

I checked this against the source data and the omission is real. data/capabilities.json and docs/01 have only a bare 'INP.DEV.gamepads Gamepads' row and no row for stick deadzones, response curves or drift. Materiality: stick processing affects every gamepad title, and accessibility guidance (XAG 107) expects configurable deadzones and curves. Without a row, no agent owns this, so the input layer would have an undefined contract.

Scope: aim assist is genre-specific, but docs/06 C.2 explicitly allows the game-specific boundary to be challenged per genre. It also sets the bar for moving things into the engine, which is formats shared across four or more domains. Aim assist meets that bar: it crosses input, prediction (NET.PRED.input-commands), anti-cheat and gameplay. The framework already puts comparable shooter mechanics in the engine (GAM.SYS.projectiles with server-side rewind validation and anti-cheat, GAM.SYS.hit-detection), so the proposal follows precedent rather than contradicting a recorded scope decision.

Soundness: the proposal is technically sound. Stick processing fits input-system (it could arguably sit under INP.DEV, but that is minor). Aim assist in gameplay-systems-toolkit with contributions from input, prediction and anti-cheat matches the projectiles pattern. 'Major' fits: this is a shipping requirement for console and crossplay shooters and a baseline input need, but it is not a blocker for the whole framework.

This is a real, material gap. I confirmed it in data/capabilities.json. NET.SESS.handshake covers version/auth/capability negotiation only. XC.EXT.mod-loading, mod-compat, ugc and ugc-integrity cover local loading, patch compatibility and the UGC/Workshop pipeline, but nothing covers a server pushing its content set when a client joins. No capability owns the config/ruleset files for a redistributable player-hosted server or the internet query/listing protocol. The indie-2d-online-moddable-client/server pair (M4) and sandbox-online-server (M5) are real configurations whose reason to exist depends on this. K-NET independently raised the same session content-set gap, which corroborates it. The finding is within K-COMPLETE's mandate (missing capabilities, compared against shipped engines). It does not contradict the docs/06 C.3 backend-services exclusion. Listing registration is an integration boundary like PLAT.SVC.matchmaking, and the proposal makes online-services-liveops a contributor rather than having the engine own a backend. The query protocol and mod-manifest download are engine/server-process concerns. The proposal is technically sound: net-session owns content-sync with modding-ugc contributing and C-SIGN verification before load, and dedicated-server owns community-hosting. Registering both in untrusted-inputs.json is correct: the only mods entry is hostile-local, but server-pushed content and query responses are hostile-remote. Major is the right severity, because without this, joining a modded server is impossible in a stated configuration. It is not critical, because other configurations are unaffected.

The finding holds as a minor omission. I checked the data directly. UI.FW has 18 capabilities and none is a web view. PLAT.SVC.identity says "account linking" but no capability covers the browser or device-code flow that linking needs on TV and console. untrusted-inputs.json has no entry for web content loaded into a web view. The nearest entries do not cover it: browser-bridge is the WASM host bridge, web-sources is agent research input, and invites-deep-links, auth-tickets and service-responses are other surfaces.

The omission is not covered by a recorded scope decision. The backend-services non-goal (docs/00, docs/06 C3) is about server backends. A client-side web view and the client OAuth flows sit on the engine's integration boundary, which docs/06 C3 says the engine owns. The finding is inside K-COMPLETE's mandate, which is missing capabilities compared against shipped engines and platform requirements. UE's WebBrowser module and platform OAuth rules (RFC 8252, RFC 8628, ASWebAuthenticationSession, Custom Tabs) are valid evidence for that.

It is material for autonomous agents. Without an owner, an agent building account linking or an in-game news or store page has no capability to claim. It could also embed OAuth in a web view, which RFC 8252 advises against, or leave out navigation allow-lists and isolation on a hostile-remote input.

Minor severity is defensible. It is one optional capability plus one untrusted-inputs entry under existing owners, and it causes no multi-owner or cross-skill breakage. It could be argued up to major for the security surface, but minor is not clearly wrong.

The proposal is sound in substance but needs one change. It puts two concerns in one UI.FW capability owned by ui-architect: the embedded web view (a UI surface) and the external-browser and device-code auth flows. The auth flows are identity work, and device-code linking needs no web view at all. The better fix is:
- UI.FW.web-view, owned by ui-architect with contributor security-engineering.
- The external-browser and device-code linking flows added to PLAT.SVC.identity or a sibling PLAT.SVC capability, owned by platform-services.

That is a fix to where the proposal places things, not a reason to reject the finding.

The finding holds, and "minor" is the right severity. RND.VFX in data/capabilities.json lists seven capabilities: gpu-sim, graph, primitives, collision, budgets, volumes and volume-playback. None of them is a CPU simulation path. The vfx-particles purpose field names only "GPU particle simulation", and I found no CPU or deterministic particle capability anywhere else. The skill runs under every profile ("all"), including the indie 2D and minimal configurations. The framework's own principles already reject the GPU-only assumption. docs/00 row 95 makes the CPU-culled batched path first-class on TBDR/lite3d and names "GPU-driven dogma on mobile" as the pattern to avoid. docs/06 section C and the non-goals list do not exclude CPU particles. The proposal is technically sound: one E-maturity capability, owned by vfx-particles, that keeps the same graph semantics, which mirrors Niagara's CPU/GPU sim targets. It is an omission, not a correctness break, so minor is appropriate.

The finding is material, falls within the critic's mandate, and the fix is technically sound. I checked data/capabilities.json. ANM.DEF has skinning, morphs, ML deformers, RT updates, motion vectors, crowd, geometry cache and modular assembly, but no damage, dismemberment or slicing. PHY.DEST has only runtime fracture, replication, propagation and structural. PHY.CTRL has vehicles, vehicle-net, aero, orbital and watercraft, but no body deformation or part detachment. RND.CHAR has no wound or damage masks. PHY.SOFT.softbody is generic and does not cover vehicle damage. Nothing in the data, the radar or the docs/06 §C decisions puts these out of scope. §C2 excludes game content, but it moved into the engine anything whose formats are shared across four or more domains. Damage data qualifies: it spans ANM skinning (runtime re-skinning or cap geometry), RND (layered masks and decals), PHY (physics hand-off and detachment), NET (replication) and QA.CERT.ratings (gore toggles), so the critic applies the recorded criterion correctly. The K-COMPLETE mandate covers missing capabilities, and its note says it searched first. The techniques ship widely (id Tech GORE, RE Engine, Dead Space, Forza/GT/BeamNG), so maturity E is correct. Owners are reasonable: deformation-skinning with character-rendering and destruction-fracture contributing, and vehicle-physics for vehicle damage. Severity: minor is not inflated. It is arguably slightly low, since the protocol defines minor as a wording or placement issue. I checked this against the data files and the finding holds. AUD.CONTENT has events, music, dialogue, authoring, haptics, licensed-music, speech and music-clock. "Spline" appears only in the editor spline tools (ED.WORLD.splines) and math curves. "Emitter" appears only for VFX and volumetric media, apart from the C-AUDIO contract summary "Emitter/listener data". Rating it minor is reasonable, because C-SIGNIF and the asymptotics duty cover part of the scaling concern.

This is a real gap. None of the AUD.* capabilities covers area, spline or volume emitters, or ambience beds. "ambien" and "soundscape" appear nowhere in data/, and the only "emitter" matches are VFX, plus the C-AUDIO contract's generic emitter/listener data. AUD.ARCH.voices ("Voice management & virtualization") covers voices, not the emitters placed in the world. However, audio is not listed as a contributor to WLD.PART.activation, and no audio capability claims shaped emitters or ambience. Shipped engines treat these as standard open-world features (UE Soundscape and audio gameplay volumes, Wwise spline and room emitters), so this is within K-COMPLETE's mandate. I found no recorded scope decision in docs/06 or docs/00 that excludes it. The proposal is sound: a new capability under AUD.CONTENT owned by audio-content-runtime, with spatial-audio-acoustics and world-architect as contributors. It would be better if it named C-SIGNIF and WLD.PART.activation as the culling and partition mechanisms rather than implying new ones. Minor is the right severity: shared mechanisms reduce the scaling risk, but the emitter types themselves have no owner.

This is a real gap, though a small one. BLD.CI.build-distribution ("Build distribution to QA, playtesters, betas & devkits", owner ci-cd-automation) only covers delivery. XC.SEC has 27 rows, including tamper/DRM, supply-chain, secrets, key-custody and incident. None of the scope decisions in docs/06 §C (NDA parameters, game-specific systems, backend services, may-be-built membership, critic misses) excludes it, and docs/00 doesn't either. It falls within K-COMPLETE's mandate, since it is a missing engineering discipline. The proposal is technically sound. Per-recipient visible overlays and forensic marks are standard pipeline steps at distribution time. The owner (ci-cd-automation) and contributor (security-engineering) match the existing owners, and E maturity is right. Minor is the right severity. Leaving it out would not cause architectural rework or lock in a legacy design. It is a small capability addition, and a new row can be added later without disturbing the existing structure. I confirmed the gap in data/capabilities.json. ED.UI has toolkit, inspectors, asset-browser, ux, asset-editor-host, thumbnails, curves-timeline, tabular, toolkit-basis and localization. **The fact is confirmed.** data/capabilities.json line 2836 defines CNT.COOK.ddc as "Derived-data cache keyed by source path & file modification time". That wording contradicts three other places in the data:
- the owner's purpose in skills.json: "derived-data cache and content-addressed store";
- the shared-ddc registry limit in untrusted-inputs.json: "content-addressed/verified";
- the C-COOK "cache keys" obligation.

**Why it is material.** An agent working from this capability would build a cache keyed on path and file modification time. That cache:
- cannot be shared across machines, so CNT.COOK.shared-cache is not achievable;
- gives false hits when the processor version, settings or platform variant change but the source does not;
- invalidates everything after a VCS sync, because checkouts rewrite modification times;
- makes CNT.COOK.incremental-equivalence (an incremental cook matching a clean cook) unprovable.

This is exactly the "silent legacy architecture" that PROTOCOL.md uses to define "major".

**Scope.** Nothing in docs/06 or docs/00 records a decision in favour of path/timestamp keys. No seed-map entry covers this capability, so it is not a planted seed.

**Mandate.** Accidental legacy architecture is K-LEGACY's mandate. Adding a legacy pattern matches its check ("each pattern in data/legacy-patterns.json absent or justified by an ADR").

**The proposal is sound.**
- The content-addressed key it proposes (source content, processor id and version, settings, platform variant, dependency keys) matches UE DDC and Bazel practice.
- The pattern's stance capabilities, CNT.COOK.ddc and CNT.COOK.contract, are both owned by content-pipeline-architect.
- One small gap: the new pattern also needs a "detection" field and a "justification_owner" of content-pipeline-architect to fit the legacy-patterns.json schema. The finding text omits these, but the fuller entry in gauntlet/round-3/K-LEGACY.md names the owner.

**Duplicates.** K-ARCH, K-SEC, K-TOOLS and K-PERF raised the same issue independently. That supports the finding; it will probably be merged with them in dispositions.

The main deficiency checks out against the data.

1. **Missing contracts.** fluid-simulation lists profiles aaa, sandbox and massim. Both rts-2d-massim-client and rts-3d-massim-client combine massim with online-lockstep, so the skill is in the lockstep configurations. It owns PHY.FLUID.cellular (E, described as "deterministic"). Its consumes list is only C-PHYS, C-RG?, C-RSCENE? and C-ENV?, so C-DET, C-TASK and C-SNAPSHOT are all missing.

2. **Its peers do declare them.** rigid-body-dynamics consumes C-PHYS, C-TASK and C-DET. physics-2d consumes C-PHYS and C-DET. crowd-simulation and systems-simulation consume C-DET and C-TASK, and systems-simulation also consumes C-SNAPSHOT?. Neither C-DET nor C-TASK is a universal contract. check.py only proves that configurations are closed under dependencies, not that a deterministic capability's owner consumes C-DET, so nothing machine-proves this.

3. **Partial mitigation.** C-PHYS requires C-DET and C-SNAPSHOT, so determinism-replay is present in those configurations anyway. That keeps configuration closure intact, but fluid-simulation's own grid reductions are still not bound to C-DET's ordered-execution rules. Merging them is a design suggestion, not a demonstrated defect. The core dependency-error still holds.
