K-SIM owns this area: fluids and systems-simulation are both in its scope. Even so, the finding is overstated in two places and one of its proposed changes is unsound.

(1) The claim that fluid-simulation skips determinism is mostly wrong. fluid-simulation consumes C-PHYS, and C-PHYS itself requires C-DET and C-SNAPSHOT. C-PHYS also carries the snapshot/restore/resimulate participation and the state-hash conformance. So C-DET's rules and snapshot participation are already in fluid-simulation's closure in both RTS configurations, and the "lockstep desync source" claim does not follow. What remains is a convention gap. The sibling skills rigid-body-dynamics, physics-2d and crowd-simulation list C-DET (and C-TASK) directly even though C-PHYS already requires C-DET, and fluid-simulation does not. Adding C-DET and C-TASK is a fair minor fix. Adding C-SNAPSHOT? is redundant, because C-PHYS already covers it.

(2) Making GAM.SIM.fields the single grid substrate is unsound as stated. systems-simulation is a gameplay skill and provides no contract. A physics skill (C-PHYS sits at L3) consuming its substrate would need a new contract from a higher layer, which breaks the no-upward-module-links rule in docs/00. The proposal also ignores the aaa profile, where fluid-simulation ships without systems-simulation. The heat/diffusion overlap is real, but the data already records the boundary: systems-simulation routes "Cellular fluids" to fluid-simulation. A sound fix would place a shared grid substrate at or below the physics layer, or state the split in both skills, not point physics at a gameplay substrate.

(3) The shallow-water point is a wording issue. The capability data already records WLD.ENV.water-interaction as owned by water-ocean, with fluid-simulation as a contributor. So there are not two owners, only loose wording in fluid-simulation's purpose, which is minor.

Net: the valid parts are minor fixes, and the headline change is unsound, so "major" is inflated.

The facts are right but the proposal is unsound, and the risk it targets is already owned elsewhere. (1) The DoS concern is covered by two budgeted capabilities. PHY.COL.runtime-build is literally "Runtime/incremental collision generation for edited geometry (voxel chunks, ..., UGC), async and budgeted", with voxel-worlds and modding-ugc as partners. NET.SRV.budgets (dedicated-server) is "Per-connection memory/CPU/RPC quotas & limits on client-triggered work", which is exactly the per-player edit/rebuild bounding cited from Minecraft and Space Engineers. (2) untrusted-inputs.json records trust-boundary input classes that are parsed (packets, mods, ugc-graphs, assets, replicated-state, input-commands). Collision geometry is data the engine derives from inputs that are already registered: edit requests come in as packets, input-commands or replicated-state, and UGC meshes come in as mods or assets under modding-ugc and serialization-schema limits. Registering derived data as an input and making collision-detection its "validating owner" puts the validation in the wrong place. Whether an edit is legal, and its rate, belong at the edit/RPC boundary (voxel-worlds, replication, dedicated-server). Mesh sanity belongs to the UGC validator. "Rebuild time per tick" is a runtime budget, not an input limit, and runtime-build already declares that budget. (3) The registry is K-SEC-1 territory under security-engineering, so this is outside K-SIM's physics mandate. The only possible gap left, degenerate-triangle robustness, is collision-robustness work (cook/runtime-build), not a missing registry entry. The most this deserves is a note on runtime-build or modding-ugc limits, not a new input class. If it were upheld, "minor" would be the right severity.

The QA and CI agents also get no contract edge to the protocol they are meant to use, which invites private control channels. That is a real dependency gap for a framework that coordinates autonomous agents, not a matter of style. Nothing in docs/06 section C or docs/00 records a decision against these consumers, and CI and automation tooling falls within the K-TOOLS mandate. The fix is technically sound: I applied all four additions to a copy of the data, and scripts/check.py still reports 0 errors and 0 warnings. The case is weaker for perf-benchmarking and render-validation, and an optional C-AUTOMATION? dependency might fit them better, but that does not make the proposal unsound. Minor severity is right: this is a missing consumer edge on a contract that is already frozen, not a broken proof.

What holds: the registry in data/untrusted-inputs.json has no entry for code that runs when a project is opened (in-project Python/tool scripts, startup scripts, importers). Why this does not hold:

I checked this against the data files and both halves of the finding hold.

1. **L37 points at the wrong capability.** In data/legacy-patterns.json, L37 ("Modal, blocking editor operations", default stance "Asynchronous, cancellable editor jobs with progress") lists only ED.ARCH.process as its stance capability. In data/capabilities.json, ED.ARCH.process is "Editor process architecture (in-process vs out-of-process runtime)". That is a different concern: an in-process editor can still run async jobs, and an out-of-process one can still block. No ED.* capability owns the editor background-job model. The C-EDCMD contract summary covers commands, transactions, undo scopes, the journal and cross-process transactions, but not job progress, cancellation, or how a finishing job's writes interact with open transactions and undo. editor-architect's purpose text and its consumes list (no C-TASK) don't cover it either. For autonomous agents, a stance with no owner is a real coordination gap: nobody specifies what happens when an async import or compile finishes during an open transaction. check.py only proves that the stance capability exists and is owned by the justification owner, not that it matches the stance. So this is a real wrong-boundary defect that the machine checks can't catch.

2. **No outliner capability.** ED.UI has an asset browser, inspectors, a tabular editor and more, but nothing for the scene outliner or hierarchy panel. No capability, skill or doc in the data mentions an outliner. ED.ARCH.scale ("Editor performance for large projects") covers it only implicitly. docs/06 A2 names a synthetic 10⁶-object world as the measurement target, so the gap is anchored in the framework's own documents. Nothing in docs/06 section C excludes it.

**Proposal:** It is sound. Owners and contributors match the existing split: editor-architect is the lead for ED.ARCH, editor-ui-framework owns ED.UI and provides C-EDHOST, and world-data-model is an existing skill. Two optional refinements: editor-architect should consume C-TASK (owned by job-system-task-graph, which targets tools) and C-EDCMD should state how jobs interact with transactions, and world-architect is arguably a better contributor for data-layer/cell filtering. Neither makes the proposal unsound.

**Severity:** Minor is right. This is a missing boundary and a mis-mapped stance, not a broken contract or a failed proof.

**What the data shows.** In data/capabilities.json, PLAT.PAL.cloud-streaming has maturity M, owner platform-architect and no contributors. Its entry in data/radar.json gives the fallback "Treat as a PC target". The radar entry's own evidence already says "Shipping services (GeForce NOW, xCloud)".

- The fallback is wrong architecture, not just wrong wording. Xbox Cloud Gaming streams console builds. - Every named skill exists: runtime-scalability, frame-orchestration, platform-console, platform-desktop, input-system and ui-architect.

Wanting per-platform, platform-tagged store backends is a design preference. It does not fix an ownership or closure hole. What remains true is that no configuration carries a storefront axis, even though the platform matrix names store. That is a minor gap, not a major missing contract.

This is not a material missing-contract defect, and the proposed change is unsound.

1. The gap does not exist. C-SVC (data/contracts.json) is owned and provided by platform-services. That skill has no platform tag, targets client, headless-client, server and tools, and has profile "all". Its purpose explicitly covers "entitlements and commerce through first-party stores", identity, achievements, cloud save and so on. When a contract is not needs_implementer, the owner is the implementation. The check.py closure then already requires platform-services in every configuration that consumes C-SVC, so Steam, EOS, StoreKit and Play backends do have an owner with closure. C-NETLINK's summary confirms this: "platform-SDK transports (Steam/EOS/console relays) register as backends implemented by platform-services and online-services-liveops". platform-console implements C-SVC only because the console slot is NDA (PLAT.CON.user-model, PLAT.CON.confidential-slots). That is a deliberate carve-out, not evidence that the other platforms are unowned.

2. The proposal contradicts a recorded decision without new evidence. docs/00 (line 119) puts first-party platform services in platform-services, reasoning that the work is "NDA SDKs plus certification". Moving Steamworks, GDK-on-PC, StoreKit, Play Billing and portal SDKs into platform-desktop, platform-mobile and platform-web would scatter that expertise into OS-integration skills.

3. Splitting by platform does not fit how stores work. Stores cut across the OS platform axis. EOS runs on PC, console and mobile. Steamworks runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. GDK spans PC and Xbox. Tagging store backends to one platform each would duplicate one SDK integration across several agents, the same drift problem K-PLATFORM-8 criticises for D3D12.

4. A storefront configuration axis would prove nothing. configurations exist to prove skill membership closure. Store variance does not change which skills are members, because platform-services is already present. Store variants in packaging and submission belong to packaging-release-patching (store-submission artifacts) and to the ARCH.REQ.platform-matrix capability.

What survives is at most minor: the store dimension of ARCH.REQ.platform-matrix is named but not carried in data, and there is no explicit list of the non-console store backends platform-services must cover. So "major" is inflated.

The data matches the finding. In data/skills.json, rhi-d3d12 has platforms ["pc"] and no access class. Its purpose covers only the PC Agility SDK, and it lists "Other API backends" as a non-responsibility. rhi-console (access nda:per-platform-holder, "one agent per platform-holder family") says it "Implements C-RHI on each console graphics API". RND.RHI.console, "Console graphics API backends (confidential, per platform holder)", belongs to rhi-console alone, and rhi-d3d12 is not a contributor to it. Nowhere in data/ or docs/ is Xbox, GDK, a shared D3D12 base, or D3D12 code reuse between the PC and console backends modelled. The closest generic mechanisms are PLAT.PAL.confidential-extensions ("segregated modules/repos, public stubs", owned by platform-architect) and ARCH.STRUCT.platform-backends. Neither makes rhi-d3d12 the base owner of a console D3D12 variant, so the Xbox D3D12 work falls to the separate rhi-console NDA agent and the drift risk stands. The same split holds for GDK PAL code: platform-desktop has expertise "Win32/GameInput" and platforms ["pc"], while platform-console is a separate NDA skill, and there is no shared-GDK module. check.py does not prove this. It only checks that "console-only skills carry an NDA access class", which if anything enforces the split. The finding is not a planted seed: seed-map.json lists RND.RHI.d3d12 only as domain coverage. K-PLATFORM-1 exists, so the cross-reference is valid. Major severity fits the protocol's definition: a wrong boundary that would cause duplicated backend work and rework.

The finding holds and "major" is the right severity. In data/skills.json, rhi-d3d12 has platforms ["pc"], implements C-RHI, and has no access class. rhi-console "implements C-RHI on each console graphics API" as a separate backend, with access nda:per-platform-holder and one agent per holder. Neither skill provides a contract the other could build on, and every dependency edge must go through a contract. So an Xbox-class rhi-console instance cannot reuse the D3D12 backend: it has to re-implement barrier translation, descriptor heaps, PSO and DXC handling, and so on. That is a real, material defect for autonomous agents: the largest API backend gets duplicated, and the NDA copy drifts where the public agent cannot see it. Only a shared contract (C-RHI) and its conformance oracle limit that drift.

Scope: docs/00 section 8 records "one skill per graphics API backend", but the reason given is that "each API has its own specification, validation layers and release cadence". The finding challenges that premise with a new fact: the Xbox API is a D3D12 superset, not an independent specification. It is therefore not re-arguing a settled decision without evidence. docs/06 section C has no recorded decision on this.

Mandate: the K-PLATFORM mandate covers "consoles, graphics APIs", and rhi-d3d12 is explicitly in its scope.

Soundness: the proposed change mirrors PLAT.PAL.confidential-extensions ("segregated modules/repos, public stubs, access classes") and the UE D3D12RHI-plus-platform-extension model, so the direction is sound. One caveat: it depends on K-PLATFORM-1's module-level access class. Without that, check.py lines 236-239 ("NDA skill ... not confined to the console platform") reject an NDA module inside a skill tagged pc. The proposal states this dependency. A variant would keep the Xbox instance in rhi-console and have it consume a shared D3D12-core module published by rhi-d3d12. That variant fixes the same defect, which confirms the defect is real, not a matter of style.

Severity: "major" fits. The flaw is structural duplication and drift, not something that blocks the build, so it is not a blocker. It is more than minor because it duplicates a whole backend and extends to the GDK PAL code shared by platform-desktop and platform-console (GameInput, XGameRuntime).

The finding holds. Every claim checks out against the data:

No capability gathers external browser-capability share: OBS.LOG.analytics covers gameplay analytics only, and the platform-web purpose has nothing on audience measurement. On severity, "major" is defensible. The fallback shows the WebGPU-only web target is a conscious choice. But the trigger that is supposed to re-open the decision can never fire, and the smallest configurations and the M2 exit promise web shipping to an audience that partly has no WebGPU.

The finding holds and "major" is the right severity. Every factual claim checks out against the data:
- data/contracts.json gives C-PAL the oracle_author "accessibility". C-PAL is a layer-0 boundary contract and its summary covers OS services, thread QoS and affinity, clock-domain correlation, the suspend/resume quiesce protocol, memory pressure and display.
- Five skills implement C-PAL: platform-desktop, platform-console, platform-mobile, platform-web and platform-server-host. platform-console carries the access class nda:per-platform-holder.
- accessibility sits in the ui workstream and has no NDA access class.
- test-runtime-harness sits in the quality workstream, consumes C-PAL and owns QA.HOST.runner and QA.HOST.fault-points. It also contributes to PLAT.PAL.event-injection alongside certification-compliance.

Materiality. The framework's defence against agents gaming their own tests is the oracle author (docs/00 lines 102, 124 and 128; QA.AGENT.oracle-independence). An oracle author outside the domain writes weak acceptance suites, and five autonomous implementers would then pass the certification-critical lifecycle, clock and thread cases unchallenged. That is silent rework risk on the most widely consumed platform contract, which fits PROTOCOL's definition of major.

Mandate and scope. C-PAL is owned by platform-architect, which is inside K-PLATFORM's scope (subtree:platform-architect), and the check "certification requirements traced" applies. No recorded decision in docs/00 or docs/06 section C covers how oracle authors are assigned.

Soundness. test-runtime-harness is in a different workstream from every implementer, so it passes the independence-matrix and check.py rules. It also consumes C-PAL, so the suite stays consumer-driven. Co-signature fits the existing QA.AGENT.oracle-change-control mechanism.

One weakness does not sink the finding. Neither test-runtime-harness nor certification-compliance has an NDA access class today. The NDA part of the proposal therefore depends on the per-holder confidential partition proposed in K-PLATFORM-1 rather than working on its own. The core reassignment stands without it.

The central claim is that shared Apple frameworks "get implemented twice" because platform-desktop and platform-mobile split Apple support. The data does not support that. Each framework the finding names already has exactly one cross-platform owner outside both platform experts:
- GameController: INP.DEV.gamepads, owned by input-devices-haptics.
- GameKit: PLAT.SVC.achievements and PLAT.SVC.leaderboards, owned by platform-services.
- StoreKit: PLAT.COMM.iap and PLAT.COMM.receipts, owned by platform-services.
- CAMetalLayer surfaces: PLAT.PAL.windowing (platform-architect) and RND.RHI.present (rhi-core). platform-desktop also lists "Swapchain" as a non-responsibility routed to rhi-core.
- AVAudioSession/CoreAudio: AUD.ARCH.devices (audio-architect) and PLAT.PAL.system-events for audio endpoints.
- Signing and notarization: BLD.REL.packaging, owned by packaging-release-patching.
- TCC: appears only once, in PLAT.DESK.os-security.

check.py already proves each capability has exactly one owner. rhi-metal is a single backend tagged for the pc, mobile and xr-standalone platforms, so it is not split either.

The only real split is the C-PAL backend: PLAT.DESK.pal covers macOS and PLAT.MOB.pal covers iOS/visionOS. That is a per-OS-family PAL assignment, not duplicate ownership of the named frameworks.

The tvOS part is factually true: no file under data, docs or scripts mentions tvOS. But ARCH.REQ.platform-matrix is a register the project fills in, not a list of every OS. Other TV platforms, such as Android TV and smart TVs, are equally unlisted, so on its own this is at most a very minor note. Because the main deficiency is already covered under other names, the finding does not hold as described.

This finding is not material, and most of it is not true of the data. The framework does not split the shared Apple frameworks by form factor. Each is already owned once, by a domain skill that serves every platform:
- GameController belongs to input-devices-haptics (gamepads).
- GameKit and StoreKit belong to platform-services (PLAT.SVC.entitlements, achievements).
- CAMetalLayer surfaces belong to rhi-core (RND.RHI.present) and rhi-metal. rhi-metal's platforms are pc, mobile and xr-standalone.
- Signing and notarization belong to packaging-release-patching (BLD.REL.packaging, "incl. notarization, hardened runtime").
- TCC appears only in PLAT.DESK.os-security. iOS permission prompts are a different mechanism, so nothing is duplicated there.

The only overlap left is PAL code for the Darwin layer (threads, clocks, file IO) inside the C-PAL backends. Even there, the AppKit and UIKit lifecycles and windowing really do differ. Under the split rule in docs/00 section 1 (different literatures, validated separately), keeping the two apart is justified. docs/00 section 9 also defers per-module file globs and code layout to M0, so where shared Darwin code lives is not a phase-1 boundary defect.

The proposed change is also technically unsound. Having platform-desktop consume a module owned by platform-mobile is a skill-to-skill dependency. docs/00 section 3 says skills depend on contracts, never on skills, so this would need a contract, and the finding does not propose one. Giving the mobile expert ownership of macOS code also works against the form-factor expertise the split exists for.

The tvOS point is valid but small. tvOS is not mentioned anywhere in data/ or docs/. Recording it as supported or as a non-goal in the ARCH.REQ.platform-matrix / radar non-goal list would be a trivial housekeeping fix. It is better handled under K-PLATFORM's broader platform_variants finding, which targets ARCH.REQ.platform-matrix, and it does not rescue the wrong-boundary claim.

Minor is not an understated severity; the most this finding could justify is a minor note.

The finding holds. This is in scope for K-PLATFORM, it is a real gap, and "minor" is the right severity. I found no scope decision against it in docs/06 section C or docs/00.

What the framework already has (data/capabilities.json, data/contracts.json):
- PLAT.PAL.windowing is a generic "Windowing & surfaces" line with no contributors.
- PLAT.MOB.pal and PLAT.WEB.pal are PAL backends that list "windowing, display, events" only generically.
- The C-PAL summary mentions display, lifecycle and system events, including overlay/focus.
- C-COLOR defines a static-looking output display descriptor (peak luminance, paper white).
- CORE.FRAME.host-loop covers requestAnimationFrame together with platform-web.
- PLAT.PAL.lifecycle lists platform-console and platform-mobile as contributors, but not platform-web.

So the three behaviours are only implied by generic PAL-backend lines. Agents route work by explicit capabilities and contributor lists, so each gap has a concrete cost:
- Mobile windowing: iPadOS 26 deprecates UIRequiresFullScreen and Android 16 enforces resizability on large screens. Mobile games can no longer assume a fixed fullscreen surface. None of platform-mobile's capabilities or purpose mention resizing, multi-window or foldable posture.
- HDR headroom: it changes while the game runs (EDR on Apple). The descriptor must then be updated at runtime rather than read once at startup. That is not stated anywhere.
- Browser lifecycle: page visibility, background-tab throttling, bfcache and tab discard map directly onto PLAT.PAL.lifecycle's suspend, resume and terminate. Yet platform-web is the only mobile-like target missing from that contributor list.

The proposed changes are small and technically sound:
- A new PLAT.MOB.windowing line fits the style of the existing PLAT.MOB lines.
- Adding contributors to a PAL capability has precedent: non-platform skills such as test-runtime-harness already contribute to PLAT.PAL.event-injection.
- Adding platform-web to PLAT.PAL.lifecycle matches how console and mobile are listed.

Why it is not more than minor: generic coverage does exist through the PAL-backend lines and C-PAL, so this is a missing explicit line, not a structural hole. The one weak point is platform-desktop: it is also absent from PLAT.PAL.lifecycle and the finding does not mention it. That makes the web part look like an inconsistency rather than a pure omission, but it does not make the finding wrong.

The finding holds. In data/capabilities.json (PRF.METH area), PRF.METH.budgets reads word for word "Budgets measured on the reference high-end PC and scaled proportionally to lower tiers" and is owned by performance-architect. The contract C-BUDGET in data/contracts.json says "Budget numbers per hardware tier × configuration × refresh class, derived from the performance model", which directly contradicts it.

The framework's other entries side with per-tier bottlenecks, so no other capability already corrects this:

- PRF.METH.scalability: "knob budgets per tier"
- RND.ARCH.submission-strategy: "per hardware tier ... TBDR suitability"
- PLAT.MOB.thermal: ADPF and iOS thermal state
- The performance-architect purpose: "budgets per subsystem and hardware tier"

Every one of these is either adjacent to the proportional-scaling wording or inconsistent with it. None supersedes it.

No legacy pattern covers single-machine scaled budgets. Patterns run L02 to L57, and L58 is free. The closest, L12 on draw-call submission, is a different issue. scripts/check.py proves structural closure only (configuration closure / scale-down proof) and never checks capability wording, so it cannot catch this.

Major severity is justified. This is the budget-defining capability of the owner of a universal contract, and it contradicts that contract. Budgets derived this way would be wrong for mobile, console and server tiers.

Confirmed in data/capabilities.json. PRF.METH.budgets reads "Budgets measured on the reference high-end PC and scaled proportionally to lower tiers" and is owned by performance-architect. In data/contracts.json, C-BUDGET, owned by the same skill, says "per hardware tier × configuration × refresh class, derived from the performance model". The skill's purpose also says "budgets per subsystem and hardware tier". The framework therefore contradicts itself in a core methodology capability.

This is a material defect. An autonomous agent reading only the capability name would produce scaled-down PC budgets. Those budgets are wrong for TBDR mobile, UMA consoles with an OS reserve, thermally throttled handhelds and fixed-SKU consoles. They are meaningless for server tick and CCU budgets, since ARCH.REQ.hardware-tiers includes server instance classes. The framework's own RND.ARCH.submission-strategy ("per hardware tier ... TBDR suitability") and PRF.METH.model ("unit costs × counts per tier/configuration") assume that bottlenecks differ per tier.

No recorded scope decision covers this. docs/06 section C and docs/00 say nothing that justifies PC-first proportional scaling, and docs/00 favors scale-down. The finding is within the mandate of a performance critic.

The proposed change is technically sound. The rename lines the capability up with C-BUDGET and PRF.METH.model. Measuring at the thermally sustained state is established practice (ADPF, iOS thermal state). L58 fits the legacy-pattern schema and passes the check.py rule, because performance-architect owns PRF.METH.budgets.

Minor notes:
- K-SYSTEMS's variant, which allows cross-tier scaling as an initial estimate that is then validated, is compatible, because the model-derived number already serves as the prior.

I confirmed this in the framework's source data. In data/capabilities.json (lines 1243-1244), PLAT.WEB.runtime reads "WASM threads (SharedArrayBuffer required; cross-origin isolation assumed on every host) & memory limits". That contradicts the framework's own principles. docs/00 line 90 says "The same graph runs inline on 0–2 workers (web, low-end)". CORE.JOBS.degenerate (capabilities.json line 1956) exists to provide exactly that 0–2 worker inline mode, and platform-web contributes to it (docs/03 line 2204). Neither docs/06 section C nor docs/00 records any scope decision that makes cross-origin isolation mandatory, so the finding does not go against a reasoned exclusion. The facts are also correct: SharedArrayBuffer needs COOP/COEP, and many iframe portals cannot provide it. As written, the web configurations would fail to start on those hosts, and nothing on the platform side would own the fallback. indie-2d-online-web-client (web only) is proven at M4 (docs/09 line 284), and the M2 exit claims indie-2d ships on web. So this is a material wrong-boundary and scale-down defect that would cause rework, which meets the protocol's definition of major. It is within K-PERF's mandate: its scope is "all" plus runtime-scalability, and scaling down to a zero-worker configuration is a scalability concern. The proposed fix is technically sound. It keeps WASM threads where the page is cross-origin isolated, adds a separately built single-threaded variant (Emscripten pthread builds cannot run without SharedArrayBuffer, so this has to be a build variant) that maps to CORE.JOBS.degenerate, and detects isolation at load. Godot 4.3 and Unity ship this same split. Several other critics raised the same finding independently (K-ARCH, K-FUTURE, K-PLATFORM, K-SYSTEMS, K-LEGACY), so it should be merged with them rather than fixed separately. The only issue is minor: the proposal targets the M2 claim, but the web-only client configuration is proven at M4, so the threads-off variant should be checked at both points.

The facts check out in data/capabilities.json. BLD.CI.devices is "Device-farm fleet scheduling & pooling" (ci-cd-automation, team-large). The finding holds. I checked every claim against the data and check.py.

(a) I joined contracts.json (owner plus implements) with the skill workstreams, skipping layer P. In exactly 41 of 110 code contracts the oracle_author shares a workstream with the owner or an implementer; in 40 of them it is the owner itself. The examples are accurate:
- C-RHI: oracle author gpu-memory-resources (rendering); owner rhi-core and all rhi-* backends are also rendering.
- C-REP: oracle author prediction-rollback, owner replication, both online.
- C-PREDICT: oracle author anti-cheat-integrity, owner prediction-rollback, both online.
- C-TESTHOST: oracle author test-architect, owner test-runtime-harness, both quality.
- C-MEM, C-SAVE, C-SCRIPT, C-BUILD, C-PKG, C-SERVER, C-SHARD and C-AUTOMATION are all on the list as well.

(b) security-engineering, security-runtime, test-runtime-harness, robustness-fuzzing and privacy-data-protection are all in the quality workstream. security-runtime owns CORE.TYPES.crypto, XC.SEC.signed-artifacts and XC.SEC.pqc-signatures.

(c) The framework does claim that workstream separation enforces independence:
- docs/00-design-principles.md says workstreams "are also the co-hosting unit, so the independence matrix ... implementer vs oracle author ... is enforced by keeping each pair in different workstreams".
- docs/04-cross-cutting.md line 42 says "check.py proves they sit in different workstreams".
- ARCH.ORG.staffing is "co-hosting of skills per organization scale (by workstream)".

(d) check.py does not prove this for these pairs. Its independence-matrix loop only compares pairs where both entries are real skills, so the rows ('security-engineering','owning-skill') and ('test-architect','owning-skill') are never checked for workstream. The oracle rule only errors when the oracle author is the owner and no skill implements the contract; it never compares workstreams.

No other capability, contract or doc covers this under different wording. The ARCH.ORG.independence text "co-hosting capped by capability count" does not stop a small organization from co-hosting one workstream in one agent, which docs/00 line 82 explicitly allows.

Blocker severity is justified: this contradicts an invariant the docs present as machine-proved, and it enables the self-grading that L56 and QA.AGENT.oracle-independence exist to prevent.
